1. The deceased is [NAME OF THE DECEASED], son/daughter of [NAME], aged [AGE], resident of [ADDRESS].

**II. FACTS**

3. On 20 June 2024, at about [TIME], at [PLACE OF OCCURRENCE], within the jurisdiction of this police station, the accused intentionally inflicted injuries on the deceased with [WEAPON / MEANS USED] on [PARTS OF THE BODY INJURED].

4. The accused inflicted the injuries intending to cause the death of the deceased. The nature of the weapon, the part of the body struck, the force used and the number of blows are as follows: [PARTICULARS OF THE WEAPON, THE INJURIES AND THE NUMBER OF BLOWS].

6. The incident was seen by [NAMES AND ADDRESSES OF EYEWITNESSES, IF ANY]. The motive or background, so far as known to me, is [MOTIVE / PRIOR ENMITY, IF ANY].

7. The incident occurred on 20 June 2024. I am approaching the police on 25 June 2024. The reason for the interval is [REASONS FOR THE DELAY IN REPORTING, e.g. performance of the last rites, hospital formalities, fear or threats].

**III. OFFENCE DISCLOSED AND THE SECTION UNDER WHICH THE ACCUSED IS TO BE CHARGED**

8. **Penal section: Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860** (punishment for murder), read with the first clause of Section 300 of the Indian Penal Code (culpable homicide is murder if the act causing death is done with the intention of causing death). [Corresponding provision of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Section 103, cited only as the new equivalent.]

9. The offence was committed on 20 June 2024, before the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 came into force on 1 July 2024. Section 358(2)(c) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita saves the Indian Penal Code, 1860 for offences committed before that date, and Article 20(1) of the Constitution forbids punishing an act under a law not in force when it was done. The Indian Penal Code therefore governs the charge.

10. Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code provides that whoever commits murder shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine.

11. On the facts above, the accused's act of intentionally inflicting injuries to cause death falls within the first clause of Section 300. No exception to Section 300 is made out on the facts given in this information, such as grave and sudden provocation under Exception 1. [CONFIRM FROM THE FACTS WHETHER ANY PROVOCATION OR SUDDEN QUARREL IS ALLEGED.]

12. **Registration: Section 154(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.** This section requires every information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence, if given orally to an officer in charge of a police station, to be reduced to writing, read over to the informant and signed by the informant, and its substance to be entered in the prescribed book. Where the information is given in writing, it must likewise be signed by the person giving it and entered in the book. Murder is a cognizable offence. This information is given in writing, and I request that the First Information Report be registered on it. [Corresponding provision of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023: Section 173, cited only as the new equivalent.]

13. **Investigation: Section 156(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973**, which governs the investigation of a cognizable case by an officer in charge of a police station. [Corresponding provision of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023: Section 175, cited only as the new equivalent.]

14. This proceeding began on 25 June 2024, before 1 July 2024, and was therefore pending immediately before that date. By Section 531(2)(a) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, the registration, investigation and subsequent proceedings continue under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, and evidence in them is governed by the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (Section 170(2) of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023).

**V. PRAYER**

 (a) register the First Information Report under Section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, for the offence under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, against [NAME OF THE ACCUSED] and any other person found involved;

BEFORE THE STATION HOUSE OFFICER,
[NAME OF POLICE STATION], [DISTRICT], [STATE]

WRITTEN COMPLAINT / INFORMATION UNDER SECTION 173 OF THE BHARATIYA NAGARIK SURAKSHA SANHITA, 2023 [Section 154, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (repealed)]

IN THE MATTER OF: Death of [NAME OF THE DECEASED], caused on 1 July 2024

Date: 1 July 2024 [TIME OF PRESENTING THE COMPLAINT]

To,
The Station House Officer,
[NAME OF POLICE STATION]

From,
[NAME OF THE COMPLAINANT], [AGE], [OCCUPATION], resident of [ADDRESS], [RELATIONSHIP TO THE DECEASED]

Subject: Complaint for registration of a First Information Report and investigation of the murder of [NAME OF THE DECEASED] by [NAME OF THE ACCUSED] under section 101 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023

Sir,

I, the complainant named above, give the following information and request that an FIR be registered and the offence investigated.

**A. FACTS**

1. The deceased, [NAME OF THE DECEASED], was [RELATIONSHIP / DESCRIPTION] and resided at [ADDRESS].

2. The accused, [NAME OF THE ACCUSED], [DESCRIPTION AND ADDRESS], is known to the complainant [DETAILS OF ACQUAINTANCE / RELATIONSHIP, IF ANY].

3. On 1 July 2024, at about 00:01 hours, at [PLACE OF OCCURRENCE], the accused intentionally inflicted [NATURE AND NUMBER OF INJURIES] on the deceased with [WEAPON / MEANS, IF KNOWN] [DETAILS OF HOW THE ASSAULT OCCURRED AS WITNESSED OR LEARNT BY THE COMPLAINANT].

4. The injuries were inflicted on [PARTS OF THE BODY]. The deceased died [AT THE SPOT / ON BEING TAKEN TO [NAME OF HOSPITAL]] as a result of those injuries.

5. [MOTIVE OR PRIOR ENMITY, IF ANY, AS KNOWN TO THE COMPLAINANT.]

6. The persons who witnessed the occurrence or have knowledge of it are: [NAMES AND ADDRESSES OF EYE-WITNESSES / OTHER WITNESSES].

7. The accused [FLED / WAS LAST SEEN AT [PLACE]]. [PRESENT WHEREABOUTS, IF KNOWN.]

8. The complainant approached the police on 1 July 2024, the same day, and there has been no delay in reporting the matter.

**B. THE PENAL PROVISION**

9. The death was caused on 1 July 2024, which is the date the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 came into force. The offence was therefore committed on or after the commencement of that Sanhita, and the Indian Penal Code, 1860 does not apply to it. The accused is to be charged under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.

10. The accused is to be charged with murder under **section 101 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023** [section 300 read with section 302, Indian Penal Code, 1860 (repealed)]. The punishment is provided by section 103 of the Sanhita, the text of which is not reproduced here.

11. Under section 101, subject to the exceptions, culpable homicide is murder if the act causing death is done with the intention of causing death (clause (a)). It is also murder if the act is done with the intention of causing such bodily injury as the offender knows to be likely to cause the death of the person harmed (clause (b)). Clause (c) covers an act done with the intention of causing bodily injury that is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.

12. On the facts stated above, the accused intentionally inflicted the injuries by which the deceased died. The case therefore falls under section 101, clause (a), (b) or (c), depending on what the investigation shows of the intention with which the injuries were inflicted.

13. Under the corresponding provisions of the repealed Code, the Supreme Court has held that intention to kill is not the only intention that makes culpable homicide murder. The intention to cause an injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death also does so, if death is caused. Where the intention to inflict the particular injury is established and the injury is objectively sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, the offence is murder unless an exception applies (*Jai Prakash v. State (Delhi Administration)*, [1991] 1 S.C.R. 202 (Supreme Court, full bench), on clause Thirdly of section 300 IPC). That intention is inferred from the act or acts resulting in the injury (*Anbazhagan v. State represented by the Inspector of Police*, [2023] 10 S.C.R. 1091, on section 300 IPC, following the same principle). Section 101(c) BNS is the successor of that clause.

**C. THE PROCEDURAL PROVISIONS**

14. This information is given and the case is to be registered under **section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023** [section 154, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (repealed)]. The text of section 173 is not shown here. The proceeding begins with this information, lodged on 1 July 2024, and nothing was pending immediately before that date. Section 531(2)(a) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, which saves the Code of Criminal Procedure, does not apply. The case must be registered under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 and the evidence in it will be governed by the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023.

15. The offence is to be investigated under **section 176 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023** [section 157, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (repealed)]. Under sub-section (1), the officer in charge of the police station, having reason to suspect the commission of an offence which he is empowered to investigate under section 175, shall forthwith send a report to the Magistrate empowered to take cognizance. He shall also proceed in person, or depute a subordinate officer of the prescribed rank, to the spot to investigate the facts and circumstances. If necessary, he shall take measures for the discovery and arrest of the offender.

16. The offence is a serious one, being murder. The proviso to section 176(1) permitting the officer not to attend the spot does not apply to it. Section 176(3) also provides for a forensic expert to visit the crime scene and for videography of the process, for offences punishable with seven years or more, from the date notified by the State Government. The complainant requests that this be done to the extent the notification applies in [STATE].

**D. PRAYER**

The complainant respectfully requests that the Station House Officer:

(a) register an FIR on this complaint under section 101 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 against [NAME OF THE ACCUSED], and under such other provisions as the investigation may disclose;

(b) register the case under section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 and give the complainant a free copy of the FIR;

(c) send the report to the Magistrate and proceed to the spot to investigate under section 176 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023;

(d) secure the scene, the weapon and the body, have the post-mortem conducted, and arrest the accused; and

(e) record the statements of the witnesses named above.

**VERIFICATION**

I, [NAME OF THE COMPLAINANT], state that the contents of this complaint are true and correct to the best of my knowledge and belief, that nothing material has been concealed, and that the facts I did not witness are stated as learnt from [SOURCE].

Place: [PLACE]
Date: 1 July 2024

(Signature / thumb impression of the Complainant)
[NAME OF THE COMPLAINANT]

[Advocate's signature block, if the complaint is settled by counsel: [NAME OF ADVOCATE], [ENROLMENT NO.], [ADDRESS AND CONTACT]]

**ANNEXURES**

- Annexure A-1: Copy of the identity proof of the complainant [TO BE ADDED]
- Annexure A-2: [INQUEST / HOSPITAL / MEDICAL RECORDS OF THE DECEASED, IF AVAILABLE]
- Annexure A-3: [PHOTOGRAPHS, MESSAGES OR OTHER DOCUMENTS RELIED ON, IF ANY]

---
*Note for the advocate:* the penal section is section 101 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, punishable under section 103. The registering section is section 173 and the investigating section is section 176 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. The code is decided by the date alone. The offence date, 1 July 2024, is on or after commencement, so the stated time of 00:01 hours is not needed for the choice of code. Please verify the time of occurrence and the section 103 punishment text before filing.

**Subject:** Complaint for registration of a case for culpable homicide not amounting to murder, punishable under section 105 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, and for investigation under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023.

**I. FACTS**

1. The complainant is [DESCRIPTION OF THE COMPLAINANT AND HIS OR HER RELATIONSHIP TO THE DECEASED].

2. On 1 July 2024, at about [TIME], at [PLACE OF OCCURRENCE, WITH LANDMARKS AND POLICE STATION LIMITS], the accused, [NAME OF THE ACCUSED], [DESCRIBE THE ACT OF THE ACCUSED, THE WEAPON OR MEANS USED, AND THE INJURY CAUSED].

5. On the facts stated, the death was caused by the act of the accused, but the act was not done with any of the intentions that make culpable homicide murder under section 101 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. On the complainant's information, the accused did not set out to cause death, did not intend a bodily injury that he knew to be likely to cause death, and did not intend an injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. [ADD THE FACTS THAT SUPPORT THIS, FOR EXAMPLE THE SUDDENNESS OF THE ENCOUNTER, THE ABSENCE OF PREPARATION, THE NATURE OF THE FORCE USED.]

6. The complainant reported the matter to the police on 1 July 2024, the same day. The earlier history of the matter, if any, is [DETAILS, IF ANY, OF ANY EARLIER INTIMATION TO THE POLICE OR OTHER AUTHORITY].

**II. THE PENAL PROVISION**

7. The act complained of was committed on 1 July 2024, the day the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 came into force. The offence therefore falls under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and not the Indian Penal Code, 1860. Where the offence is placed within that day (for example 00:01 hours) does not alter the position.

8. Section 100 of the BNS defines culpable homicide. It is committed by whoever causes death by doing an act with the intention of causing death, or with the intention of causing such bodily injury as is likely to cause death, or with the knowledge that he is likely by such act to cause death.

9. Under section 101 of the BNS, culpable homicide is murder if the act is done with an intention of the kind set out in clauses (a), (b) and (c), or with the knowledge described in clause (d), subject to the stated exceptions. Section 101 is not attracted on the facts stated in paragraph 5, because the intention required for murder is absent.

10. The Supreme Court has explained how the two offences are distinguished. Culpable homicide can be committed on the basis of knowledge alone, without any intention to cause death. It is the intention or knowledge with which the act is done that decides whether the offence is murder or culpable homicide not amounting to murder (*Alister Anthony Pareira v. State of Maharashtra*, [2012] 1 S.C.R. 145, paras 27–29; *Rampal Singh v. State of U.P.*, [2012] 7 S.C.R. 160, paras 15–16, approving the staged approach in *State of A.P. v. Rayavarapu Punnayya*, (1976) 4 SCC 382). Those decisions were rendered under sections 299 and 300 of the Indian Penal Code. Their corresponding provisions are sections 100 and 101 of the BNS.

11. Where culpable homicide does not amount to murder, the punishment is provided by **section 105 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023**. The complainant therefore asks that the accused be charged under **section 105 of the BNS** [corresponding to section 304 of the Indian Penal Code, cited for reference only]. Section 105 prescribes two grades of punishment:
   - (a) Where the act causing death is done with the intention of causing death, or of causing such bodily injury as is likely to cause death, the punishment is imprisonment for life, or imprisonment of either description for not less than five years and up to ten years, and also fine.
   - (b) Where the act is done with the knowledge that it is likely to cause death, but without any intention to cause death or such bodily injury, the punishment is imprisonment of either description for up to ten years, and fine.

12. Which limb of section 105 applies depends on the accused's state of mind. That is a matter for investigation and for the Court. [THE COMPLAINANT'S CASE ON THE LIMB: LIMB (a) / LIMB (b) / TO BE DETERMINED ON INVESTIGATION.] The complainant also asks that the investigating officer consider, on the material collected, any other offence disclosed.

**III. THE PROCEDURAL PROVISIONS**

13. This information is given on 1 July 2024, after the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 came into force. No investigation or other proceeding on this matter was pending immediately before that date. The case must therefore be registered and investigated under the **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023**, and not under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, which is relevant only as the repealed equivalent. The evidence will be governed by the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023.

14. **Registration:** The complainant asks that a First Information Report be registered under **section 173 of the BNSS** [Cr.P.C. s. 154]. The text of section 173 is not reproduced in this draft. The offence is cognizable on the information given. [ADVOCATE TO VERIFY AND CONFIRM THE TEXT OF SECTION 173 BEFORE FILING.]

15. **Investigation:** The complainant asks that the investigation proceed under **section 176 of the BNSS** [Cr.P.C. s. 157]. Under section 176(1), an officer in charge of a police station who has reason to suspect the commission of an offence he is empowered to investigate under section 175 must:
   - forthwith send a report to the Magistrate empowered to take cognizance of the offence on a police report;
   - proceed in person, or depute a subordinate officer of the prescribed rank, to the spot to investigate the facts and circumstances; and
   - if necessary, take measures for the discovery and arrest of the offender.

16. The offence under section 105 of the BNS is punishable with imprisonment which may extend to ten years or to life. Section 176(3) of the BNSS therefore applies. It requires the officer in charge, from the date notified by the State Government, to cause a forensic expert to visit the crime scene to collect forensic evidence, and to cause the process to be videographed on a mobile phone or other electronic device. The complainant requests compliance with section 176(3) to the extent it is in force in [STATE]. [STATE NOTIFICATION, IF ANY, TO BE ADDED.]

**IV. PRAYER**

The complainant therefore prays that the Station House Officer may be pleased to:

(a) register a First Information Report under section 105 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 against [NAME OF THE ACCUSED], and supply a free copy of it to the complainant;

(b) investigate the case under section 176 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, including by visiting the spot, preserving and collecting forensic evidence, and sending the report to the Magistrate;

11. **Why one charge and why the BNS.** The conduct complained of began before 1 July 2024 and continued until 05 July 2024, after the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita came into force. It is pleaded as one continuing course of conduct that ended in the death, and not as a series of separate offences each complete when done. One charge is therefore proper. It is not to be split by date into an IPC charge for the earlier acts and a BNS charge for the later ones. Section 9(1) of the BNS allows one punishment for an offence made up of parts. The offence was still being committed after 1 July 2024, so liability arises under section 1(3) of the BNS. Section 358 of the BNS saves the IPC only for offences completed before that date. Acts before 1 July 2024 will be charged under the IPC, 1860 (BNS, section 358). Acts on or after that date will be charged under the BNS. For that purpose the Complainant has set out the date of each overt act in paragraph 4, and the Investigating Officer is requested to record the date of each act, and of the fatal act, in the FIR and the case diary.

 The proviso to section 176(1) permits the officer not to investigate only where there is no sufficient ground for entering on an investigation. **B. OFFENCE DISCLOSED AND SECTION UNDER WHICH THE ACCUSED IS TO BE CHARGED**

6. The incident occurred on 1 February 2024, before the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 came into force on 1 July 2024. Under section 358(2)(c) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and Article 20(1) of the Constitution, the offence is governed by the Indian Penal Code, 1860.

7. The accused is to be charged under **Section 304, Part II, of the Indian Penal Code, 1860** [corresponding to section 105 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, cited only as the new equivalent]. This is culpable homicide not amounting to murder, in which the act is done with the knowledge that it is likely to cause death, but without any intention to cause death or such bodily injury as is likely to cause death.

8. The legal basis is as follows:

   (a) Section 299 of the Indian Penal Code defines culpable homicide as causing death by an act done with the intention of causing death, or with the intention of causing such bodily injury as is likely to cause death, or with the knowledge that the act is likely to cause death.

   (b) In *Anbazhagan v. State represented by the Inspector of Police* [(2023) 10 S.C.R. 1091], the Supreme Court held that the first part of section 304 applies where there is "guilty intention", and the second part applies where there is no such intention but there is "guilty knowledge", that is, the third clause of section 299.

   (c) In *Keshub Mahindra v. State of M.P.* [(1996) Supp. 6 S.C.R. 285], the Supreme Court held that a charge under section 304 Part II requires material that at least prima facie shows that the accused did an act which caused death with the knowledge that he was likely by that act to cause death.

9. The facts in paragraphs 2 to 4 satisfy these requirements. The accused's act caused death. It was done with the knowledge that death was likely. The intention required for murder under section 300 of the Indian Penal Code is absent. The offence therefore falls under section 304 Part II and not section 302.

3. [NAME OF THE DECEASED], [age, address, relationship to the complainant].

**IV. FACTS**

4. On 1 February 2024, at about [TIME], at [PLACE OF OCCURRENCE], the accused did [DESCRIBE THE ACT OF THE ACCUSED: for example, the manner of driving, handling or operating, or the omission that took place].

5. The act was rash and negligent in that [PARTICULARS OF RASHNESS / NEGLIGENCE: speed, manner of conduct, the precaution omitted, the duty of care owed to the deceased].

6. As a direct result of that act, [NAME OF THE DECEASED] sustained [NATURE OF INJURIES] and [died at the spot / was taken to (HOSPITAL) and was declared dead on (DATE AND TIME)].

7. The accused did not intend to cause the death of the deceased and did not know that the act was likely to cause death. The act therefore falls outside culpable homicide under section 299 of the Indian Penal Code and is a case of death caused by a rash or negligent act. [FACTS TO SHOW THE ABSENCE OF INTENTION OR KNOWLEDGE, IF ANY.]

8. [WITNESSES PRESENT AT THE SPOT: NAMES AND ADDRESSES.] [DETAILS OF THE POST-MORTEM, INQUEST OR MEDICO-LEGAL RECORD, IF ANY.]

9. [REASONS FOR THE INTERVAL BETWEEN 1 FEBRUARY 2024 AND 20 JUNE 2024, TO BE STATED FAITHFULLY BY THE COMPLAINANT.]

**V. THE OFFENCE AND THE PROVISION OF LAW**

10. **Penal provision.** The act was committed on 1 February 2024, before the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 came into force on 1 July 2024. The accused is therefore to be charged under **section 304A of the Indian Penal Code, 1860** (causing death by negligence), which is saved for offences committed before that date by section 358(2)(c) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and Article 20(1) of the Constitution. [The corresponding provision of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita is section 106(1), cited only as the new equivalent.]

11. Section 304A of the Indian Penal Code provides that whoever causes the death of any person by doing any rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.

12. **Ingredients.** The offence requires: (i) the death of a person; (ii) that the accused caused that death; and (iii) that the act of the accused was rash or negligent and did not amount to culpable homicide (*Raj Kumar Jain v. State*, Delhi High Court, 2024, Crl.M.C. 4183/2023). The rash or negligent act must be the proximate and efficient cause of the death, the *causa causans* and not merely a *causa sine qua non* (*Ambalal D. Bhatt v. State of Gujarat*, Supreme Court, as applied by the Karnataka High Court in *Mohan Das Shetty v. State of Karnataka*, Crl.P. 7560/2021). The Supreme Court has also held that section 304A excludes the ingredients of sections 299 and 300; where intention or knowledge is the direct motivating force of the act, section 304A makes room for the graver charge of culpable homicide (*State v. Sanjeev Nanda*, [2012] 12 S.C.R. 881). This complaint pleads the facts on which each ingredient rests.

The proceeding therefore began before the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 came into force and continues under the **Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973**, as preserved by section 531(2)(a) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita. [The corresponding provisions of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita are cited only as new equivalents: section 173 for section 154, and section 175 for section 156.]

(a) register this information as a First Information Report under section 154(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, read with section 304A of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, enter its substance in the prescribed book, and supply a free copy to the complainant;

(b) investigate the case under section 156(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, record the statements of the witnesses, and secure the post-mortem report and the other relevant material;

(c) on completion of the investigation, submit the report to the jurisdictional Magistrate and take action against the accused according to law; and

VERSUS

[NAME OF THE ACCUSED], son of [FATHER'S NAME], resident of [ADDRESS] [AND OTHER RELATIVES OF THE HUSBAND, IF ANY, AGAINST WHOM THERE IS MATERIAL] ... ACCUSED

---

**PART A: THE CODES UNDER WHICH THE CASE IS TO BE CHARGED AND REGISTERED**

1. **Penal section: Section 304-B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (dowry death).** [Its new equivalent is section 80 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.] The offence was committed on 30 June 2024, before the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita came into force on 1 July 2024. Section 358(2)(c) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita keeps the Indian Penal Code for offences committed before that date, and Article 20(1) of the Constitution forbids punishing a person under a law not in force when the act was done. The accused must therefore be charged under section 304-B IPC, not section 80 BNS. The one-minute margin makes no difference to this rule: what matters is that the act fell on 30 June 2024.

2. **Procedural section: Section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023** [corresponding to section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973]. The information was given to the police on 5 July 2024. Section 531(2)(a) BNSS saves the Code of Criminal Procedure only for an appeal, application, trial, inquiry or investigation pending immediately before 1 July 2024. Nothing was pending on that date, since the proceeding began on 5 July 2024. The date of the offence does not enter this test. The FIR is to be registered, and the investigation conducted, under the BNSS, and evidence in it is governed by the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023. The presumption of dowry death is therefore to be invoked under section 118 BSA [corresponding to section 113-B of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872]. **[Advocate to verify the BSA section number against the enacted text before filing.]**

3. Section 173(1) BNSS permits the information to be given orally or by electronic communication, requires it to be signed by the informant, and under section 173(2) a copy must be given free of cost to the informant. Dowry death carries imprisonment of not less than seven years, so the preliminary enquiry option in section 173(3) (offences punishable with three years or more but less than seven) does not apply. The offence is cognizable and an FIR should be registered.

---

**PART B: FACTS**

4. The complainant is [RELATIONSHIP] of the deceased, [NAME OF THE DECEASED], who was married to the accused on [DATE OF MARRIAGE], at [PLACE]. The marriage was therefore solemnised within seven years of her death.

5. After the marriage, the deceased lived with the accused at [MATRIMONIAL HOME ADDRESS].

6. The accused, [AND HIS RELATIVES, IF ANY], demanded dowry from the deceased and her family in the form of [PARTICULARS OF THE DEMAND]. [DATES, PLACES AND NATURE OF THE DEMANDS AND OF THE CRUELTY OR HARASSMENT, TO BE STATED SPECIFICALLY.]

7. The deceased was subjected to cruelty and harassment in connection with that demand, including [PARTICULARS OF ACTS OF CRUELTY]. This continued until shortly before her death. [PARTICULARS OF THE LAST INCIDENT OF HARASSMENT AND ITS DATE, SHOWING PROXIMITY TO THE DEATH.]

8. On 30 June 2024, at about 23:59 hours, the deceased died at [PLACE] [MANNER OF DEATH: BURNS / BODILY INJURY / OTHERWISE THAN UNDER NORMAL CIRCUMSTANCES], in the circumstances that [PARTICULARS OF HOW THE COMPLAINANT LEARNT OF THE DEATH AND WHAT WAS SEEN].

9. The complainant approached the police on 5 July 2024. [REASON FOR ANY INTERVAL BETWEEN THE DEATH AND THE REPORT, IF ANY, TO BE EXPLAINED.]

10. [DETAILS OF POST-MORTEM, INQUEST OR ANY EARLIER INFORMATION OR UNNATURAL DEATH REPORT, IF ANY.]

---

**PART C: GROUNDS**

11. The ingredients of the offence of dowry death are: (a) the death of a woman caused by burns or bodily injury, or otherwise than under normal circumstances; (b) within seven years of marriage; (c) cruelty or harassment by the husband or his relative soon before her death; and (d) that the cruelty or harassment was for, or in connection with, a demand for dowry. Each is disclosed by paragraphs 4 to 8 above.

12. The presumption of dowry death arises only on proof of cruelty or harassment for dowry in reasonable contiguity with the death, and such proof is the foundation on which the presumption stands. On the presumption under section 113-B of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (now section 118 BSA), the Supreme Court in *Kans Raj v. State of Punjab*, [2000] 3 S.C.R. 662, held that a proximate and live link must exist between the cruelty or harassment and the death, and that lapse of time alone is not a defence. The complainant has accordingly pleaded dates and particulars of the harassment in paragraphs 6 and 7 so that this link can be investigated and proved.

13. The accused, being the husband, is liable to be deemed to have caused the death.

---

**PART D: PRAYER**

It is respectfully prayed that:

(a) the information be registered as a First Information Report under section 173 BNSS for the offence under section 304-B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 [section 80 BNS], together with [SECTION 498-A IPC AND SECTIONS 3 AND 4 OF THE DOWRY PROHIBITION ACT, 1961, IF THE FACTS SUPPORT THEM];

(b) the investigation be conducted under the BNSS, including the seizure of dowry-related material, recording of statements and preservation of the post-mortem record;

(c) a copy of the FIR be furnished free of cost to the complainant under section 173(2) BNSS; and

(d) such other order be passed as this Court deems fit.

The death occurred within seven years of the marriage.

4. 5. The cruelty and harassment was one continuing course of conduct. It began before 1 July 2024 and continued without break after that date until 31 December 2024. [FACTS SHOWING THE LINK BETWEEN THE LAST ACTS OF HARASSMENT AND THE DEATH, INCLUDING DATE OF LAST DEMAND OR ASSAULT.]

6. The complainant approached this police station on 15 January 2025 with this complaint. [EXPLANATION OF ANY INTERVAL BETWEEN THE DEATH AND THE COMPLAINT, IF ANY.]

**B. THE PENAL PROVISION**

7. The offence disclosed is **dowry death, punishable under section 80(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023** [corresponding to section 304-B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860]. Section 80(1) provides that where the death of a woman is caused by any burns or bodily injury, or occurs otherwise than under normal circumstances, within seven years of her marriage, and it is shown that soon before her death she was subjected to cruelty or harassment by her husband or any relative of her husband for, or in connection with, any demand for dowry, such death is called "dowry death", and such husband or relative is deemed to have caused her death. Section 80(2) provides imprisonment for a term of not less than seven years, which may extend to imprisonment for life.

8. **Why the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and not the Indian Penal Code.** The cruelty and harassment was a continuing course of conduct that ran from 10 January 2023 across 1 July 2024 to 31 December 2024. It is one continuing offence, not separate offences each complete when done. It is therefore charged once and is not split by date into an IPC charge and a BNS charge (section 9(1) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita allows one punishment for an offence made up of parts). The conduct was still being committed after 1 July 2024, so liability arises under the Sanhita (section 1(3) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita). The Indian Penal Code, 1860 is cited only as the repealed equivalent.

9. The accused may also be charged with cruelty by a husband or his relative under section 85 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [corresponding to section 498-A, Indian Penal Code, 1860]. The text of section 85 is not set out here and should be confirmed by the advocate. It is to be treated as part of the same continuing conduct and charged under the Sanhita. The complainant also relies on the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, to the extent the facts disclose an offence under it: [PROVISIONS, IF ANY].

**C. THE PROCEDURAL PROVISIONS**

10. **Registration.** The information discloses a cognizable offence. This proceeding was begun on 15 January 2025, after 1 July 2024, and nothing in it was pending immediately before that date. Section 531(2)(a) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 therefore does not continue the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, and the date of the offence does not enter that test. The case is to be **registered under section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023** [section 154, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (repealed)]. The text of section 173 is not reproduced here.

11. **Investigation.** The case is to be **investigated under section 176 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023** [section 156, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (repealed)], read with section 175, which empowers the officer in charge of a police station to investigate. Under section 176(1), on information giving reason to suspect the commission of a cognizable offence that he is empowered to investigate, the officer in charge shall forthwith send a report to the Magistrate empowered to take cognizance of such offence upon a police report. He shall proceed in person, or depute a subordinate officer of the prescribed rank, to the spot to investigate the facts and circumstances and, if necessary, to take measures for the discovery and arrest of the offender. Because the offence is punishable with imprisonment of seven years or more, section 176(3) also applies. Under it, the officer in charge shall, from the date notified by the State Government, cause a forensic expert to visit the crime scene to collect forensic evidence and cause videography of the process. The complainant requests that this be done to the extent notified in this State.

12. Evidence in the case will be governed by the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023. The presumption as to dowry death, formerly under section 113-B of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, is to be looked for in the corresponding provision of that Adhiniyam: [CORRESPONDING SECTION OF THE BHARATIYA SAKSHYA ADHINIYAM — TO BE VERIFIED].

**D. GROUNDS**

13. Every ingredient of the offence is disclosed on the facts above: (i) the death of a woman caused by burns or bodily injury or otherwise than under normal circumstances; (ii) within seven years of her marriage; (iii) subjection to cruelty or harassment by her husband or his relative; (iv) for, or in connection with, a demand for dowry; and (v) soon before her death. These are the ingredients identified by the Supreme Court in *Manohar Lal v. State of Haryana* [2014] 6 S.C.R. 263 (Supreme Court of India, 2014), where the Court observed that it is only when such ingredients are established by acceptable evidence that the death is called a "dowry death" and the husband or relative is deemed to have caused it. The citation and the statement should be verified against the full report before filing.

14. In *Kans Raj v. State of Punjab* [2000] 3 S.C.R. 662 (three-Judge Bench), the Supreme Court held that proximate or live links must exist between the course of cruelty or harassment and the death. It also held that mere lapse of time does not by itself give the accused a defence that the cruelty was not "soon before" the death. Later treatment of this judgment has not been checked and should be verified. Here the harassment continued until 31 December 2024, and the death followed on [DATE OF DEATH]. This shows the proximate and live link.

15. The conduct from 10 January 2023 to 31 December 2024 is one continuing course of conduct, as set out in paragraphs 5 and 8 above.

**Offence: Section 108 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (abetment of suicide)**

Date: 01 July 2024
Place: [PLACE]

**1. PARTIES**

Complainant: [NAME OF THE COMPLAINANT], [AGE], [OCCUPATION], [RELATIONSHIP TO THE DECEASED], resident of [ADDRESS], [MOBILE NUMBER].

Deceased: [NAME OF THE DECEASED], [AGE], resident of [ADDRESS].

Accused: [NAME OF THE ACCUSED], [AGE/DESCRIPTION], resident of [ADDRESS], [RELATIONSHIP OR CONNECTION TO THE DECEASED].

**2. THE APPLICABLE CODES**

2.1 **Penal provision.** The incident occurred on 01 July 2024, the day the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 ("BNS") came into force. The offence was therefore committed on or after the commencement of the BNS. The accused is to be charged under **Section 108 of the BNS** [corresponding to Section 306 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, with Section 107 IPC for the definition of abetment]. The BNS definition of abetment is in Section 45.

2.2 **Procedural provisions.** This information is given on 01 July 2024, the same day the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 ("BNSS") came into force. No investigation, inquiry or trial was pending immediately before that date, so Section 531(2)(a) BNSS, which saves the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, does not apply. The case is therefore to be:
   (a) registered under **Section 173 BNSS** [Section 154 CrPC], and
   (b) investigated under **Section 176 BNSS** [Section 157 CrPC], with evidence governed by the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023.

**3. FACTS**

3.1 The complainant is [RELATIONSHIP] of the deceased, [NAME OF THE DECEASED].

3.2 The deceased and the accused were known to each other as [NATURE OF RELATIONSHIP/DEALINGS].

3.3 On 01 July 2024, at about [TIME], at [PLACE], the deceased died by suicide by [MANNER OF DEATH, AS KNOWN]. [DETAILS OF DISCOVERY OF THE BODY, WHO FOUND IT AND WHEN.]

4.1 The Supreme Court has held that an offence of abetment of suicide requires proof of direct or indirect acts of instigation or incitement by the accused. These acts must be in close proximity to the suicide and must reveal a clear mens rea. Mere harassment does not suffice without a positive action proximate to the occurrence that led or compelled the deceased to commit suicide. *Patel Babubhai Manohardas v. State of Gujarat*, 2025 INSC 322, [2025] 3 S.C.R. 432, paras 21–25, reaffirming *Rajesh v. State of Haryana* (2020) 15 SCC 359 and *Prakash v. State of Maharashtra* (2024 INSC 1020); *Jayedeepsinh Pravinsinh Chavda v. State of Gujarat*, [2024] 12 S.C.R. 439, paras 22–25, citing *Ude Singh v. State of Haryana* (2019) 17 SCC 301. Whether they amount to abetment is a matter for investigation, and the information discloses the commission of a cognizable offence.

This is how the Bombay High Court (single bench), in *Durgeshwari Wd/o Narendra Thakre v. State of Maharashtra* (APL/999/2025, Bombay High Court), set out the principle on Section 306 IPC. In that judgment the Bombay High Court itself refers to the Supreme Court's decision in *Sanju @ Sanjay Singh Sengar v. State of M.P.*, (2002) 5 SCC 371, on instigation and mens rea; that Supreme Court decision is cited here only as quoted in the Bombay judgment, and it has not been verified against the original report. The same passage on active role and instigation also appears in *Kamlesh Suryavanshi @ Kamlesh Ahirwar v. State of Madhya Pradesh* (CRR/1116/2023, Madhya Pradesh High Court, division bench). The Bombay High Court and the Gauhati High Court (*Rudra Kumar Pathak v. State of Assam*, AB/1874/2025, Gauhati High Court, quoting an earlier decision in the passage relied on; the passage is attributed to that quoted decision and not stated as the Court's own holding) both stress positive action proximate to the time of death. The Gauhati High Court passage treats a continuous course of conduct that leaves the victim with no option but to end life as capable of amounting to abetment. These are High Court decisions and are cited for their reasoning only. The Supreme Court in *Lalita v. Vishwanath & Ors.* (2025, division bench), an appeal concerning abetment of suicide and mere harassment or cruelty, may be consulted on this point; no holding from it is relied on here until its text is verified. [ADVOCATE TO ADD VERIFIED SUPREME COURT AUTHORITY, IF POSSIBLE OF A LARGER BENCH.]

**1. COMPLAINANT**

[NAME OF THE COMPLAINANT], [AGE], [OCCUPATION], resident of [ADDRESS], [CONTACT DETAILS], [RELATIONSHIP, IF ANY, TO THE ACCUSED].

**2. ACCUSED**

[NAME OF THE ACCUSED], [AGE], [OCCUPATION], resident of [ADDRESS], [RELATIONSHIP, IF ANY, TO THE COMPLAINANT].

**3. SUBJECT**

Complaint against the accused for attempting to commit culpable homicide not amounting to murder, by a continuing course of conduct from 10 January 2023 to 31 December 2024, and a request for the registration of an FIR.

---

**FACTS**

4. The complainant is the person against whom the conduct described below was directed.

5. From 10 January 2023 until 31 December 2024 the accused engaged in a continuing course of conduct towards the complainant. The conduct was done with such intention or knowledge, and in such circumstances, that if death had been caused by it the accused would have been guilty of culpable homicide not amounting to murder. The complainant describes this conduct as cruelty.

6. [PARTICULARS OF EACH ACT OR INCIDENT: DATE, PLACE, MANNER, WEAPON OR MEANS USED, IF ANY].

7. [INJURIES SUFFERED, IF ANY, MEDICAL TREATMENT TAKEN, NAME OF HOSPITAL AND DOCTOR]. If hurt was caused by any of the acts, the complainant asks that this be recorded.

8. [WITNESSES TO THE INCIDENTS: NAMES AND ADDRESSES].

9. [REASONS FOR THE DELAY IN APPROACHING THE POLICE BEFORE 15 JANUARY 2025, IF ANY].

10. The conduct was a single course of conduct that began before 1 July 2024 and was still going on after that date. The complainant therefore asks that it be treated as one continuing offence and not divided by date.

---

**LAW AND GROUNDS**

11. **Penal provision.** The offence is the attempt to commit culpable homicide not amounting to murder. It is punishable under **section 110 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS)**, whose text is not set out here. Its equivalent in the repealed Indian Penal Code, 1860 is section 308. That section provided punishment of up to three years' imprisonment, or fine, or both, and, where hurt is caused, up to seven years, or fine, or both.

12. **Why the BNS and a single charge.**
   - The conduct is alleged to be one continuing offence. It began on 10 January 2023, before 1 July 2024, and was still being committed on and after that date.
   - Section 9(1) of the BNS allows one punishment for an offence made up of parts. Section 1(3) of the BNS makes liability for an offence still being committed after commencement one under the Sanhita "and not otherwise". Under section 518 of the BNSS, a continuing offence is treated as committed afresh at every moment it continues.
   - The offence should therefore be charged once, under section 110 of the BNS, and not split into an IPC charge for the period before 1 July 2024 and a BNS charge for the period after it. Section 308 of the IPC is cited only as the equivalent of section 110.
   - If the investigation shows that the acts were separate offences, each complete when done, each should be charged under the code in force on the day it was done. Acts before 1 July 2024 would then fall under the IPC, as saved by section 358 of the BNS, and acts on or after that date under the BNS.

13. **Procedure: registration.** This information is given on 15 January 2025, after 1 July 2024, and no investigation was pending before that date. The case must therefore be registered and proceeded with under the BNSS and not the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. The offence is cognizable and the information is to be recorded as an FIR under **section 173 of the BNSS** [section 154, CrPC]. The text of section 173 is not shown here. The complainant requests that the information be read over to the complainant, signed, and entered in the prescribed book, and that a free copy be given.

14. **Procedure: investigation.**
   - Under **section 175(1) of the BNSS** [section 156(1), CrPC], an officer in charge of a police station may, without the order of a Magistrate, investigate any cognizable case that a court having jurisdiction over the local area would have power to inquire into or try.
   - Under **section 176(1) of the BNSS**, an officer who has reason to suspect the commission of such an offence must forthwith send a report to the Magistrate empowered to take cognizance, and must proceed in person, or depute a subordinate officer, to the spot to investigate the facts and circumstances. If necessary, he must take measures for the discovery and arrest of the offender.
   - Under section 176(3) of the BNSS, where the offence is punishable with seven years or more, the forensic and videography requirements apply from the date notified by the State Government. This is mentioned in case the offence as investigated attracts that threshold.

15. If the information is not registered, the complainant reserves the right to apply to the Magistrate under section 175(3) of the BNSS, supported by an affidavit under section 173(4) of the BNSS, for an order directing investigation.

---

**PRAYER**

The complainant prays that the Station House Officer may:

(a) register an FIR on this information under section 173 of the BNSS, 2023, for the offence under **section 110 of the BNS, 2023** (equivalent of section 308 of the IPC), as one continuing offence from 10 January 2023 to 31 December 2024, adding any other offence the facts disclose;

(b) investigate under sections 175 and 176 of the BNSS, 2023, and forward the report to the Magistrate;

(c) arrange medical examination of the complainant and preserve the evidence; and

(d) give the complainant a free copy of the FIR and take any other action the law requires.

---

**VERIFICATION**

**(Signature of the Complainant)**

B. THE OFFENCE AND THE PENAL PROVISION

8. The offence disclosed is voluntarily causing hurt. The accused did acts intending to cause hurt, or knowing that he was likely thereby to cause hurt, and thereby caused hurt to the complainant.

9. The section under which the accused is to be charged is section 115(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [section 323 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, which is its equivalent, now repealed]. Section 115(2) provides for imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees, or both. This is subject to the exception for the case provided for by section 122(1) of the BNS.

10. Why one charge under the BNS and not an IPC charge for the earlier period:

(a) On the complainant's case, the accused's conduct is one continuing course of conduct that ran without break from 10 January 2023 to 31 December 2024. It is not a set of separate offences, each complete when done.

(b) A continuing offence is one susceptible of continuance, as distinguished from one committed once and for all. The offence is committed on every occasion it recurs (State of Bihar v. Deokaran Nenshi, as applied in Jafar Abbas Rasoolmohammad Merchant v. State of Gujarat, High Court of Gujarat, 2015, a single-bench decision persuasive only outside that High Court).

(c) The Supreme Court in Vikas Chaudhary v. State of NCT of Delhi, [2010] 9 S.C.R. 1076, held that where the accused's conduct in pursuit of the same object continued, the offence did not end with the first act. The date on which the conduct last continued was taken as the date of the offence.

(d) Section 9(1) of the BNS permits one punishment for an offence made up of parts. The conduct was still being committed on and after 1 July 2024, so liability arises under the BNS (section 1(3) of the BNS). The complainant therefore asks that the offence be charged once, under section 115(2) of the BNS, and not split by date into an IPC charge and a BNS charge. The IPC section is cited only as the equivalent of the BNS section.

(e) [Note for the advocate: if, on the facts, the acts of hurt prove to be separate incidents, each complete when done, each would be charged under the code in force on its date. Those before 1 July 2024 would fall under section 323 IPC (saved by section 358 of the BNS), and those on or after that date under section 115(2) of the BNS. The particulars in paragraph 3 decide this and should be settled before filing.]

C. THE PROCEDURAL PROVISIONS

11. This complaint is made under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, and not the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. The proceeding began on 15 January 2025, after 1 July 2024. Nothing was pending immediately before that date, so section 531(2)(a) of the BNSS does not continue the old Code. The date of the offence does not enter that test. The evidence will likewise follow the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (section 170 of the BSA).

12. Registration: the information is to be registered under section 173 of the BNSS [section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973] (the text of this section is not reproduced here).

13. Investigation: the case is to be investigated under sections 175 and 176 of the BNSS [section 156 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973]. Section 176(1) requires the officer in charge, on suspecting the commission of an offence he is empowered to investigate, to send a report forthwith to the Magistrate empowered to take cognizance on a police report. He must then proceed in person, or depute a subordinate officer, to the spot to investigate the facts and circumstances, and if necessary take measures for the discovery and arrest of the offender. The first proviso to section 176(1) contemplates cases where the officer need not proceed to the spot, or need not investigate, and section 176(2) requires reasons to be recorded in such cases.

14. [Classification of the offence under the First Schedule to the BNSS (cognizable or non-cognizable) to be verified by the advocate before filing. If the offence is non-cognizable, the police may investigate only with the Magistrate's order, and the alternative prayer (c) below applies.]

D. GROUNDS

16. The conduct continued after 1 July 2024, so the whole course of conduct is governed by the BNS.

17. The complainant is ready to produce medical and other evidence and to name witnesses.

The complainant respectfully states as follows:

**A. PARTIES AND BACKGROUND**

1. The complainant is a woman residing at [ADDRESS]. [RELATIONSHIP OR ACQUAINTANCE BETWEEN THE COMPLAINANT AND THE ACCUSED, IF ANY].

2. The accused, [NAME OF THE ACCUSED], resides at [ADDRESS] and [OCCUPATION / POSITION OF THE ACCUSED RELATIVE TO THE COMPLAINANT, IF ANY].

**B. FACTS**

3. From 10 January 2023 until 31 December 2024 the accused assaulted the complainant and used criminal force to her, intending to outrage her modesty or knowing it to be likely that he would thereby outrage her modesty.

4. The conduct was not a single act. It was a continuous and connected course of conduct by the same accused against the same complainant over the whole period. It began before 1 July 2024 and continued after that date until 31 December 2024.

5. The particulars of the acts complained of are:
 (a) [PARTICULARS OF THE ACTS, WITH DATES AND PLACES, FOR THE PERIOD 10 JANUARY 2023 TO 30 JUNE 2024];
 (b) [PARTICULARS OF THE ACTS, WITH DATES AND PLACES, FOR THE PERIOD 1 JULY 2024 TO 31 DECEMBER 2024];
 (c) [WITNESSES PRESENT, IF ANY];
 (d) [ANY MESSAGES, RECORDINGS, MEDICAL OR OTHER MATERIAL, IF ANY].

6. [REASONS FOR NOT APPROACHING THE POLICE EARLIER, IF THE COMPLAINANT WISHES TO STATE THEM.]

7. The complainant approached the police on 15 January 2025, and this complaint is made on that date. [DETAILS OF ANY EARLIER COMPLAINT OR REPRESENTATION TO ANY AUTHORITY, IF ANY.]

**C. THE PENAL SECTION UNDER WHICH THE ACCUSED IS TO BE CHARGED**

8. **Section: section 74 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023** (assault or criminal force to a woman with intent to outrage her modesty). It is the successor of section 354 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. The accused is to be charged once, under this section alone.

9. The reasons are as follows:
 (a) Section 354 IPC punished whoever assaults or uses criminal force to any woman, intending to outrage or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby outrage her modesty, with imprisonment of either description for a term of not less than one year, extendable to five years, and also with fine. The conduct described in paragraphs 3 to 5 falls within that description. It is a cognizable offence for the purposes of registration (see paragraph 12).
 (b) A continuing offence is one susceptible of continuance, as distinguished from one committed once and for all. Where it continues, the offence is committed on every occasion it recurs. This principle, taken from State of Bihar v. Deokaran Nenshi, is recorded in *Jafar Abbas Rasoolmohammad Merchant v. State of Gujarat* (High Court of Gujarat, Criminal Misc. Application No. 14361 of 2010, 2015), a decision persuasive here and not binding outside that High Court. [CITATION OF THE SUPREME COURT'S JUDGMENT IN DEOKARAN NENSHI TO BE VERIFIED AND ADDED FROM THE OFFICIAL REPORT.]
 (c) The complainant describes one unbroken course of conduct by the same accused against the same woman, which was still being committed after 1 July 2024. For such an offence, section 9(1) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita permits a single punishment where the offence is made up of parts. Since the offence was still being committed after the Sanhita came into force, the accused is liable under the Sanhita (section 1(3)). A continuing offence is treated as committed afresh at every moment it continues (section 518 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita). The offence is therefore not split by date into a charge under the Indian Penal Code and a charge under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita. Section 354 IPC is cited only as the equivalent provision.
 (d) [DRAFTING NOTE FOR THE ADVOCATE, TO BE DELETED BEFORE FILING: This course of conduct is pleaded as one continuing offence, on the complainant's instructions. If the investigation shows only discrete acts, each complete when done, each act is charged under the code in force on its date. Acts before 1 July 2024 are then charged under section 354 IPC, saved by section 358 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, and acts on or after that date under section 74 BNS. The facts in paragraph 5 should be settled with this in mind.]

**D. THE PROCEDURAL SECTIONS UNDER WHICH THE CASE IS TO BE REGISTERED AND INVESTIGATED**

10. **Registration: section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023** [section 154, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973]. The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 continues to govern only an appeal, application, trial, inquiry or investigation pending immediately before 1 July 2024 (section 531(2)(a) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita). Nothing was pending before the police on that date. The proceeding began with this complaint on 15 January 2025, after 1 July 2024. The date of the offence does not enter that test. The case is therefore to be registered, and the FIR headed, under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita. The Indian Evidence Act, 1872 does not apply to it, and the evidence will be governed by the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (section 170(2) of that Adhiniyam).

11. **Investigation: section 176 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023.** Under sub-section (1), an officer in charge of a police station who has reason to suspect the commission of an offence he is empowered to investigate shall forthwith send a report to the Magistrate empowered to take cognizance on a police report. He shall proceed in person, or depute a subordinate officer of the prescribed rank, to the spot to investigate the facts and circumstances and, if necessary, to take measures for the discovery and arrest of the offender. Examination of witnesses, including the complainant, is to follow under section 180 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita [section 161, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973].

12. **Recording by a woman officer.** The complainant is the woman against whom an offence of the kind in section 74 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita [section 354 IPC] is alleged. She requests that her information be recorded by a woman police officer, as the corresponding proviso to section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita requires. The text of that proviso is to be verified against the enacted section before filing. The proviso to section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, as set out in the sources, so provided for an offence under section 354 of the Indian Penal Code.

**Subject: Information of the commission of the cognizable offence of assault on a woman with intent to outrage her modesty (section 354 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860) on 10 May 2024, and request to register the First Information Report and investigate.**

---

**I. PARTIES**

1. **Complainant:** [NAME OF THE COMPLAINANT], [AGE], [OCCUPATION], resident of [ADDRESS], a woman. [CONTACT DETAILS]

2. **Accused:** [NAME OF THE ACCUSED], [AGE], [OCCUPATION], resident of [ADDRESS]. [RELATIONSHIP OR ACQUAINTANCE WITH THE COMPLAINANT, IF ANY]

---

**II. FACTS**

3. The complainant states that on 10 May 2024, at about [TIME], at [PLACE OF OCCURRENCE], within the jurisdiction of this police station, the accused assaulted her with the intention of outraging her modesty.

4. [DESCRIBE THE ACT: WHAT THE ACCUSED DID, THE WORDS USED, AND THE FORCE APPLIED, IN THE COMPLAINANT'S OWN ACCOUNT.]

5. [NAMES OF WITNESSES PRESENT OR TO WHOM THE COMPLAINANT DISCLOSED THE INCIDENT, IF ANY.] [INJURIES, DAMAGE TO CLOTHING, OR MEDICAL EXAMINATION, IF ANY.]

6. The complainant is approaching the police on 20 January 2026, about twenty months after the incident. The reasons for the delay are as follows: [REASONS FOR DELAY, AS STATED BY THE COMPLAINANT, FOR EXAMPLE FEAR, SOCIAL EMBARRASSMENT, THREATS, FAMILY CIRCUMSTANCES, WITH DATES].

7. No earlier complaint or information about this incident has been made to any police station or Magistrate. [DETAILS OF ANY EARLIER COMPLAINT, IF ANY.]

---

**III. THE OFFENCE AND THE PROVISIONS APPLICABLE**

8. **Penal provision.** The offence was committed on 10 May 2024, before the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 came into force on 1 July 2024. The accused is therefore to be charged under **section 354 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860** (assault or criminal force to a woman with intent to outrage her modesty). The Indian Penal Code continues to govern offences committed before 1 July 2024 by virtue of section 358 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, and Article 20(1) of the Constitution forbids punishment under a law not in force when the act was done. The corresponding provision of the new code is section 74 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, cited only as its equivalent. [ADD ANY FURTHER OFFENCE DISCLOSED BY THE COMPLAINANT'S ACCOUNT, WITH ITS DATE.]

9. **Procedural provisions.** The proceeding begins with this information, given on 20 January 2026. Nothing was pending before 1 July 2024, so section 531(2)(a) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 does not apply. The procedure therefore follows the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023:
   (a) The case is to be **registered** under **section 173** of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita [section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973].
   (b) It is to be **investigated** under **section 176** of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita [section 156 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, in the power to investigate a cognizable case]. Under section 176(1), an officer in charge who has reason to suspect the commission of an offence he is empowered to investigate must forthwith send a report to the Magistrate empowered to take cognizance, and proceed in person or depute a subordinate officer to the spot to investigate the facts and circumstances.
   (c) The corresponding proviso of the repealed section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which names section 354 of the Indian Penal Code among the offences covered, required information given by the woman against whom the offence is alleged to have been committed to be recorded by a woman police officer. The complainant requests that her information be recorded accordingly by a woman police officer, in line with the corresponding provision of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita.

---

**IV. GROUNDS**

10. **Delay.** The Supreme Court in *Vidyadharan v. State of Kerala* [[2003] Supp. 5 S.C.R. 524] observed in a prosecution under section 354 of the Indian Penal Code that delay in lodging the FIR is natural in a tradition-bound society, where a woman wishes to avoid the embarrassment that arises when her reputation is concerned. Delay in every case cannot be a ground for suspicion. It arouses suspicion only where it is unexplained. The reasons for the delay here are stated in paragraph 6.

11. **Ingredients of the offence.** In *Vidyadharan* (above) the Supreme Court also observed that, for the offence under section 354 of the Indian Penal Code, intention to outrage modesty is not the sole criterion, and that knowledge that the modesty of a woman is likely to be outraged is sufficient. The facts in paragraphs 3 to 5 disclose a cognizable offence under section 354 of the Indian Penal Code.

12. **Limitation.** The complainant states the following for the Magistrate's examination:
   (a) Section 468 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 [the corresponding provision of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita is section 514, whose text is not shown here] bars cognizance only for offences in the categories of sub-section (2): fine only (six months), imprisonment up to one year (one year), and imprisonment above one year up to three years (three years).
   (b) It is submitted that the offence under section 354 of the Indian Penal Code is punishable with imprisonment exceeding three years and so falls outside those categories. Limitation under that section is therefore not a bar to registration or investigation. [ADVOCATE TO VERIFY THE PUNISHMENT PRESCRIBED AND THE CORRESPONDING BNSS PROVISION BEFORE FILING.]
   (c) Any question of cognizance is for the Magistrate after the police report. It is no ground to refuse to register the information.

---

**V. PRAYER**

It is respectfully prayed that the Station House Officer may:
(a) register the First Information Report under section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 for the offence under section 354 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 [section 74 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023] and any other offence disclosed;
(b) have the complainant's information recorded by a woman police officer and provide her a free copy;
(c) investigate under section 176 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, recording the statements of the complainant and the witnesses and, if required, arranging her medical examination;
(d) send the report required by section 176(1) to the jurisdictional Magistrate and take the lawful steps to arrest the accused and complete the investigation; and
(e) pass any other order deemed fit.

---

**VI. ANNEXURES**

- Annexure A-2: [MEDICAL RECORDS, IF ANY]
- Annexure A-3: [MESSAGES, PHOTOGRAPHS, OR OTHER DOCUMENTS, IF ANY]

---

Ranjini v. State of Tamilnadu, WP/1812/2015, Madras High Court (2017)).

7. The facts above disclose a cognizable offence. Section 154(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure requires every information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence, if given to the officer in charge of a police station, to be reduced to writing, signed by the informant and entered in the prescribed book.

8. Section 75(1) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 provides that a man who commits any of the following acts is guilty of sexual harassment: (i) physical contact and advances involving unwelcome and explicit sexual overtures; (ii) a demand or request for sexual favours; (iii) showing pornography against the will of a woman; or (iv) making sexually coloured remarks.

10. Under section 75(2), an offence under clause (i), (ii) or (iii) is punishable with rigorous imprisonment which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. Under section 75(3), an offence under clause (iv) is punishable with imprisonment of either description which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both.

11. **Clause(s) attracted:** [CLAUSE(S) OF SECTION 75(1) ATTRACTED, TO BE FILLED FROM PARAGRAPH 5].

---

**IV. WHICH CODE APPLIES, AND WHY**

12. **Penal code.** The conduct began on 15 June 2024, before 1 July 2024, and continued until 5 July 2024, after that date. The complainant's case is that this was one continuing course of sexual harassment directed at her in the same workplace. It was one undivided course of conduct, and it was still being committed after 1 July 2024. It is therefore charged **once**, under **section 75 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023**, and is not split by date into an IPC charge and a BNS charge. Section 9(1) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita permits one punishment for an offence made up of parts. Section 1(3) of the Sanhita makes the Sanhita govern liability for an offence still being committed after its commencement. The Indian Penal Code provision of which section 75 is the successor is cited only as its equivalent: [SECTION 354A OF THE INDIAN PENAL CODE, 1860].

13. **Alternative.** If the investigation finds that the conduct consisted of separate acts, each complete when done, each act must be charged under the code in force on the day it was done. Acts on or before 30 June 2024 would then attract the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (section 358(2)(c) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita saves it for them). Acts on or after 1 July 2024 would attract section 75 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita. The complainant therefore asks that the investigation record the date of each overt act (paragraph 5) so that the charge can be framed correctly. Article 20(1) of the Constitution protects the accused from conviction for any act that was not an offence under the law in force when it was done, and from a penalty greater than that then provided. See Directorate of Revenue Intelligence v. Raj Kumar Arora & Ors. (Supreme Court of India, 2025) 4 S.C.R. 960, which applies Article 20(1) and, following Soni Devrajbhai Babubhai v. State of Gujarat (1991) 4 SCC 298, holds that an accused cannot be tried under a new, more stringent offence for an act done before it came into force. [Authority on continuing offences to be added separately.]

14. The proceeding was begun on 10 July 2024, after 1 July 2024. 8. The offence alleged is kidnapping from lawful guardianship. Section 137(1)(b) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) defines it as taking or enticing any child out of the keeping of the lawful guardian, without the guardian's consent. The Explanation to the clause includes within "lawful guardian" any person lawfully entrusted with the care or custody of the child. Section 137(2) BNS provides imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and also liability to fine. Its equivalent is section 363 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC), which provides the same punishment.

9. **Which code applies, and why.** The code follows the nature of the offence. The statutory act of kidnapping from lawful guardianship is the taking or enticing of the child. It is complete when the child is taken or enticed, and it is not an offence that continues from day to day. [AUTHORITY TO BE ADDED.] The alleged cruelty is not an ingredient of section 137(1)(b) BNS or section 363 IPC. Because the offence is complete on the taking, the date of the taking decides the code, and the later course of conduct does not change it.

10. The conduct is alleged to have begun on 10 January 2023, before 1 July 2024. If the taking or enticing occurred before 1 July 2024, the accused is to be charged under **section 363 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860** [equivalent: section 137(2) BNS], which section 358(2)(c) BNS saves. The date of the taking is not yet pleaded, so it is left open here: [DATE OF THE TAKING — BEFORE 1 JULY 2024: SECTION 363 IPC; ON OR AFTER 1 JULY 2024: SECTION 137(2) BNS].

11. If the facts show that a distinct act, complete in itself, was done on or after 1 July 2024, it is a separate offence. It is to be charged under the BNS provision applicable to it: [SECTION OF BNS, TO BE IDENTIFIED ON THE PARTICULARS OF THE ALLEGED CRUELTY OR OTHER ACT]. No such section is named here because the request does not describe the act.

12. The advocate should note that if the complainant's case is that the taking or the restraint is itself a single continuing offence, it would have to be charged once, under the BNS, with the IPC section named only as its equivalent (sections 1(3) and 9(1) BNS; section 518 BNSS). This draft does not adopt that view, for the reasons in paragraph 9.

The case is therefore to be registered and investigated under the **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023**, and the evidence in it is governed by the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023.

Under section 176(1), an officer in charge of a police station who has reason to suspect the commission of an offence he is empowered to investigate under section 175 must forthwith send a report to the Magistrate empowered to take cognizance. He must then proceed in person, or depute a subordinate officer, to the spot to investigate the facts and circumstances and, if necessary, to take measures for the discovery and arrest of the offender. Section 176(3) also applies to offences punishable with seven years or more, from the date notified by the State Government, and so applies to this offence, which is punishable with up to seven years.

Sir/Madam,

**I. FACTS**

1. The Complainant is an adult woman residing at the address above. The Accused is [RELATIONSHIP OR ACQUAINTANCE OF THE ACCUSED WITH THE COMPLAINANT, IF ANY].

2. Between 15 June 2024 and 5 July 2024 the Accused committed rape upon the Complainant. The conduct complained of ran from 15 June 2024 to 5 July 2024, and so began before 1 July 2024 and continued after it.

3. The particulars of the acts are as follows. The Complainant will supply each, and the officer recording the information is requested to enter them in the Complainant's own words:
   (a) Act 1: date [DATE], place [PLACE], manner [DESCRIPTION OF THE ACT AND OF ABSENCE OF CONSENT / COERCION, AS GIVEN BY THE COMPLAINANT].
   (b) Act 2: date [DATE], place [PLACE], manner [DESCRIPTION].
   (c) [FURTHER ACTS, EACH WITH DATE, PLACE AND MANNER].
   (d) The last act complained of was on or about 5 July 2024 at [PLACE].

4. The acts are listed separately and dated so that each can be placed before or after 1 July 2024. The Complainant relies on every act so listed.

5. The Complainant approached the police on 10 July 2024. The reason for the interval between the last act and this complaint is [REASON FOR ANY DELAY, AS GIVEN BY THE COMPLAINANT].

6. [DETAILS OF ANY WITNESS, MEDICAL EXAMINATION, MESSAGES, CALL RECORDS, PHOTOGRAPHS OR OTHER MATERIAL, IF ANY].

**II. THE PENAL PROVISION UNDER WHICH THE ACCUSED IS TO BE CHARGED**

7. Rape is complete on each act of penetration or other act that constitutes the offence. It is not an offence that merely continues. Each act of 15 June 2024 to 5 July 2024 is therefore a separate offence, complete when done. The Complainant's case is not that one single offence ran continuously across the period. The charge cannot be fixed until it is known which dated acts the Complainant relies on, and paragraph 3 supplies them.

8. Each offence is charged under the penal code in force on the day it was committed (section 358 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 saves the Indian Penal Code, 1860 for offences before 1 July 2024):
   (a) **Each act on or before 30 June 2024:** section 376(1) of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, read with section 375 [now section 64(1), read with section 63, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023]. The punishment is rigorous imprisonment of either description for not less than ten years, which may extend to imprisonment for life, and fine.
   (b) **Each act on or after 1 July 2024 (including that of on or about 5 July 2024):** section 64(1) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, read with section 63. The punishment is rigorous imprisonment of either description for not less than ten years, which may extend to imprisonment for life, and fine.
   (c) **Aggravated form:** section 64(2)(m) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 applies where a person "commits rape repeatedly on the same woman". The punishment is rigorous imprisonment for not less than ten years, which may extend to imprisonment for the remainder of the person's natural life, and fine. If the investigation shows that the acts were repeated on the Complainant, the Complainant requests that this provision be invoked for the acts on or after 1 July 2024. The acts before that date are charged under the Indian Penal Code, 1860, and are not merged into a charge under the Sanhita. [SUBSECTION (2) CLAUSES (a) TO (l) TO BE ADDED ONLY IF THE FACTS OF THE RELATIONSHIP OR CIRCUMSTANCES SUPPORT THEM: TO BE CONFIRMED FROM THE COMPLAINANT'S ACCOUNT.]

9. If the investigation instead shows that the conduct was one continuing course of conduct and not separate acts, the whole of it should be charged once. It would then be charged under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (section 1(3) and section 9(1)), since it was still being committed after 1 July 2024. That does not suit rape, which is complete with each act, and it is not the Complainant's case.

**III. THE PROCEDURE UNDER WHICH THE CASE IS TO BE REGISTERED AND INVESTIGATED**

10. This information was given on 10 July 2024. No investigation, inquiry or trial on it was pending immediately before 1 July 2024. Section 531(2)(a) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 therefore does not save the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, and the date of the offence does not enter that test. The FIR must be registered under **section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023** [section 154, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973]. It must be investigated under **section 176 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023** [section 157, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973]. Evidence will follow the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023. This applies even to the acts of 15 June 2024 to 30 June 2024.

11. Under the first proviso to section 176(1) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, in relation to an offence of rape the recording of the victim's statement shall be conducted at the residence of the victim or in the place of her choice. As far as practicable it shall be recorded by a woman police officer, in the presence of her parents or guardian or near relatives or a social worker of the locality. It may also be recorded through audio-video electronic means, including a mobile phone. The Complainant requests that her statement be recorded accordingly. Information given by a woman about rape is to be recorded by a woman police officer or woman officer (see the proviso to the repealed section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973). The Complainant requests the same course.

12. Section 176(3) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 provides that on every information of an offence punishable with seven years or more, the officer in charge shall, from the date notified by the State Government, cause a forensic expert to visit the crime scene and cause videography of the process. The Complainant requests compliance to the extent the State's notification applies.

**IV. PRAYER**

The Complainant prays that the Station House Officer may be pleased to:
(a) register an FIR on this complaint under section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 for the offences described in paragraph 8, and give the Complainant a free copy of it;
(b) investigate under section 176 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, and record the Complainant's statement as requested in paragraph 11;
(c) arrange her medical examination and the collection and preservation of the evidence; and
(d) take all other steps the law requires, including the arrest of the Accused.

**V. DECLARATION**

I declare that the facts stated above are true to my knowledge and belief and that nothing material has been concealed.

Place: [PLACE]  Date: 10 July 2024

(Signature / thumb impression of the Complainant)
[NAME OF THE COMPLAINANT]

[Advocate's signature block, if the complaint is filed through counsel: NAME, ENROLMENT NO., ADDRESS]
