comparative_analysis.agreements_between_courts: Davinder Singh [2] and Dharmendra Kumar [1] agree that Scheduled Castes are not beyond sub-classification. [1] describes the class as heterogeneous and relies on Constitution Bench interpretation of Articles 15 and 16. All sources agree that SC/ST and OBC are constitutionally distinct categories.
comparative_analysis.conflicts_or_differences: The Bombay High Court passages in [3], [4] and [5] (2019) hold that Scheduled Castes form a class by themselves and cannot be sub-classified, reading Indra Sawhney as excluding SC/ST from sub-division. Davinder Singh [2] rejects that reading of Indra Sawhney. As a Constitution Bench ruling it prevails under Article 141, and the 2019 High Court view cannot be relied on as good law to the extent of the conflict. Whether Davinder Singh also overruled E.V. Chinnaiah is not stated in the excerpt.
comparative_analysis.trend_analysis: The law has moved from treating Scheduled Castes as an indivisible Presidential List class to permitting sub-classification where constituent groups are not comparably placed. This follows the substantive equality rationale in [2]. A 2025 Bombay High Court Division Bench [1] describes the class as heterogeneous, consistent with that shift.

answer.conclusion: The governing authority is the Constitution Bench in State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh [2], which in the excerpted passages rejects the argument that sub-classification cannot apply to Scheduled Castes and makes it available where constituents are not comparably placed. The older Bombay High Court view that Scheduled Castes form an indivisible class [3][4][5] conflicts with it and should not be relied on. The sources do not show how [2] resolved the Article 341 deeming fiction, its majority and separate opinions, the Chinnaiah question, or any conditions on State action. Before citing it, obtain the certified copy of the full judgment and the official report, confirm the operative conclusions and any later treatment, and cite the High Court passages only as contrary history.
answer.issue: Whether Scheduled Castes constitute a homogeneous, integrated class under Article 341 that cannot be sub-classified for reservation under Articles 14, 15(4) and 16(4), and what authority governs that question today.

precedents.case_name: The State of Punjab & Ors. v. Davinder Singh & Ors.
precedents.holding_summary: The excerpted passages reject the view that Indra Sawhney's recognition of sub-classification was confined to OBCs to the exclusion of Scheduled Castes. They state that sub-classification applies to Scheduled Castes where the social positions of constituent castes or groups are not comparable. They then take up whether the Article 341 deeming fiction creates an integrated homogeneous class that cannot be further classified. The excerpt breaks off at the discussion of Chinnaiah, so the final answer on the deeming fiction, the opinions, the majority and any directions are not in the sources.

precedents.case_name: Dharmendra Kumar v. Union of India, Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions (WP/1834/2024)
precedents.holding_summary: The excerpt notes that sub-classification of Scheduled Castes was upheld as permissible under Articles 15(4) and 16(4), describing the class as heterogeneous. It treats SC/ST as a class distinct from OBC, so that differing criteria (such as unlimited attempts for SC/ST in the Civil Services Examination) are not arbitrary. The question here was attempts under the Civil Services Examination Rules, not SC sub-classification, so the SC observations are secondary to its ratio. It also relies on Union of India v. M. Selvakumar (2017) 3 SCC 504, which I have not independently verified.

precedents.case_name: Ketan Tirodkar v. State of Maharashtra (PIL/140/2014)
precedents.holding_summary: The excerpt records a view that Scheduled Castes form a class by themselves, that further sub-classification is impermissible, and that Indra Sawhney's OBC sub-classification cannot be applied to the Presidential List. It then notes Atyant Pichhara Barg Chhatra Sangh v. Jharkhand State Vaishya Federation (2006) 6 SCC 718 on backward and more backward classes. The same text also appears in [4] and [5] under different case titles and numbers, so attribution to a particular matter is uncertain. This view runs contrary to Davinder Singh [2].

precedents.case_name: Ketan Tirodkar v. State of Maharashtra (CAI/68/2019)
precedents.holding_summary: Identical text to [3]. It reflects the pre-Davinder Singh Bombay High Court position that Scheduled Castes cannot be sub-classified.

precedents.case_name: Prof. Dr. S.M. Dahiwale v. Save Democracy Foundation and Ors. (CAI/45/2017)
precedents.holding_summary: Identical text to [3] and [4]. This is a repetition of the same passages and not independent authority.

answer.reasoned_analysis: ISSUE: The proposition that Scheduled Castes are a homogeneous class incapable of sub-classification is the position associated with the Article 341 deeming fiction and with E.V. Chinnaiah. The question is whether it survives. LAW: Article 341(1) lets the President specify castes, races or tribes, which are deemed Scheduled Castes, and Article 366(24) defines the class by that deeming. Articles 14, 15(4) and 16(4) govern classification and affirmative action. COURT POSITION: In Davinder Singh [2], the Constitution Bench excerpt states that a nine-Judge Bench has already extended sub-classification to beneficiary classes under Articles 15 and 16. It says it does not find that the observations in Indra Sawhney on sub-classification were meant to limit the principle to OBCs to the exclusion of Scheduled Castes. It adds that the principle applies to Scheduled Castes if the social positions of the constituents are not comparable. It acknowledges that OBCs and Scheduled Castes differ, because Scheduled Castes suffer a common form of backwardness through untouchability, which is why the Constitution groups them separately. It then identifies the deeming fiction as the remaining question and begins examining Chinnaiah, where the opinions of Justice Santosh Hegde and Justice Sema had treated Scheduled Castes as acquiring a new status by Presidential notification. The excerpt ends there. I therefore cannot state from these sources how the Bench resolved the deeming-fiction argument, who wrote for the majority, whether there were dissents, or what limits or conditions it imposed. The High Court material is secondary. The 2019 Bombay passages [3][4][5] adopt the homogeneous-class view and are contrary to [2]. They also appear in three differently titled matters, so they should not be cited as three authorities. Dharmendra Kumar [1] (2025) describes the class as heterogeneous, but its issue was examination attempts, so its observations on sub-classification are not its ratio. APPLICATION: An advocate resisting sub-classification can no longer argue homogeneity as an absolute bar. The opposing position will rest on [2]. The remaining arguments are that the deeming fiction preserves the Presidential List, that groups within it must genuinely be non-comparable, and that the state must justify any sub-classification. The excerpt does not record the evidentiary standard required. RISKS: The summary of [2] is from excerpts only. Any later treatment, review or reference of [2] has not been checked, nor has the effect of the Act or notification being challenged. COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The respondent in a challenge will say the Constitution itself keeps the list out of State interference, as [3] reasons, and that only Parliament can alter it under Article 341(2). The answer is that sub-classification for reservation does not alter the list, a point I cannot confirm from the excerpt. ADVICE: Obtain the certified copy of the full judgment and confirm the operative conclusions before relying on it.

relevant_law.summary: Article 14 permits reasonable classification (intelligible differentia with rational nexus). Articles 15(4) and 16(4) are the enabling sources of affirmative action for backward classes, including Scheduled Castes. They are the provisions through which any sub-classification of Scheduled Castes would be defended or attacked.

Article 341(1) empowers the President to specify castes, races, tribes or parts or groups within them, which are 'deemed' to be Scheduled Castes. Article 366(24) defines Scheduled Castes by reference to that deeming. The 'homogeneous class' argument rests on the deeming fiction, and Davinder Singh [2] examines it.

The law declared by the Supreme Court binds all courts. A Constitution Bench ruling in Davinder Singh [2] therefore displaces contrary High Court views, including the Bombay High Court passages in the sources.

comparative_analysis.agreements_between_courts: The Andhra Pradesh High Court in Ivax Paper Chemicals [9] follows the Constitution Bench and holds that stamping objections are not for the Section 8 or 11 court. All the sources agree that Section 35 bars admission and acting upon the instrument until duty and penalty are paid, and that the defect is curable.
comparative_analysis.conflicts_or_differences: Before 2023 there was a conflict between SMS Tea Estates, Garware and the Karnataka High Court extract [6] (an unstamped arbitration clause does not exist or cannot be acted upon) and N.N. Global [5] (the same result, but reasoned on Section 35). The Constitution Bench in Interplay [7][9] resolved the position by holding that the defect is curable and the instrument is not void. The Karnataka High Court extract [6] pre-dates or ignores that resolution.
comparative_analysis.trend_analysis: The law has moved from treating the stamping defect as going to the existence of the arbitration agreement towards treating it as an inadmissibility defect that is curable and decided by the Tribunal. This accords with minimal judicial intervention at the referral stage (Section 11(6A), as discussed in [5]). The proposition in the query is no longer good law.

answer.conclusion:
The proposition that an arbitration agreement in an unstamped instrument is void and unenforceable is no longer the law. The Constitution Bench in Interplay [7] holds that such an instrument is inadmissible under Section 35 but not void, that the defect is curable, and that the objection is for the Arbitral Tribunal rather than the Section 8 or 11 court [9]. SMS Tea Estates, Garware paras 22 and 29 and N.N. Global (2) are overruled. If you act for the party resisting arbitration, you will have to distinguish this decision. If you act for the party seeking reference, rely on it and prepare to cure the stamping defect. Before filing, check the full text of para 235 of Interplay in the official report, whether the 2021 N.N. Global decision [5] is the one overruled, and any later treatment.

answer.issue: Whether an arbitration agreement contained in an unstamped or insufficiently stamped instrument is void and unenforceable, or whether that proposition has been displaced by the Constitution Bench decision on the interplay between the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 and the Indian Stamp Act, 1899.

precedents.case_name: In Re: Interplay between Arbitration Agreements under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996 and the Indian Stamp Act 1899
precedents.holding_summary: As reproduced in [9], unstamped or inadequately stamped agreements are inadmissible under Section 35 but are not void, void ab initio or unenforceable. The defect is curable, and the stamping objection is not for determination under Sections 8 or 11, where the court examines only whether the arbitration agreement prima facie exists. Stamping objections fall to the Arbitral Tribunal, and N.N. Global (2), SMS Tea Estates and paras 22 and 29 of Garware Wall Ropes are overruled. [7] confirms the Bench and its identification of the earlier conflicting line.

answer.reasoned_analysis:
STATUTORY PRECEDENCE (NON-OBSTANTE ANALYSIS)

Prevailing provision: s. 3, The Indian Stamp Act, 1899
Yields:               s. 3, The Indian Stamp Act, 1899
Rule applied:         subordination
Reasoning:            s. 3, The Indian Stamp Act, 1899 is expressed as subject to other provisions, which is the converse of an overriding clause. It yields.
Authority:
  - Ashok Leyland Ltd v State of Tamil Nadu, (2004) 3 SCC 1

Verify the current commencement and amendment status of every provision named above before relying on this precedence in a filing.

ISSUE: The query proceeds on the premise that an arbitration agreement in an unstamped instrument is void and unenforceable. On the sources, that premise has been rejected by the Constitution Bench, and an advocate relying on it before the Supreme Court would be citing overruled law.

LAW: Section 7 of the Arbitration Act requires only a written agreement to arbitrate [1]. Section 35 of the Stamp Act bars admission in evidence of, and acting upon, a chargeable instrument that is not duly stamped, but its proviso permits admission on payment of the duty and penalty [4]. Section 33 imposes the impounding duty [3]. Section 3 is the charging provision, and on the precedence analysis it is expressed as subject to other provisions and yields [2]. Nothing in the extracted text of these sections declares an unstamped instrument void.

COURT POSITION: The older line (SMS Tea Estates, Garware paras 22 and 29, and N.N. Global [5]) held that the arbitration clause could not be acted upon, or did not exist in law, until the instrument was stamped [5][7]. The Constitution Bench in Interplay [7] reconsidered that line. As reproduced in [9], at para 235 it held that: (i) such agreements are inadmissible under Section 35 but are not void, void ab initio or unenforceable; (ii) the defect is curable; (iii) the objection does not fall for determination under Sections 8 or 11, where the court examines only prima facie existence of the arbitration agreement; (iv) the objection is for the Arbitral Tribunal; and (v) N.N. Global (2), SMS Tea Estates and Garware paras 22 and 29 are overruled. A five-Judge Bench decision binds Benches of lesser strength under Article 141 (well-established constitutional authority; verify against the official report). The Andhra Pradesh High Court has applied it [9]. The Karnataka High Court extract [6] follows the old line and appears not to have considered the Constitution Bench.

APPLICATION: In a Section 8 or 11 application, the stamping objection cannot be a ground to refuse reference. The court looks only at prima facie existence. The Tribunal will deal with the stamping objection, and the instrument cannot be relied on as evidence until duty and penalty are paid and the Section 33 and 35 process is followed.

COUNTER-ARGUMENT AND RISKS: A party seeking to resist arbitration would say that Section 35 still bars the instrument from being acted upon, and would cite [5] and [6]. The answer is that [5] stands overruled to the extent described in [7] and [9], and [6] does not consider that decision. A genuine risk is that the extracts of Interplay in the sources are secondary, via [7] and [9], and the extent of overruling of the 2021 decision [5] is unclear because the sources cite a differently reported 'N.N. Global (2)'. Whether any later larger Bench or a review has qualified Interplay is not addressed by the authorities cited here. Practically, the advocate should argue that the defect is curable and for the Tribunal, and should be ready to pay duty and penalty to avoid inadmissibility at trial.

relevant_law.summary: Defines an arbitration agreement as an agreement to submit disputes to arbitration, which may be a clause in a contract or a separate agreement, and which must be in writing [1]. The question is whether stamping affects the existence of that agreement for Sections 8 and 11 purposes.

An instrument chargeable with duty is not to be admitted in evidence for any purpose or acted upon unless duly stamped, but the proviso allows admission on payment of the duty and penalty [4]. The bar is therefore one of admissibility and is curable.
Imposes a duty on every person authorised to receive evidence to impound an instrument that appears not to be duly stamped [3]. This is the mechanism through which the defect is cured.

Makes the listed instruments chargeable with duty, but opens with 'Subject to the provisions of this Act and the exemptions' [2]. On the precedence analysis supplied, Section 3 is expressed as subject to other provisions and therefore yields. It is the charging provision and does not itself declare an unstamped instrument void.

comparative_analysis.agreements_between_courts: Islamic Academy [1], Indian School, Jodhpur [3] (relying on T.M.A. Pai and Modern Dental College), Jain Heritage [2] and the Telangana decisions [4][5] all agree on two points. Private unaided institutions may charge fees and have real autonomy, and the State may legitimately stop capitation fee and profiteering.
comparative_analysis.conflicts_or_differences: The sources diverge on how far regulation may go. Jain Heritage [2] places private unaided schools wholly outside fee-regulating provisions of the Karnataka Act. The Telangana decisions [4][5] uphold a government-fixed fee for professional colleges through a committee. Indian School [3] says that regulation at the initial stage is permissible. These are reconcilable only by distinguishing school from professional education, and none of the sources decides that point expressly. The sources also do not show how Islamic Academy's own directions (fee committees, quotas) later fared in P.A. Inamdar.
comparative_analysis.trend_analysis: The trend runs from the Unni Krishnan nationalising scheme, to its rejection, to a settled middle position. Autonomy is the rule, with regulation confined to preventing capitation fee and commercialisation. Seat-sharing is not addressed in the supplied extracts.

answer.conclusion: On the sources, the position is that State schemes which take over fee-fixing and admissions in private unaided institutions are unconstitutional (Islamic Academy [1], citing the rejection of Unni Krishnan). Regulation to prevent capitation fee and profiteering remains valid, including initial-stage fee regulation (Indian School, Jodhpur [3]). If you appear for the institution, press autonomy and show the scheme overrides cost and surplus considerations. If you appear for the State, frame it as anti-profiteering regulation with a cost-based fee committee. Before filing, obtain the certified copies of T.M.A. Pai, Islamic Academy, P.A. Inamdar and Modern Dental College and check the operative directions and the position on seat-sharing quotas, which none of the supplied extracts decides. Also confirm the later treatment of each judgment and the applicable State statute.
answer.issue: Whether, and to what extent, the State may impose a scheme of fee regulation and seat sharing (a fixed quota of seats surrendered to the State) on private unaided educational institutions, in light of Article 19(1)(g) and Article 30(1), and what the present governing authority is.

answer.reasoned_analysis: ISSUE: The question is whether a State may impose a fee-regulation and seat-sharing scheme on private unaided institutions. LAW: Article 19(1)(g) protects the institution's occupation, subject to reasonable restrictions under Article 19(6). Article 30(1) adds protection for minority institutions and secures parity with other institutions. COURT POSITION: Islamic Academy [1] is the strongest authority in the sources on the Unni Krishnan scheme. The extract records that the scheme nationalised education in its important features, namely the right to admit and to fix fees, and was therefore unconstitutional. Its ratio, on the extract, is that a scheme which makes private unaided institutions indistinguishable from government institutions is neither fair nor reasonable. Paras 138-139 are quoted from T.M.A. Pai. Unaided institutions are assured maximum autonomy in fees and admissions, subject to recognition conditions that cannot whittle down Article 30. I treat the extract as stating the Court's position on autonomy. The operative directions of Islamic Academy are not in the extract and must be checked. Indian School, Jodhpur [3] is a Division Bench ruling, but it expressly relies on the Constitution Bench in Modern Dental College for the proposition that commercialisation is impermissible. The Government may regulate fees at the initial stage and may direct reduction of excessive fees. The extracted passages show it permitting passive euthanasia, laying down guidelines until Parliament legislates, and requiring High Court approval before life support is withdrawn from an incompetent patient (paras 126-127). The passage mentioning Gian Kaur (para 30 in the extract) appears among reasoning drawn from English authority and counsel's submissions. It records that Gian Kaur held no right to die exists under Art 21, yet a dying person may be permitted to terminate life without crime. From the extract alone I cannot say this is the Court's own holding, so please check the full report before attributing it.

Common Cause [2] is a Constitution Bench. A concurring passage states that Gian Kaur does not conclusively rule on passive euthanasia, that Aruna Shanbaug proceeds on an incorrect perception of Gian Kaur, that its act-omission reasoning is flawed, and that its underlying basis is flawed. The headnote passage adds that Gian Kaur does not lay down that passive euthanasia could be made lawful only by legislation. The sources carry a caution that these passages are not confirmed as the majority opinion, so attribute each to the opinion it came from. Common Cause [2] nonetheless upheld passive euthanasia and advance directives on Art 21 (liberty, dignity, autonomy, privacy), issuing directions under Art 142.

If you assert that Gian Kaur approved passive euthanasia and cite Aruna Shanbaug [1] for it, opposing counsel or the Bench will point to Common Cause [2] as having disapproved that reading. Candour requires you to cite Common Cause [2] yourself.

(3) Gian Kaur at most establishes that there is no right to die under Art 21 and does not foreclose passive euthanasia; this is the formulation in Common Cause [2]. That argument can be defeated only by not advancing the proposition. Pramendra Dobal [3] is merely a High Court recital and gives no help on this point. LAW: Section 7 of the Arbitration Act [1] defines and requires writing for an arbitration agreement, and nothing in it ties validity to stamping. Section 3 of the Stamp Act [2] is the charging section. Section 33 [3] imposes the impounding duty. Section 35 [4] makes an instrument inadmissible and not to be acted upon unless duly stamped, but its proviso allows admission on payment of duty and penalty. The statute, on its text, creates a curable evidentiary bar and does not say that the instrument or its arbitration clause is void.

COURT POSITION: The 2021 passage [5] reproduces the reasoning in SMS Tea Estates: because of s. 35, the court cannot act upon the arbitration clause within an unstamped instrument, and s. 35 has no collateral-purpose proviso like s. 49 of the Registration Act. That reasoning is the high-water mark of your proposition. Even there, the language is that the court cannot act upon the document until duty and penalty are paid; it is not a holding that the agreement is void. The extract also notes the effect of s. 11(6A) and Duro Felguera on the scope of s. 11. The Andhra Pradesh High Court [6] quotes para 235 of the Constitution Bench decision in the Interplay reference: unstamped agreements are inadmissible but not void, void ab initio or unenforceable (235.1); the defect is curable (235.2); stamping objections do not arise under ss. 8 or 11 (235.3); they belong to the Tribunal (235.4); and N.N. Global (2), SMS Tea Estates, and paras 22 and 29 of Garware are overruled (235.5). The Delhi High Court is bound by that decision under Art 141 (well-established constitutional authority; verify against the official report). The Delhi decision in Ahluwalia Contracts [7] deals with the MSMED Act and is of no assistance.

APPLICATION: A submission that the agreement is void and unenforceable would run directly against 235.1, and a submission that the court should refuse to refer or act on the clause would run against 235.3 and 235.5. Citing N.N. Global (2) as a live authority would be citing an overruled decision. If you act for the party resisting arbitration, the opposing side will cite the Constitution Bench decision at once.

COUNTER-ARGUMENT AND LIMITS: The strongest opposing case is that para 235 disposes of the point entirely. What could be left to you is narrow: (i) inadmissibility under s. 35 survives, so the instrument cannot be relied on in evidence until duty and penalty are paid; (ii) the stamping objection must be raised before the Tribunal, which is a forum for it and not a way to avoid it; and (iii) whether the instrument is chargeable at all, or whether any ground other than stamping defeats the arbitration agreement under s. 7. None of the sources decides how a Delhi High Court bench is applying the Constitution Bench ruling, and I cannot confirm from them whether it has been reviewed or modified since.

PRACTICAL ADVICE: Do not advance the voidness proposition. Obtain the Constitution Bench judgment from the official report and confirm that para 235 reads as quoted in [6] before you rely on it.

Unni Krishnan [3] imposed a scheme on affiliating authorities to remove management discretion in admissions, whereas the passage in Islamic Academy [1] records that the larger Bench in T.M.A. Pai held that scheme, and the directions to implement it, unconstitutional. On that Bench-strength and recency ranking, the Unni Krishnan scheme is not good law for private unaided institutions. The passage in [1] also records the overruling of the dictum that education is not an occupation under Art 19(1)(g). The sources do not show how far the Unni Krishnan reasoning on recognition and affiliation survives beyond that.

Modern School [2] frames the present question as a balance between autonomy and prevention of commercialisation, to be worked out through statute. Later treatment of these judgments has not been checked.

ISSUE: The instruction is to build submissions on Unni Krishnan for a scheme of fee regulation and seat sharing on private unaided institutions. That proposition cannot safely be put to the Delhi High Court as stated, and the submissions need to be re-framed. LAW: The Unni Krishnan headnote passages [3] record that the right to establish an institution does not include a right to recognition or affiliation. They also record that the recognising authority is the State, bound by Art 14 to impose conditions securing standards and fair, equal treatment in admissions, and that the Court framed a scheme to remove management discretion in admissions. COURT POSITION: Islamic Academy [1] records that T.M.A. Pai, a larger Bench, declared the scheme and the directions to implement it unconstitutional as to privately managed institutions. It also overruled the dictum that education is not an occupation under Art 19(1)(g), and held that institutions cannot be made to adopt the scheme as a condition of affiliation, since this destroys institutional autonomy. [AUTHORITY NOT CONFIRMED — no retrieved passage could be identified as the majority opinion of the Bench] It nonetheless preserved the bar on capitation fee and profiteering and the principle that merit governs professional admissions. Modern School [2] (headnote) treats fee autonomy as real but subject to a reasonable-surplus limit and to the Delhi School Education Act, 1973 and Rules. Those passages are not confirmed as the majority holding, and I attribute them only to the passages. APPLICATION: What can still be argued from Unni Krishnan [3] is limited to the following. (a) The State may attach conditions to recognition and affiliation that ensure standards and fairness. (b) Commercialisation is contrary to public policy. (c) Rights under Art 19(1)(g) are subject to Art 19(6). Fee regulation should be pursued through the Delhi School Education Act and Rules, in particular ss. 17(3) and 18 and Rules 172 to 177 considered in [2], and through the anti-profiteering principle preserved in [1]. Seat sharing as a compulsory scheme cannot be argued as binding law. If seat sharing is relied on, it should rest on T.M.A. Pai as summarised in [1], where a percentage may be fixed by Government according to local needs, but I have only a fragment of that passage and its application to schools is not shown. RISKS: The opposing side will say Unni Krishnan was overruled on the scheme, so reliance on it as authority for imposed fee and seat regulation risks being treated as citing overruled law, which is a serious credibility problem. Its strongest point is autonomy and the reasonable-surplus principle. Our answer is to cite Unni Krishnan only for the surviving propositions, and the statutory and anti-profiteering route. LIMITS: None of the sources decides the extent of Delhi's statutory power over fee fixation, the meaning of reasonable surplus in operation, or whether any other part of Unni Krishnan survives. answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The proposition that the Constitution contains no right to privacy is no longer tenable. The question is what authority displaces it and how far the right extends.

LAW AND COURT POSITION: The text of the Constitution does not name privacy. The 2015 reference order [1] records that it had been inferred from Article 21, and that M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh, read literally, would 'denude' Article 21 of vigour. The order stresses that smaller benches cannot ignore larger-bench pronouncements without giving reasons, and it identified an unresolved contradiction. For that reason it referred the matter to a larger bench. That order does not itself decide the question, and the advocate should not cite it for the right. The ratio is in Puttaswamy (2017) [2]. The headnote extracts show the Court rejecting the argument that recognising privacy needs a constitutional amendment. It held that the argument wrongly assumes privacy exists apart from the liberties in Part III. Privacy is an element of human dignity and is intrinsic to Article 21 and freedom and liberty. Common Cause (2018) [5] confirms that the nine-judge bench held privacy to be the constitutional core of human dignity and an intrinsic part of Article 21 protected under Part III.

SCOPE AND LIMITS: The right is not absolute. An invasion must pass three tests: legality (a law exists), need (a legitimate state aim) and proportionality (a rational nexus between object and means). Article 14 infuses Article 21, so the law must be fair, just and reasonable. Informational privacy is a recognised facet, and the Court noted that threats may come from non-State actors, leaving a data-protection regime to the Union Government. Common Cause [5] extends the right to bodily integrity and decisions at the end of life. Md. Majid Hussain [3] shows how a High Court balanced privacy against public interest and matrimonial exceptions, though it predates Puttaswamy and is only persuasive.

PRECEDENT WEIGHT: The Supreme Court's nine-judge bench binds the Delhi High Court under Article 141. Common Cause, a constitution bench, follows it. Bihar Public Service Commission [4], a division-bench ruling, yields to these authorities where they differ.

COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The State may say that privacy is qualified, and that the claimed intrusion is backed by statute, serves a legitimate aim and is proportionate, and that the right is not available against purely private conduct. The petitioner's answer is the three-fold test in [2], applied to the particular law. Note that the Supreme Court recognised non-State threats but left the remedy to a legislative regime, so a horizontal claim needs separate authority.

ISSUE: Whether an Article 368 amendment can be tested against Part III as 'law' under Article 13(2).

LAW: Article 13(2) restrains 'the State' from making 'law' abridging Part III rights, and Article 13(3)(a) defines 'law' without mentioning constitutional amendments [1]. Article 13(4), as set out in [1], provides that Article 13 does not apply to any amendment under Article 368. On the text, an amendment is outside Article 13.

COURT POSITION: Kesavananda Bharati [2] records that the amending power is a facet of the constituent power; that when Parliament amends the Constitution 'it is not legislating'; and that an amendment under Article 368 'is constituent law and not law within the meaning of Article 13(2) and law as defined in Article 13(3)(a)'. It also records that the 24th Amendment made explicit what was implicit and so changed nothing in the prior position, and that assimilating the procedure to ordinary legislation does not make the two powers the same. Because the extracts do not identify the opinions, I cannot say from the sources how many judges concurred on this point. The constitutional notes state that Golak Nath held otherwise and was overruled by Kesavananda. Both are from the notes and need verification.

APPLICATION: The proposition is therefore good law, but with an important qualification. An amendment is not 'law' under Article 13, so a challenge cannot be founded on Article 13(2) alone. The extracts in [2] also record that Parliament cannot make itself supreme sovereign by amendment and cannot damage or destroy the essential features of the Constitution. The constitutional notes identify this as the basic structure doctrine. A challenger must therefore plead breach of basic structure (for example Article 21, judicial review, or equality) and not simply Part III abridgement.

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The proposition that 'Section 309 IPC is unconstitutional' is not the present law as declared by the Supreme Court. The binding position is the opposite, and the advocate must plan accordingly.

LAW: IPC s. 309 [1] punished an attempt to commit suicide with simple imprisonment up to one year, or fine, or both. For offences committed on or after 1 July 2024 the BNS applies. BNS s. 226 does not replicate s. 309; it punishes only an attempt to commit suicide intended to compel or restrain a public servant in the discharge of official duty (simple imprisonment up to one year, or fine, or both, or community service). A bare attempt to commit suicide, without that intent, is therefore not an offence under the BNS text shown. For offences before 1 July 2024, IPC s. 309 is saved by BNS s. 358 and the charge lies under it. Because s. 226 narrows the offence, a different code applies depending on the date of the offence; confirm the date in your matter.

COURT POSITION: The Constitution Bench in Gian Kaur upheld ss. 306 and 309 IPC and held that Art. 21 does not include the right to die; suicide involves positive overt acts which cannot be traced to the protection of the right to life, and extinction of life cannot be read into 'protection of life'. Common Cause (2018) [3] paras 36-38 restates this: 'the legal position which stands as of today is that right to life does not include right to die'. The Law Commission [2] records that the Supreme Court rejected the Art. 14 challenge as well, reasoning that the sentence can be tailored and probation used. These are the ratio of Gian Kaur; the passages in Common Cause on s. 309 are a restatement by a Constitution Bench and, in that context, arguably obiter, but they are binding in effect under Art. 141. The Law Commission reports [2] [4] [5] are advisory, not law; they note that Gian Kaur dealt with constitutionality and not the wisdom of retaining s. 309.

APPLICATION: A direct constitutional attack on s. 309 before the Delhi High Court is foreclosed by Art. 141; a Division Bench cannot depart from a Constitution Bench. The attack on BNS s. 226 is a different proposition: it is a new provision, narrower, tied to coercion of a public servant, and Gian Kaur did not consider it. Arguments available: (i) the provision is not a restatement of s. 309, so the validity reasoning must be reapplied; (ii) overbreadth or vagueness of 'compel or restrain'; (iii) proportionality. Each is untested on the sources and carries real risk, since Gian Kaur's reasoning (no right to die; sentence tailoring) would be used to support s. 226, whose purpose, preventing coercion of public servants, is arguably stronger.

COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The State will say Gian Kaur is binding, the Law Commission recommendations are not law, and Parliament has already softened the position. What defeats the State is a showing that s. 226 raises a distinct question (e.g., expression or protest-related conduct under Art. 19(1)(a)), which none of the authorities cited here decides.

LIMITS: The full text of Gian Kaur, the Bombay High Court and P. Rathinam decisions, and any Delhi High Court authority on s. 226 are not among the sources.

ISSUE: The proposition that an arbitration agreement in an unstamped instrument is void and unenforceable is no longer the law. LAW: Section 7 of the Arbitration Act [1] requires the agreement to be in writing and says nothing about stamping. Under the Stamp Act, Section 35 [4] makes an unstamped chargeable instrument inadmissible and bars it from being acted upon, but its proviso allows admission on payment of duty and penalty. Section 33 [3] requires impounding by the person receiving evidence. Section 3 [2] is a charging provision that yields to the other provisions of the Act, so it cannot be read as declaring nullity. COURT POSITION: In re Interplay (2023) [6], a Constitution Bench, concluded at para 235 (as reproduced in Ivax [5]) that such agreements are inadmissible under Section 35 but are not void, void ab initio or unenforceable. Non-stamping is a curable defect. The objection does not fall for determination under Sections 8 or 11, where the court examines only whether the arbitration agreement prima facie exists, and stamping objections lie within the arbitral tribunal. N.N. Global (2) and SMS Tea Estates are overruled, and paras 22 and 29 of Garware are overruled to that extent. Para 209, extracted in Krish Spinning [7], adds that examination and impounding at the Section 8 or 11 stage is among the 'other issues' the referral court should not undertake, because impounding is not time-bound. Krish Spinning [7] confirms that the Section 11 enquiry is confined to prima facie existence. Ivax [5] applies Interplay and holds that the law as on the date of decision governs, so an order based on N.N. Global cannot stand. APPLICATION: In Delhi, if the opposing party relies on Garware, SMS Tea or N.N. Global (2), the answer is that these authorities are overruled and bind no court under Art 141. If the instrument is unstamped, the Section 8 or 11 court should refer or appoint without impounding. The stamping objection is then raised before the tribunal, where the party relying on the instrument can cure it by paying duty and penalty under the proviso to Section 35. COUNTER-ARGUMENT AND RISKS: The opposing side may argue that Section 35 bars the instrument from being 'acted upon', so the clause cannot be given effect. The answer is that Interplay treats inadmissibility as curable and assigns the question to the tribunal. The opponent may also invoke Vidya Drolia for wider referral-stage scrutiny, but Krish Spinning [7] doubts that scrutiny after Interplay. The extracts do not show whether Interplay has been the subject of later review or curative proceedings, and the instrument still needs to be stamped before it is relied on in evidence. Interplay concerns the arbitration agreement and the referral stage. The extracts do not address enforcement of an award founded on an instrument that remains unstamped, so that point needs separate verification.

relevant_law.summary: Defines an arbitration agreement as an agreement to submit defined disputes to arbitration, in the form of a clause or a separate agreement, and requires it to be in writing. The extract [1] contains no requirement of stamping. The question is therefore whether the Stamp Act supplies one.

Makes instruments listed in Schedule I chargeable with duty, subject to the Act and its exemptions. The precedence analysis treats Section 3 [2] as expressed to be subject to other provisions of the Act, so it yields to them. It is a charging provision and does not itself declare an unstamped instrument void.

Requires a person authorised to receive evidence to impound an instrument that appears not to be duly stamped [3]. In re Interplay (2023) [6] holds that examination and impounding by the referral court at the Section 8 or 11 stage is among the 'other issues' the court should not undertake.

An instrument chargeable with duty is inadmissible in evidence and cannot be acted upon unless duly stamped. The proviso allows admission on payment of the duty and penalty [4]. The consequence is inadmissibility, which is curable, not nullity.

answer.reasoned_analysis: ISSUE: The question has two limbs: (a) how far the State may regulate fees of private unaided institutions, and (b) how far it may impose a seat-sharing scheme. LAW: Both limbs sit within Article 19(1)(g)/19(6) and, for minorities, Article 30(1). COURT POSITION on fees: The sources are consistent. The passages from P.A. Inamdar quoted in the Delhi decisions [1] [3] state that the essence of a private unaided institution is autonomy, that fixing a rigid fee structure is unacceptable, and that the quantum of fee is an essential ingredient of management. The Delhi single-judge decision [1] (paras 129-132) synthesises the Supreme Court position: fee setting is a facet of the right to administer; reasonable surplus is permissible; profiteering and capitation fee are not; and the Government cannot fix a rigid fee structure. The constitution-bench-labelled Delhi decision [3] summarises the same limits. The Islamic Academy passage [4] states the Unni Krishnan scheme, which controlled admissions and fees, was rejected as nationalising education, and that minority and non-minority unaided institutions enjoy equal maximum autonomy; but the note on [4] warns that the passages are not confirmed as the majority opinion, so attribute them only to the passages. The Karnataka decision [2] applies the same principles to hold the State fee-regulation section inapplicable to unaided schools; it is persuasive only. SEAT-SHARING: None of the sources decides whether the State can compel unaided institutions to surrender seats. The passages in [4] speak of the Unni Krishnan scheme's control over admissions as unconstitutional, which suggests autonomy in admission, but this is by passage only and is not a holding on current quota schemes. From the constitutional notes (verify against official reports): Article 21A and the RTE Act 2009 s. 12 impose a 25 per cent EWS entry quota; Society for Unaided Private Schools of Rajasthan (2012), Pramati (2014; minority exemption) and Article 15(5) (93rd Amendment) bear on this. These cannot be extracted as reasoned holdings from the sources and must be read in full. APPLICATION AND COUNTER-ARGUMENT: A school resisting a fee-regulation order can argue that the order amounts to a rigid fee structure or demands accounts beyond what is needed to detect profiteering [1]. The Directorate's strongest answer is that the school's land was allotted on conditions, which [3] shows the Supreme Court directed the Directorate to examine, and that review for profiteering and capitation fee requires some scrutiny; that answer defeats a blanket autonomy argument where such conditions exist. For seat-sharing, the State will rely on Article 21A and statutory quotas; the school's argument depends on authority outside the sources. RISKS: [1] is a single-bench decision and [3] and [4] are extracts; [1] and [3] recite Supreme Court law by quotation, so verify against the Supreme Court reports. Later treatment of all these judgments has not been checked. PRACTICAL ADVICE: Frame fee arguments on the profiteering/capitation line and on land-allotment terms; for seat-sharing, obtain and analyse the Supreme Court decisions themselves.

Authority in the sources, led by In Re Article 370 (2023) [2], supports limited judicial review: a reasonable nexus with the object of the Proclamation, a prima facie showing of mala fides or extraneous exercise by the challenger, and then an onus on the Union. The non-justiciability passage reproduced in the Chhattisgarh decision [3] is likely a separate opinion in Bommai and should be treated cautiously. answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The proposition that the President's satisfaction under Article 356 is beyond judicial scrutiny is not the present law. The better statement is that the satisfaction is reviewable on a limited, deferential standard.

LAW: Article 356(1) rests on the President's satisfaction. Under Articles 74 and 75 and Samsher Singh [1][4], that satisfaction is the Council of Ministers', so it is an executive determination like any other.

COURT POSITION: First, the authority in the sources that squarely states the current standard is In Re Article 370 (2023) [2], a constitution bench. Per Chandrachud CJI (with Gavai and Surya Kant JJ.), the exercise of power after a proclamation under Article 356 is subject to judicial review, must have a reasonable nexus with the object of the Proclamation, and a challenger who prima facie shows mala fides or extraneous exercise shifts the onus to the Union to justify it. Kaul J. concurred and emphasised that emergency powers are bound by judicial and constitutional scrutiny; Khanna J. concurred. Second, the Constitution notes record that S.R. Bommai (1994) held President's Rule subject to judicial review, requiring relevant material and a floor test (verify against the official report). Third, the passage reproduced by the Chhattisgarh High Court [3], at paras 214 and 216 of a Supreme Court judgment, says the satisfaction is subjective and not justiciable on manageable standards. This is the source of the proposition in the query. However, the same extract is an outlier on the sources: the extract does not identify which opinion it is, and it cannot override the majority position in Bommai or the 2023 bench.

RANKING: Constitution bench authority (2023) [2] and the nine-judge Bommai outrank High Court judgments [3][4][5]. Where the Chhattisgarh extract conflicts, the Supreme Court's statement of reviewability prevails.

APPLICATION: For the Delhi High Court, the argument against the proposition is that (a) the satisfaction is that of the Council of Ministers, an executive act; (b) the court asks whether relevant material existed and whether there is a nexus with the Proclamation's object; (c) the petitioner must prima facie show mala fides or extraneous considerations, after which the Union must justify. Note that the 2023 holding is framed around power exercised after the Proclamation, so the Union may argue it does not extend to the initial satisfaction; the answer is Bommai, as recorded in the notes.

COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The Union will rely on the passage in [3] on political questions and subjective satisfaction, and on parliamentary approval of the Proclamation. That passage's own reasoning about parliamentary approval ('judicial review becomes unavailable') should be checked, since the extract is incomplete. A petitioner defeats it by citing the majority in Bommai and the 2023 bench.

LIMITS OF THE RECORD: The sources do not give paragraph references for Bommai's majority holding, nor identify the opinion in [3]. None of the sources applies the reviewability test to a specific factual proclamation. Bench, opinion and paragraph details must be verified from the certified official reports.

answer.reasoned_analysis: ISSUE: The advocate wants the settled position on quashing common entrance test notifications. [AUTHORITY NOT CONFIRMED — no retrieved passage could be identified as the majority opinion of the Bench] LAW: The forum is Article 226 of the Constitution before the Delhi High Court, and the grounds are the usual grounds of judicial review: arbitrariness under Art 14, lack of jurisdiction or statutory authority, breach of natural justice, and unreasonableness. Common Entrance Test only incidentally, because the headnote says admissions should have been routed through it. It is not a decision on quashing a notification. APPLICATION: Anyone relying on Andhra Kesari [1] can say only this. Courts will not use interim relief to override the educational authorities' compliance requirements, and the admission process should follow the prescribed common entrance route. comparative_analysis.agreements_between_courts: Sankari Prasad [2] holds that Article 13 'law' means ordinary legislative power, not constituent power. Article 13(4) [1] now states the same result in the text. Ashoka Kumar Thakur [3] and Manoj Narula [4] are consistent with this only to the limited extent that Article 13(2) is not the test applied to amendments.
comparative_analysis.conflicts_or_differences: The sources record that Golak Nath (1967) is 'referred to' in Ashoka Kumar Thakur [3] and the notes say it held Part III unamendable and was overruled by Kesavananda Bharati. The notes add that Sajjan Singh (1965) followed Sankari Prasad. None of the judgments supplied states the Golak Nath holding or the extent of the Kesavananda overruling, so verify these from the reports. Manoj Narula [4] recites Kesavananda opinions that amending power is limited by basic elements.
comparative_analysis.trend_analysis: The law moved from Sankari Prasad (amendments are outside Article 13) to Golak Nath (the contrary) to the position that amendments are outside Article 13 but subject to the basic structure limit (Kesavananda Bharati, per the notes and [3], [4]). Sankari Prasad survives only for the narrow Article 13 point, not as authority for unlimited amending power.

answer.conclusion:
Argue that Sankari Prasad [2], reinforced by Article 13(3)(a) and 13(4) [1], means an Article 368 amendment is not 'law' under Article 13(2), so a challenge founded only on Article 13 must fail. Concede candidly that this does not shield an amendment from basic structure review, as Ashoka Kumar Thakur [3] and Manoj Narula [4] show, and that Sankari Prasad was displaced on its wider reach by later larger benches. Before filing, verify from the official SCR report the bench composition, the exact passage and page numbers, and the AIR citation; confirm the Article 13(4) insertion history from the official text; and read Kesavananda Bharati and Golak Nath in the official reports to state the current rule accurately.

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: Your proposition is that a constitutional amendment is not 'law' under Article 13. It is sound but must be framed as a limited one.

LAW: Article 13(2) [1] restrains the State from making 'law' abridging Part III, and Article 13(3)(a) [1] defines 'law' by listing ordinary instruments (Ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom, usage) with no mention of amendments. Article 13(4) [1], on the text supplied, expressly excludes amendments under Article 368 from Article 13.

COURT POSITION: Sankari Prasad [2] is your anchor. The passage supplied records that 'law' in Article 13 means rules or regulations made in exercise of ordinary legislative power and not amendments made in exercise of constituent power, so Article 13(2) does not affect amendments under Article 368. The same passage held Articles 31A and 31B valid without ratification: they neither textually nor in effect altered Articles 226, 132 or 136; they removed a class of cases from Part III's purview, so the courts' powers were not curtailed.

SUBMISSIONS TO ADVANCE: (1) Textual: the Article 13(3)(a) definition [1] is of legislative and executive instruments, and amendment is absent. (2) Constituent versus ordinary power, as drawn in Sankari Prasad [2]. (3) Article 13(4) [1] now confirms the result, so the point is settled irrespective of how Sankari Prasad is viewed historically. (4) If the challenge to an amendment rests only on Article 13(2), it fails at the threshold. (5) Where the impugned amendment resembles Articles 31A/31B, argue that the High Court's Article 226 jurisdiction remains intact and the amendment merely narrows the substantive field, as the Court reasoned in [2].

RISKS AND COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The opposing side will say that Sankari Prasad is not the whole law. The notes record that Golak Nath (1967) departed from it and Kesavananda Bharati (1973) then settled that amendments are subject to the basic structure. Ashoka Kumar Thakur [3] tests the Ninety-Third Amendment against the basic structure, and Manoj Narula [4] quotes Sikri CJ, Shelat and Grover JJ that 'amendment' has a limited meaning. The Bombay High Court is bound under Article 141 by the later Supreme Court position, so you must not assert that amendments are immune from review. What defeats the counter-argument is limiting your claim: Article 13 is not the yardstick, and the challenger must instead establish violation of the basic structure, which is a heavier burden.

LIMITS OF THE RECORD: None of the sources supplied states the bench strength in Sankari Prasad, its AIR citation, or the full Golak Nath and Kesavananda holdings. Sajjan Singh and Golak Nath appear only in the notes (well-established constitutional authority; verify against the official report). The 1951 date in your query and the 1952 report year both appear in the sources, so cite the SCR report.

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The advocate proposes to rest on Naz Foundation (Delhi HC, 2009) for the proposition that a High Court may read down s. 377 IPC. The first point to make is that the brief as framed is defective. Naz Foundation was set aside by Koushal (2013) [2][3][4], so it is not good law as an authority. It can only be cited as reasoning that the Supreme Court adopted when it overruled Koushal in Navtej Singh Johar (2018), whose conclusions are quoted at [5]. Lead with Navtej Singh Johar and use Naz Foundation as background.

LAW: IPC s. 377 [1] criminalises carnal intercourse against the order of nature. Challenge lies under Articles 14, 15, 19 and 21, with Article 13 supplying voidness for pre-constitutional law and Article 226 supplying the forum.

COURT POSITION: Per the quoted conclusion at [5], s. 377 is violative of Articles 14, 15, 19 and 21 insofar as it criminalises consensual adult sexual acts in private, with free consent required. It continues for non-consensual acts, acts with minors and bestiality, and concluded prosecutions are not reopened but the ruling applies to pending matters. Koushal was overruled. Article 141 binds the Bombay High Court. Navtej Singh Johar is a Constitution Bench ruling and sits above the Delhi High Court and the Gujarat single-judge descriptions.

SUBMISSIONS TO ADVANCE: (1) The reading-down is binding law under Article 141, so the High Court need not itself exercise reading-down power; it applies the declaration. (2) If the facts involve consensual adult conduct in private, the proceeding is liable to be quashed because Navtej Singh Johar applies to pending trial, appellate and revisional stages [5]. The quashing route, the BNSS s. 528 petition (CrPC s. 482), should be pleaded. (3) The Delhi High Court's reasoning, that constitutional morality prevails over public morality [2], supports the same result and was endorsed in substance. (4) If the offence post-dates 1 July 2024, IPC s. 377 has no BNS equivalent, which strengthens the argument that no offence exists for consensual conduct.

RISKS: The State will argue that the declaration leaves s. 377 operative for non-consent, minors and bestiality, and that consent must be free of duress [5]. The record contains no client facts, so I cannot say whether these exceptions apply; the nature of the alleged act, the ages and the question of consent must be supplied. Any reliance on the Uttarakhand passage that consent is irrelevant [5] must be treated cautiously, since it predates the Navtej Singh Johar reading-down and the extent to which it survives is not settled by these sources. Do not cite the Gujarat decisions [2][3][4] for the validity of s. 377.

ADVICE: Cite Navtej Singh Johar from the official report, cite Naz Foundation only as the reasoning it adopted, and disclose Koushal's overruling candidly.

ISSUE: The instruction is to build a submission on N.N. Global 2, (2023) 7 SCC 1 for the proposition that an arbitration agreement in an unstamped instrument is void and unenforceable. That proposition is no longer good law. The 25 April 2023 decision was overruled by In Re: Interplay (13 December 2023), and it cannot be advanced as a current authority. [7][9]

LAW: Section 35 of the Stamp Act makes an unstamped chargeable instrument inadmissible and not to be acted upon, but its proviso permits admission on payment of duty and penalty. [3] Section 33 imposes the duty to impound. [2] Section 7 of the Arbitration Act contains no stamping requirement for an arbitration agreement. [4]

COURT POSITION: The 2023 majority held that the unstamped instrument is void under s. 2(g) of the Contract Act, that 'existence' under s. 11(6A) means existence in law, and that the s. 11 court must impound. [7] As quoted in the Andhra Pradesh High Court judgment, para 235 of In Re: Interplay holds that such agreements are inadmissible but are not void, void ab initio or unenforceable. It holds that the defect is curable, that stamping objections are not for ss. 8 or 11 but for the Arbitral Tribunal, and that N.N. Global (2) and SMS Tea Estates are overruled. [9] The Bombay High Court orders of 2023 in this very litigation are procedural, record payment of duty and penalty and appointment of an arbitrator, and do not help. [5][6]

APPLICATION: A submission that the agreement is void and unenforceable would contradict binding Constitution Bench law under Art. 141 (well-established constitutional authority; verify against the official report). Because In Re: Interplay was decided later and by a bench of equal strength, it prevails. A High Court cannot treat the overruled decision as binding. The Andhra Pradesh High Court has applied the law as it stands on the date of decision. [9]

Global 2 has no answer to that, and advancing it risks a finding of professional impropriety for relying on an overruled authority without disclosure.

WHAT REMAINS AVAILABLE: Within the current law, the following may be argued. (a) The instrument is inadmissible under s. 35 until duty and penalty are paid, and the Arbitral Tribunal should be asked to impound under s. 33 and decide stamping. (b) The agreement must prima facie exist under s. 7 (signed, in writing). [4][9] (c) If the dispute turns on the date of the proceeding, check whether any interim order was passed on the overruled law. None of the sources states whether In Re: Interplay was made prospective, and its full text, particularly the paragraphs on impounding procedure, is not in the sources. The point should be confirmed from the certified copy.

RISKS: Misciting an overruled decision, and any argument that the court must decide stamping at the referral stage, will likely fail.

answer.reasoned_analysis: ISSUE: The proposition that surveillance infringes no fundamental right is not the present law, and an advocate should not advance it as such. LAW: Privacy is protected under Article 21, and communications privacy also engages Article 19(1)(a). Any State surveillance must satisfy the Maneka Gandhi triangle of Articles 14, 19 and 21 (per the notes). COURT POSITION: In Manohar Lal Sharma (2021) [1], the Supreme Court stated that privacy is directly infringed by surveillance by the State or any external agency. It added that State surveillance must be justified on constitutional grounds, be absolutely necessary for national security and proportionate, rest on evidence, and carry sufficient statutory safeguards under the procedure established by law. The Puttaswamy reference order (2015) [2] recites the earlier telephone-tapping reasoning that tapping infracts Article 21 unless permitted by procedure established by law, and Article 19(1)(a) unless within Article 19(2). It also records the unresolved conflict between M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh, and the notes record that the nine-judge bench decision in Puttaswamy (2017) settled it in favour of a fundamental right to privacy. The Telangana High Court in Md. Abdul Kareem (2019) [4] applied Article 21 to police surveillance through a rowdy-sheet. APPLICATION: The authority that surveillance does not infringe a fundamental right is only the older, pre-2017 line. M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh are the cases usually cited for it, and the notes record that the 2017 decision overruled ADM Jabalpur and modified Kharak Singh. If the advocate acts for the State, the defensible argument is narrower. Surveillance is lawful when it is backed by statute, necessary, proportionate and subject to oversight, so that the infringement is justified rather than absent. COUNTER-ARGUMENT: A State respondent may say that not every surveillance interferes with privacy, for example open public monitoring, and that the question depends on the facts. The 2015 reference order [2] itself says that whether privacy is infringed depends on the facts of the case. That point goes to whether the facts disclose an infringement. It does not support a blanket rule. RISKS AND LIMITS: The sources do not include the 2017 judgment text, the M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh decisions, or any Bombay High Court ruling on surveillance. Manohar Lal Sharma [1] is a general statement of principle in the extracts provided. Md. Abdul Kareem [4] is a single-judge decision of another High Court and is persuasive only.

Interception of communications engages free speech. Where it falls outside the grounds in Article 19(2), it infringes Article 19(1)(a). Restrictions must be reasonable and proportionate.

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The premise that the CJI's opinion has 'no primacy' is contrary to the present law as shown by the authorities. The only sense in which 'no primacy' is correct is the narrow one stated in the Third Judges case: an opinion formed by the CJI otherwise than in the manner indicated (that is, without the collective, plural process) has no primacy, and the Government is not obliged to act on it [1].

LAW: Articles 124(2) and 217(1) require consultation. The Second Judges case, as reproduced in [1], held that the CJI's opinion has primacy in all appointments and that no appointment may be made unless it conforms to the CJI's final opinion, formed in the manner indicated. That opinion must reflect the judiciary and have an element of plurality, formed after taking into account the views of other Judges. For the Supreme Court, the two seniormost Judges are consulted and, where relevant, others; for High Courts, the views of colleagues conversant with that Court and the High Court Chief Justice, whose opinion carries the greatest weight [1]. Where a recommendation is returned for cogent reasons and reiterated with the unanimous agreement of the Judges consulted, the appointment should be made as a matter of healthy convention [1].

COURT POSITION: In the NJAC case the Union's acceptance of the Second Judges case as binding in the Third Judges reference is recorded [1], and the Court is recorded as treating the collegium's primacy as integral to judicial independence. The constitutional notes record that the 99th Amendment and NJAC Act were struck down and the collegium restored. Mohapatra [2] is a statutory-consultation case, useful only by analogy on how courts weigh a Chief Justice's opinion. The excerpts in [1] show submissions and reproduced earlier holdings, and I cannot separate the NJAC majority's ratio from the recounting of arguments, so the operative holding must be confirmed from the full report.

answer.reasoned_analysis: ISSUE: The question is how the Explanation to Art 286(1)(a) is to be construed today. LAW: Art 286(1)(a) forbids a State from taxing a sale or purchase outside the State, and Art 286(2) authorises Parliament to lay down the principles for determining when a sale takes place in the course of inter-State trade [1]. The Law Commission paragraph [2][3] treats the Explanation as a source of controversy: it states that without a deeming provision that a sale within one State is outside all others, the Article and the Explanation yielded varying interpretations, and it recommends deleting the Explanation. A further Commission discussion [4] notes that no parliamentary law taxes sales outside a State, that States lack power over them under Art 286(1), and that sales under ss. 4 and 5 of the CST Act falling outside a State are not taxable under any law. These are advisory materials only. COURT POSITION: The only judgment provided, K.T.C. Automobiles (2016) [1], is a Supreme Court division bench decision. Its ratio is that under s. 4(2) CST Act and s. 4(4) Sale of Goods Act, motor vehicles are unascertained goods until appropriated at the registration office, so the sale occurs where that appropriation takes place. That is binding under Art 141 on the situs question it decided. It does not construe the Explanation, and nothing in it should be presented as doing so. Its observations on registration mechanics are reasoning in support of that situs finding. APPLICATION: If your matter turns on where a sale took place, K.T.C. Automobiles [1] is the controlling authority, provided the goods are comparable (unascertained goods whose delivery is regulated by statute). If the matter turns on the Explanation itself, the sources give no authority to rely on. A second risk is that the Explanation may have been deleted or altered by amendment; the sources do not say, and the current text must be checked. A third risk is that subsequent treatment of K.T.C. Automobiles [1] has not been checked. PRACTICAL ADVICE: Obtain the current text of Art 286 and its amendment history from the official Constitution text. answer.reasoned_analysis: ISSUE: Whether s.377 IPC [1] is valid as applied to consenting adults. LAW: Section 377 [1] on its face punishes any voluntary carnal intercourse against the order of nature, with no consent qualifier. It was tested under Arts 14, 15, 19 and 21. COURT POSITION: In Koushal [2], a division bench of the Supreme Court in 2013 reversed the Delhi High Court and upheld the section. The excerpt supplied records mainly the pleadings (vagueness, privacy, arbitrary classification), not the Court's reasons, so the reasoning cannot be reconstructed from the sources. A Constitution Bench in Navtej Singh Johar (2018), as quoted in [4], declared that s.377, insofar as it criminalises consensual sexual acts of adults in private, violates Arts 14, 15, 19 and 21, and overruled Koushal (para 645.4). The declaration is a reading down, not a striking out: s.377 continues to govern non-consensual acts against adults, all carnal intercourse with minors, and bestiality (para 645.3). Under Art 141 this binds every court including the Bombay High Court, and the ratio is the operative declaration; the contrary Koushal reasoning is no longer authority. RANKING: Navtej outranks Koushal by bench strength and recency, and by express overruling. The High Court decisions [3] and [4] are persuasive only outside their states and add nothing binding. APPLICATION: For an accused charged under s.377 IPC for an act with a consenting adult in private, the charge is unsustainable, and Navtej applies to pending trials, appeals and revisions though not to concluded prosecutions (para 645.2). STATUTORY PRECEDENCE (NON-OBSTANTE ANALYSIS)

Prevailing provision: s. 9, The Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957
Yields:               s. 15, MMRD Act
Rule applied:         subordination
Reasoning:            s. 15, MMRD Act is expressed as subject to other provisions, which is the converse of an overriding clause. It yields.
Authority:
  - Ashok Leyland Ltd v State of Tamil Nadu, (2004) 3 SCC 1

ISSUE: The question is whether royalty is a tax. The answer governs challenges to State levies and to GST-type claims on royalty.

LAW: s. 9 of the MMDR Act makes royalty payable by the lessee on mineral removed or consumed from the leased area, at the Second Schedule rate [1]. s. 9 overrides contrary instruments and laws, whereas s. 15 yields to it. For minor minerals, any State rule-making under s. 15 therefore cannot displace the royalty obligation fixed by s. 9. Whether s. 9 reaches minor mineral quarry leases specifically is not settled by the sources, so the advocate should check the text of s. 15 and the Second Schedule.

COURT POSITION: The Constitution Bench in MADA [2] is the governing authority. It held that royalty is not the produce, income or yield of the land. It is paid by a lessee to the lessor for exercising mineral rights, and it becomes due on exercise of those rights. It is therefore not a tax. The Bench added that, being computed on quantity extracted, it can be used as a measure for taxing mineral-bearing land under Entry 49 List II, and that a tax on land with a minerals-based measure is not a tax on minerals under Entry 50. It disapproved India Cement's view that royalty is indirectly connected with land, and it disapproved the narrow approach in Orissa Cement. As a Constitution Bench decision it binds the Bombay High Court under Art. 141. The Patna High Court in Sanjay Kumar [5] applied the same reasoning and rejected the argument that royalty is a composite regulatory and service charge. That decision is persuasive only. The Orissa decision in Royal Granite [3] quotes India Cement and should not be relied on for the proposition that royalty is a tax. Shree Balaji [4] is useful for the competence of States, not for the nature of royalty.

APPLICATION: A party asserting that royalty is a tax should expect the proposition to fail. It can be stated that royalty is a contractual consideration, though it remains a statutory payment under s. 9. A party contending it is a tax would need to distinguish MADA, which is hard.

COUNTER-ARGUMENT AND RISKS: The opposing side may point out that the MADA extracts say only that royalty is not a tax per se. The extracts do not give the full reasoning on whether royalty is a tax, and the headnote or the majority conclusion must be read in full. Later treatment has not been checked. The paragraph numbers are drawn from partial extracts. India Cement's passage in [3] is quoted second-hand.

ADVICE: Cite MADA in full from the official report, confirm the conclusions in the majority and any separate opinions, and verify whether any review or later Larger Bench consideration exists.

It records that the 'interest of the nation' proposition in Sidhajbhai and St. Xavier's stands overruled by Pai Foundation, except as read with Quadri J.'s opinion. answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The advocate asks for a settled 'test' that a statutorily incorporated institution cannot be a minority institution. The sources do not establish such a rule as binding law.

LAW AND COURT POSITION: Article 30(1) protects the right of minorities to establish and administer institutions of their choice. Sidhajbhai [3] treats this as absolute in terms but subject to regulation in the true interests of efficiency, discipline, health, sanitation, morality and public order. Inamdar [2] records the three regulatory tests and states that the national-interest limb of Sidhajbhai was overruled by Pai Foundation. Neither passage mentions statutory incorporation, so neither supports the proposition directly.

The only source that bears on the proposition is Aligarh Muslim University (2024) [1]. The passages supplied (paras 109-123) reason as follows. Article 30(1) confers conjunctive rights, so a body not established by the minority cannot claim to administer. Entry 63 of List I confers a distinct status as an institution of national importance. Reclassifying AMU as a minority institution would conflict with secular principles. The passages themselves speak of 'the majority opinion' taking a different view and of a 'revised draft opinion'. They therefore appear to be from a separate or dissenting opinion, and no passage states a holding. They must be cited as the reasoning of that opinion, not as the law declared under Article 141. [AUTHORITY NOT CONFIRMED — no retrieved passage could be identified as the majority opinion of the Bench]

Even on that opinion, the reasoning is narrower than the advocate's proposed test. It turns on the institution not being established by the minority, and on the Entry 63 designation. It does not say that every statutory body is disqualified. Paragraph 120 expressly allows that institutions of national importance may have minority character.

APPLICATION: A rule that statutory incorporation by itself bars minority status is not supported by the sources. The defensible argument is that the claimant must show establishment by the minority and, on the conjunctive reading, administration by it. Statutory creation is evidence on establishment, not an automatic bar.

COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The opposing side will say that the AMU passages [1] criticise a position that treats establishment alone as the indicium, so that position may have been what the majority held. It will also say that Inamdar [2] reads Article 30(1) widely and that Sidhajbhai [3] calls the right absolute, so incorporation cannot extinguish it. What would defeat the proposed test is a majority holding in the 2024 decision.

RISKS: The sources do not show the majority outcome, the bench, or later treatment. A High Court is bound by the ratio under Article 141, not by a dissent. The Bombay High Court would also look to State-wise minority status per Inamdar [2].

ADVICE: Obtain the certified or official report of the full 2024 judgment, identify the operative order and majority ratio, and check subsequent treatment from the Court's own records before filing.

relevant_law.summary: Minorities, religious or linguistic, have the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice, and the State must not discriminate in granting aid on the ground of minority management. The questions are whether 'establish' and 'administer' operate conjunctively and whether incorporation by statute defeats a claim.

The law declared by the Supreme Court binds all courts. A High Court must therefore apply the ratio of a larger or later Bench and cannot treat an opinion that is only a passage or a dissent as binding.

Entry 63 names the Banaras Hindu University and the Aligarh Muslim University as institutions of national importance. The passages in Aligarh Muslim University (2024) [1] treat this as bearing on the minority-character question.
A law or executive direction that infringes the substance of the Article 30(1) right is void to that extent. This is relevant to any State regulation of a minority institution.

comparative_analysis.conflicts_or_differences: The sources show no direct conflict. The area of difficulty is the extent of implied exclusion of the proviso provisions (ss. 9, 27, 37) and the seat versus venue construction. The Delhi High Court holds that exclusion need not be express [5]. The Kerala material [8] is submission-based and does not give a settled position. comparative_analysis.trend_analysis: The law moved from Bhatia International (Part I applying to foreign-seated arbitrations unless excluded) to BALCO (territorial approach), and then to the 2015 legislative proviso restoring limited Part I support, consistent with party autonomy [5]. The recent trend is strict attention to seat designation and to the parties' exclusion of the proviso provisions [5][6][7].

answer.conclusion:
The governing position is that Part I applies only where the seat is in India (s. 2(2)), subject to the 2015 proviso extending ss. 9, 27 and 37(1)(a) and (3) to foreign-seated international commercial arbitrations unless the parties have excluded them, expressly or impliedly. The primary authority is the BALCO Constitution Bench (quoted in [5]), with Roger Shashoua [7] on the effect of a foreign seat. The argument to run is that the clause designates a foreign seat, so Part I is excluded, and that any claim to the proviso provisions is displaced by the chosen rules. The main risk is a seat-versus-venue construction that favours an Indian seat. answer.reasoned_analysis:
STATUTORY PRECEDENCE (NON-OBSTANTE ANALYSIS)

Prevailing provision: s. 45, the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
Yields:               the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
Rule applied:         express reference
Reasoning:            s. 45, the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 carries an overriding clause reaching the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. Any provision of that other law which is inconsistent with it does not apply.
Caveat:               Precedence operates only to the extent of an actual irreconcilable inconsistency between the two provisions. Where both can be obeyed, both apply and no question of overriding arises.
