ISSUE: Does Part I apply to an arbitration seated outside India?

LAW: s. 2(2) confines Part I to arbitrations where the place is in India. The 2015 proviso, as set out in the Delhi High Court judgment [5], extends ss. 9, 27 and 37(1)(a) and 37(3) to international commercial arbitrations seated abroad where the award is enforceable under Part II, unless the parties agree otherwise. Foreign awards are enforced under Part II, and s. 48 [3] confines resistance to enforcement to the listed grounds, with s. 45 [2] governing the reference of parties to arbitration.

COURT POSITION: The BALCO Constitution Bench, as quoted in the Delhi High Court judgment [5], held that Part I applies only to arbitrations taking place in India, and that this declaration operates prospectively for agreements executed after the judgment. This is the governing ratio, and as a Constitution Bench decision it binds the Bombay High Court under Art. 141 (well-established constitutional authority; verify against the official report). Roger Shashoua [7] adds that a foreign seat imports the supervisory law of that country, and that a clause saying the 1996 Act governs does not make Part I applicable. The Delhi High Court in Jindal Coke [6] applies the same reasoning, and in the 2020 decision [5] holds that exclusion of the proviso provisions may be implied from a rule-based emergency framework such as the JCAA Rules, with party autonomy as the foundation.

APPLICATION: The advocate should first fix the seat by construing the clause: is the foreign place a seat or only a venue? Roger Shashoua [7] indicates that 'venue' language may be read as a seat where the surrounding indicia (institutional rules, governing law) point that way, whereas the passage quoted in Enercon in the same extract declined to treat 'venue' as seat on facts. Keller [4] shows the Bombay High Court inferring a seat from the agreed venue plus the absence of contrary indicia, though that is domestic. If the seat is abroad, Part I is excluded save the proviso provisions, and enforcement lies under Part II (ss. 45 and 48). Note that s. 45 overrides the CPC only to the extent of actual inconsistency.

COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The opposing party may say the arbitration is only venue-abroad, with the Indian Act as curial law, so Part I applies in full [6]. Alternatively it may invoke the proviso for interim relief, arguing that exclusion was not agreed. The answer is the rules selected by the parties and the implied exclusion reasoning [5][7].

LIMITS: The sources do not contain the full BALCO text, any Bombay High Court decision on the proviso to s. 2(2), or the post-2015 Supreme Court position on prospectivity in full. Keller [4] and Jindal Coke [6] have not been checked for later treatment, and Peniel Cashew [8] is largely recorded submissions.

relevant_law.section: Section 2(2) and its proviso (inserted by the 2015 Amendment)
relevant_law.summary: Part I applies where the place of arbitration is in India. The proviso, as extracted in the Delhi High Court judgment [5], applies ss. 9, 27 and 37(1)(a) and 37(3) to international commercial arbitration even if the place is outside India, where the award is enforceable under Part II, subject to an agreement to the contrary. The text of s. 2(2) is taken from that extract; the official text of the Act should be checked.

s. 2(1)(e) defines 'Court' by reference to the subject-matter of the arbitration, and s. 20 deals with the place of arbitration (s. 20(3): meetings at any place). Peniel Cashew [8] and Jindal Coke [6] show that these provisions are read together, with BALCO distinguishing 'seat' from 'venue'. The text of s. 2(1)(e) and s. 20 is not reproduced in the sources, only described in the judgments.

s. 45 [2] requires a judicial authority to refer parties to arbitration where there is an agreement under s. 44, 'notwithstanding anything contained in Part I or in the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908', unless it prima facie finds the agreement null and void, inoperative or incapable of being performed. It overrides the CPC to the extent of any actual inconsistency; where both can be obeyed, both apply.

s. 48 [3] sets out the limited grounds, to be proved by the resisting party, on which enforcement of a foreign award may be refused. These include invalidity of the agreement, lack of notice, excess of submission, improper composition, and the award not yet being binding or having been set aside by the court of the seat. They also include non-arbitrability and public policy of India under s. 48(2).

s. 2 [1] defines 'arbitration' (whether or not administered by a permanent institution) and 'arbitration agreement' (an agreement under s. 7). It supplies the base definitions for the Part I analysis.

answer.reasoned_analysis: ISSUE: The question is whether an order under s. 11(6) is merely administrative. The proposition you state, that the order is administrative and not judicial, is, on the sources provided, the position that the Supreme Court in the extract of Eminent Colonizers (2026) [2] rejects. LAW: Section 11 [1] vests the appointment power in default of party agreement. The extracts of the judgments refer to the power under s. 11(6) as conferred on the Chief Justice of the High Court or of India; the text of sub-s. (6) is not in the sources, so it must be checked from the statute as amended. COURT POSITION: In [2] the Court reasons that the Chief Justice must satisfy himself of his territorial jurisdiction, the existence of a s. 7 arbitration agreement and that the applicant is a party to it, before the conditions for s. 11(6) can be said to exist. It treats the existence of the agreement as a jurisdictional fact for appointment. It says it is difficult to say that the Chief Justice does not adjudicate a dispute when an objection is raised, and that constituting a tribunal can affect a party's rights, including by imposing expense. It concludes that it is not possible to accept that no adjudication is involved. Paragraph 39 as extracted adds that the Chief Justice can also decide whether the claim is dead or long-barred and whether the transaction was closed by satisfaction. The Karnataka High Court single bench in [3] adopts the same reasoning, stressing that conferral on the Chief Justice and not the court is not enough to make the power administrative, and that the power is not persona designata. Ratio and obiter: the passages above are reasoning on the nature of the power, and in [2] they lead into a conclusion at para 47(i) that is cut off in the extract. Whether each passage is ratio of that judgment or reproduced reasoning from an earlier one cannot be determined from the extract. APPLICATION: Before the Bombay High Court, you can argue that an administrative characterisation is untenable and that the court must examine, at the threshold, the existence of the agreement, party status and jurisdiction. Rank: the Supreme Court decision binds under Art 141 (well-established constitutional authority; verify against the official report), whereas [3] is persuasive only. COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The opposing side will say the enquiry is limited to prima facie existence and that arbitrability and the merits are for the tribunal under s. 16 (Kompetenz-Kompetenz). Against that, [3] states that s. 16 only means the tribunal can decide such questions when they arise before it. The respondent may also invoke the 'administrative' line of authority and any later amendments. The sources do not say whether such amendments exist or alter the position, and none of the judgments cited decides the limits of the prima facie standard, so those must be checked. RISKS: [2] is flagged as a recent decision whose later treatment has not been checked, and the extract is fragmentary, so the operative direction at para 47 must be read in full. ADVICE: Do not rely on [4] or [5] for this point.

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The question is how far a State may, by statute or executive scheme, fix or approve the fees of private unaided institutions and require them to share seats with the State.

LAW: The source of the right is Art 19(1)(g) and, for minorities, Art 30(1), both subject to reasonable regulation. The sources show the foundation in the Supreme Court's Pai Foundation line, but only through quotation. Islamic Academy [4] reproduces the passages that unaided minority institutions have maximum autonomy over fees and admissions and must comply only with conditions of recognition that do not whittle down the right, and that majority and minority institutions must be treated equally.

COURT POSITION ON FEES: The Delhi High Court's synthesis [1] is the fullest statement in the sources. Fee fixation is a facet of administration. The State may regulate to prevent capitation fee and profiteering but cannot fix a rigid fee structure, and a reasonable surplus is legitimate. Pai Foundation, as quoted in [5], calls a rigid fee structure unacceptable. Karnataka [2] applied this to hold a State fee-regulating section inapplicable to unaided institutions. Telangana [3] shows the other side: a statute defining capitation fee as anything above the notified fee, with a committee determining fees for professional colleges, was upheld as regulation of quantum rather than prohibition. The reconciliation is that the Supreme Court tolerates machinery that screens for profiteering (for example, a committee approving a fee after examining costs) but not machinery that dictates a uniform figure irrespective of the institution's costs. That reconciliation is my inference, and the sources do not contain a Supreme Court decision stating it.

COURT POSITION ON SEAT-SHARING: Inamdar, as quoted in [5], disapproved the Islamic Academy scheme to the extent it let States fix management/State quotas in unaided institutions. Pai Foundation as quoted in [5] allows the State at most to require merit-based selection with the management retaining discretion. Because Inamdar is a later and larger-bench decision than Islamic Academy, it prevails on this point; Islamic Academy [4] should not be cited for quota-fixing. Neither is reproduced in full in the sources, and the Madras extract is a secondary quotation.

APPLICATION: In Bombay, the first step is to identify the actual Maharashtra statute or government resolution, which the sources do not address. A challenge to a fixed fee or State quota rests on Art 19(1)(g), and Art 30(1) if the petitioner is a minority institution, relying on the Supreme Court position and persuasively on [1], [2] and [5].

COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The State will rely on [3] and on the power to prevent profiteering and capitation fee. It will say that fee-determination committees are regulation, not fixing, that the statute defines capitation fee, and that the High Court decisions in [1], [2] and [5] are persuasive only and turn on different statutes. It may also argue that for schools receiving land or aid on conditions, those conditions bind, an issue [1] flags regarding land allotment. What defeats this is evidence that the scheme sets a rigid figure or does not allow a reasonable surplus.

LIMITS OF THE RECORD: None of the sources is a Bombay High Court decision, none is a full Supreme Court judgment, and several are marked as unconfirmed as to majority opinion. Later treatment is unchecked.

relevant_law.summary: The right to establish and administer an unaided institution is treated in the sources as an occupation protected by Art 19(1)(g). Restrictions must be reasonable and in the interest of the general public, so regulation is permissible to secure academic standards and prevent maladministration, but not to nationalise the institution.

Linguistic and religious minorities may establish and administer educational institutions of their choice. Islamic Academy [4] quotes the passage that unaided minority institutions are assured maximum autonomy over fees and admissions, subject to conditions of recognition that must not whittle down the right.

Art 14 underlies the equal-treatment principle quoted in Islamic Academy [4]: laws must apply equally to majority and minority institutions. Art 141 makes the law declared by the Supreme Court binding on the Bombay High Court, so the Supreme Court authorities must be located and verified from the official reports.

A challenge in the Bombay High Court to a State fee or seat-sharing order or statute would ordinarily come by writ petition. Writ jurisdiction is available against State action even where the institution is private.

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: Whether a committee-based scheme controlling admissions and fees in private unaided institutions is valid, and in what form.

LAW: Articles 19(1)(g)/19(6) and 30(1) are the operative provisions. Islamic Academy [3] quotes T.M.A. Pai Foundation to the effect that the Unni Krishnan scheme, which nationalised admission and fee-fixing, was unconstitutional. It also quotes the statement that Art 30(1) secures equal treatment and that unaided minority institutions have maximum autonomy over admissions and fees, subject to recognition conditions that do not whittle down the right.

COURT POSITION: Two propositions can be built on the sources. First, autonomy is real: a scheme that strips an institution of its own admission and fee decisions is vulnerable (Islamic Academy [3], quoting T.M.A. Pai; the arguments recorded in P.A. Inamdar [5]). Second, autonomy is not absolute. Indian School [4], relying on the Constitution Bench in Modern Dental College (as described there), holds that the Government may regulate to stop profiteering and capitation fee. Regulation should operate at the initial stage of fee fixation. A committee that weighs location, course, cost of land and building, infrastructure, staff, administration costs and a reasonable surplus for growth was approved in the passage from Association of Private Dental and Medical Colleges v. State of M.P. quoted in [4]. AMU [2] adds that general merit rules and service-condition regulations are permissible, citing Islamic Academy, St. Stephen's and Malankara.

APPLICATION: The present position, so far as the sources show, is that a fee committee is permissible as a regulatory device against profiteering, provided it determines or approves fees by reference to the institution's cost components and a reasonable surplus. It must not fix fees at a level that nationalises the institution or deny it the surplus. For admissions, the State may prescribe general merit and transparency rules, but the sources do not establish that it may take over the selection of students. A minority institution can additionally invoke the equal-treatment limb in [3]: a rule that disadvantages it relative to non-minority institutions is bad, and reverse discrimination is also impermissible.

COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The State or committee will rely on Indian School [4] and the passage it approves to say that fee regulation is plainly valid. The institution will rely on [3] and the arguments in [5] that the committee must not displace its own decisions. What would defeat the State is a committee that fixes fees without regard to cost components and surplus, or that controls admission itself.

LIMITS OF THE RECORD: The extract of P.A. Inamdar [5] contains only counsel's submissions, not the Court's holding. The extract of Islamic Academy [3] does not show its own directions on committees. None of the sources identifies the Maharashtra statute or Bombay High Court authority in issue, and later treatment of each judgment has not been checked. The exact governing ratio on committee structure, and whether any statute or later larger bench has altered it, must be confirmed from the full reported judgments and the court's records before reliance.

relevant_law.summary: Establishing and running an educational institution is an occupation protected by Art 19(1)(g). The State may impose reasonable restrictions in the public interest, such as measures against profiteering and capitation fee. This is the basis of the P.A. Inamdar (2005) [5] arguments and the Indian School, Jodhpur (2021) [4] discussion.

Religious and linguistic minorities may establish and administer educational institutions of their choice. Islamic Academy (2003) [3] extracts the passages stating that the essence of Art 30(1) is equal treatment, that unaided minority institutions have maximum autonomy over admissions, fees and recruitment, and that recognition conditions cannot whittle down the right.
The law declared by the Supreme Court binds the Bombay High Court. Where the Supreme Court's own benches differ, the larger bench prevails. This governs how the authorities below are ranked.

precedents.holding_summary: The extract shows the Court holding that non-arbitrability can arise from an implicit statutory prohibition, where a statute creates special rights to be adjudicated by courts or public fora, and that DRT Act claims are non-arbitrable. The extract does not reach landlord-tenant disputes, which the Court's treatment of tenancy is not shown in this extract. answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The proposition is that a tenancy dispute governed by the Transfer of Property Act is not arbitrable. On the sources supplied, I cannot confirm it as a settled, general rule, and an advocate should not present it as one.

LAW: Section 105 defines a lease [1] but says nothing about arbitration. Sections 2, 7 and 8 of the Arbitration Act permit arbitration of disputes in respect of a defined legal relationship, contractual or not, and mandate referral unless there is prima facie no valid agreement [2][3][4]. The text supplied contains no exclusion of lease disputes.

COURT POSITION: The governing test is in Vidya Drolia [7]. Non-arbitrability arises from an implicit statutory prohibition where a statute confers special rights to be adjudicated by a designated court or public forum, and the extract endorses the rule that only actions in rem are non-arbitrable. The extract applies this to DRT Act claims. Emaar [6] restates that interference at the Section 8 or 11 stage is confined to manifest, ex facie non-arbitrability, and that a court should refer where the point is plainly arguable or facts are contested. Krish Spinning [5] confirms the court may consider clear and glaring non-arbitrability at the Section 11 stage.

APPLICATION: The argument for non-arbitrability must therefore be built on a specific statute conferring exclusive jurisdiction, not on the Transfer of Property Act alone. In Bombay High Court matters, that would usually be the rent-control legislation applicable to the premises. That statute is not among the sources, so I cannot state its terms or whether it ousts arbitration. Also, the Transfer of Property Act confers no special forum. The dispute's character matters too: a claim for eviction or protected-tenancy rights under a special statute is different from a claim for rent arrears or damages under the lease.

COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The opposing side will say that Section 8 mandates referral [4], that the Act has no exclusion for leases, and that under Emaar [6] any doubt favours the tribunal. They will add that the tenancy statute must be shown to contain an implied or express bar. The Court noted that disqualification might be decided on political considerations. The prejudice runs against the members facing disqualification, not against the Speaker. If the Speaker survives the motion, he may then adjudicate. The Court also noted that if a disqualification order is later set aside, the member would have lost the chance to vote on the motion. The Constitution Bench ranks highest and binds the Bombay High Court under Article 141 (constitutional notes; verify). Article 192 concerns Article 191(1) disqualifications decided by the Governor and is not engaged by Tenth Schedule petitions [4]. I cannot responsibly present the proposition as live law, and a submission put as such would expose the advocate to a candour problem and an adverse finding.

WHAT GOLAK NATH [1] ACTUALLY SAYS. The supplied passages hold three things. (i) The amending process is not a political question beyond review; the Court only checks whether Parliament acts within its amending power. (ii) Nothing in the nature of the amending power lets Parliament override express or implied limitations, and an amendment made through the legislative process is subject to Art 13(2). (iii) The Seventeenth Amendment Act 1964, insofar as it takes away or abridges fundamental rights, is void under Art 13(2). The Court expressly declined to decide whether Parliament may destroy the structure of the Constitution outside Part III, calling the argument forceful but unnecessary to decide. The structure argument was therefore left open in Golak Nath and developed in Kesavananda.

COURT POSITION AND RANKING. Golak Nath [1] was decided by an 11-judge bench (per the constitutional notes) and Kesavananda by 13 judges. The later and larger bench governs. The 24th Amendment, per the constitutional notes, also restored Parliament's power to amend fundamental rights after Golak Nath.

SUBMISSIONS THAT CAN LEGITIMATELY BE ADVANCED. (1) Justiciability: relying on Golak Nath [1], the amendment's validity is open to judicial review and is not a political question. This survives, as judicial review is itself part of the basic structure. (2) Limits on the amending power: Golak Nath [1] supports the principle that the power is not unlimited. Frame the argument as one that the impugned amendment destroys or damages the basic structure, for example by abrogating Art 14, 19 or 21 in the golden-triangle sense, or Art 32. (3) Historical foundation: Golak Nath's reasoning that fundamental rights are not ordinary legislative subject matter was carried into the basic structure doctrine, but present it as background, not as authority for an absolute bar.

COUNTER-ARGUMENT. The State will cite Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and the 24th Amendment, and say that Golak Nath is overruled and that amending fundamental rights is permissible short of destroying the basic structure. That is correct. It is defeated only by showing the specific amendment violates the basic structure, which is a heavier burden but the only sound route.

LIMITS OF THE RECORD. The sources supplied contain only Golak Nath [1] and a compensation case [2] irrelevant to this issue. They do not contain Kesavananda Bharati, Minerva Mills or the 24th Amendment. Those are cited only from the constitutional notes and must be verified. answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE. The instruction is to build submissions on Naz Foundation for the proposition that a High Court may read down Section 377 IPC. The first difficulty is that a High Court judgment cannot be the foundation of the argument when a Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court has since decided the substantive question. As recorded in Sukanya Shantha (2024) [2], para 41, Navtej Singh Johar struck down Section 377 insofar as it criminalises homosexual intercourse between consenting adults. Under Art 141 that declaration binds the Madras High Court. A submission anchored in Naz Foundation would therefore be weaker than one anchored in Navtej, and it risks the objection that it relies on a decision whose standing is uncertain. I cannot say from the sources what Naz Foundation held or how the Supreme Court treated it, so I make no representation about either.

APPLICABLE LAW. Section 377 IPC [1] punished voluntary carnal intercourse against the order of nature, with the Explanation making penetration sufficient. The IPC has been repealed and the BNS has no successor provision. For conduct before 1 July 2024 the IPC applies through BNS s. 358. For later conduct there is no corresponding offence in respect of consenting adults. The constitutional foundation is Arts 14, 15, 19 and 21 as read with Art 13, together with the doctrines of reading down, severability and the presumption of constitutionality from the interpretation notes.

COURT POSITION. The sources show the following. Navtej struck down s. 377 as to consenting adults as discriminatory. The concurring reasoning treated Art 15 as covering direct and indirect discrimination founded on stereotypes, and assessed a provision by its effect on affected individuals, not by the State's object. A facially neutral provision may have a disproportionate impact on a class, and s. 377 was seen to target the LGBTQIA+ community [2]. Joseph Shine, also recorded in [2], held that a provision must not be viewed in isolation from its social, historical and cultural contexts. Those are the authorities to cite. Para 41 of [2] is a later bench's description of Navtej and is not itself the text of Navtej. The advocate should cite Navtej from the official report and use [2] only as a confirmatory secondary reference.

APPLICATION AND SUBMISSIONS. First, on the principal submission, Navtej binds this Court under Art 141 and settles that s. 377 cannot constitutionally apply to consensual adult conduct. If Naz Foundation is cited at all, it should be cited as the earlier High Court decision whose line of reasoning the Supreme Court later took forward, but only after its standing has been confirmed from the certified copy and the Supreme Court's record. Second, if the point being argued is the technique of reading down, the answer is that the interpretation notes recognise reading down where a provision admits of two constructions, one constitutional and one not, and that it is available only where the text can bear the narrower meaning. Whether s. 377 could bear such a reading was a matter the Supreme Court resolved by striking it down to the extent stated, so a High Court has no room to adopt a different technique on the same ground. Third, the effects-based Art 15 submission drawn from the concurring reasoning in [2] can be used where the facts involve differential treatment of a class.

RISKS AND COUNTER-ARGUMENT. The State or the opposing side will say that Naz Foundation has no precedential value in the face of Navtej, that a High Court cannot reopen what the Supreme Court decided, and that the remaining operation of s. 377 (non-consensual acts, minors, animals) was left untouched, so that any wider relief overreaches. That is a strong point against any attempt to extend the argument beyond consensual adult conduct. The sources do not say what Navtej left standing, so the advocate must read the operative part of Navtej before framing relief. The BNS repeal also may make the challenge academic for future conduct, though pending proceedings for pre-July 2024 conduct remain governed by the saved IPC.

PRACTICAL ADVICE. Anchor the argument in Navtej. Use Naz Foundation only as a historical reference after verification. Confirm the factual posture: whether the client is an accused, a petitioner seeking quashing, or a challenger, and the date of the alleged conduct. None of that has been supplied, so I have not assumed it.

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: You wish to rely on Sowmithri Vishnu for the constitutional validity of Section 497 IPC. That proposition is no longer good law, and a submission built on it as a binding authority cannot be advanced candidly.

LAW AND COURT POSITION: Section 497 punished a man who had intercourse with another man's wife without his consent or connivance, and exempted the wife [1]. Sowmithri Vishnu dismissed a challenge to it; the passages available to me record the civil-remedy point, the concern that striking down would obliterate the section, and the remark that stability of marriages is not an ideal to be scorned [2]. A Madras High Court bench has described it as holding that the section does not offend Articles 14 or 15 [4]. However, the Constitution Bench in Joseph Shine struck Section 497 down as violative of Articles 14, 15 and 21, held Section 198(2) CrPC unconstitutional to the extent it applies to adultery, and expressly states that Sowmithri Vishnu, V. Revathi and W. Kalyani stand overruled [6]. Under Article 141 that binds the Madras High Court.

APPLICATION: Sowmithri Vishnu cannot be put forward as authority for validity. Nor can the earlier Madras High Court observation in Dennison Paulraj [4], which merely repeated the 1985 position and pre-dates the overruling. The Uttarakhand decision [3] shows a High Court treating cognizance under the section as unsustainable after Joseph Shine, although it is persuasive only.

COUNTER-ARGUMENT AND LIMITS: The only responsible uses of Sowmithri Vishnu are narrow and must be framed as such. First, if you act for a party who relied on the section before 2018, the 1985 decision shows the then-prevailing law, though Joseph Shine's effect on pending or concluded proceedings is a separate question that the sources do not decide and must be checked in the full judgment and later authorities. Second, you may legitimately cite the stability-of-marriage and civil-remedy observations [2] only for historical context or to distinguish, not as a binding proposition; Joseph Shine's reasoning, as quoted in [3], rejected the stability-of-marriage rationale as inapplicable to this provision. The opposing side will rely on Joseph Shine and on Article 141, and nothing in the sources displaces them. Whether any later larger bench revisited Joseph Shine is not addressed by these sources; the later treatment of Joseph Shine has not been checked.

PRACTICAL ADVICE: Do not advance validity as a submission of law. If instructions require arguing for the section, state candidly that Sowmithri Vishnu stands overruled and confine the argument to a properly framed distinction or a request for reconsideration, which a High Court cannot grant against a Constitution Bench.

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The proposition is that Part I, including s. 9, applies to a foreign-seated arbitration. Bhatia [6] is the foundation of that proposition, but the sources reveal a serious problem with it.

LAW: Section 2(1)(a) [1] defines arbitration widely. Section 9 [2] allows court interim relief before, during or after the proceedings. Section 17 [3] gives the tribunal the same power, and s. 9(3) [2] restricts court relief once the tribunal is constituted.

COURT POSITION: Bhatia, as summarised in its headnote [6], holds that (i) Part I applies to all arbitrations and proceedings relating to them; (ii) for arbitrations outside India it applies unless the parties exclude it by express or implied agreement; (iii) the omission of 'only' in s. 2(2), unlike Article 1(2) of the UNCITRAL Model Law, makes s. 2(2) inclusive and clarificatory; and (iv) ouster of jurisdiction cannot be implied. The ratio is that the court has jurisdiction in aid of a foreign arbitration unless excluded. Venture Global, quoted in Videocon [4], adopted this and said the matter was 'concluded' by Bhatia, but the Videocon extract does not show what Videocon itself decided.

APPLICATION: Submissions to advance: (1) Bhatia was a three-judge bench decision as described in Venture Global [4], so it binds the Madras High Court under Art. 141 unless a later larger bench or a bench of equal strength has displaced it. (2) The presumption is applicability, and the burden of showing exclusion lies on the party resisting. (3) Exclusion must be express or implied from the agreement. A foreign governing law of the contract alone should be argued not to exclude Part I, because Bhatia required a real exclusion and said ouster cannot be implied lightly. (4) Reliance on a foreign-seat or foreign-rules clause is answered by the Bhatia statement that the chosen rules prevail only to the extent they conflict with Part I, and that institutional rules permitting recourse to the court (the ICC Rules in Bhatia) leave s. 9 available. (5) The petitioner has no remedy elsewhere, a point Bhatia emphasised as showing the interpretation leaves no party remedyless.

RISKS AND COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The respondent will rely on Prema Container [5], where an agreement for SIAC Rules and Singapore seat law was held to shut out Part I. It will point to Vitol [8], which treats Part I as limited to arbitrations within India, and to the Bharat Aluminium line of authority referred to there. It will also invoke s. 2(2) as indicating a territorial scope [5]. Prema Container and Vitol are High Court decisions outside Madras and bind only as persuasive authority. A Supreme Court decision departing from Bhatia would bind the Madras High Court. The sources do not show whether Bhatia has been overruled or limited, and this is the critical gap. The extracts of Vitol [8] suggest that a court has declared the law differently and made it prospective for later agreements, which would matter greatly depending on the date of the agreement.

ADVICE: Before advancing the argument, establish the date of the arbitration agreement and the seat and curial law clauses, and check the current status of Bhatia in the official reports.

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: You wish to rely on Himangni for the proposition that a Transfer of Property Act tenancy dispute is not arbitrable. On the authorities supplied, that proposition is not safe as framed.

LAW: Section 105 TPA [1] defines the lease. Section 8 of the 1996 Act [3] requires reference unless prima facie no valid arbitration agreement exists. The text of s. 8 as supplied does not mention non-arbitrability, so the argument must come from case law on implied exclusion.

COURT POSITION: Himangni, as described in Vidya Drolia [8], rested on Natraj Studios and Booz Allen. Vidya Drolia [8] held that those decisions were far removed from a Transfer of Property Act situation, that Himangni noticed none of the TPA provisions, that the TPA is silent on arbitrability, and that Himangni's reasoning on exemption from the Rent Act was not correct. It added that Himangni required a relook by three judges. The Delhi High Court order in Reema Singal [5] quotes a passage overruling Himangni. Its provenance is unclear on the face of the order, but if it is a larger-bench Supreme Court passage it would settle the point against you. I cannot confirm from these sources which decision it is, or its bench strength.

APPLICATION: The honest route is to argue within the surviving exception. First, establish whether a rent control statute applies to the premises and vests exclusive jurisdiction in a designated court or forum. Booz Allen, as summarised in Vidya Drolia [8], makes tenancy disputes non-arbitrable where they are governed by a special statute, the tenant has statutory protection against eviction, and only specified courts can decide. Himangni can then be cited, if at all, only for the unchallenged point that such disputes are for the designated forum, not as authority on TPA-only disputes. Second, if the premises are outside any rent statute, argue that the relief sought operates in rem or that public-policy provisions such as ss. 111, 114 and 114A TPA exclude arbitration by necessary implication. That argument was advanced in Vidya Drolia [8] and, on the supplied extract, did not succeed.

Second, on forum: Charu Lodha [6] and Dharamvir Khosla [7] note that Vidya Drolia arose under s. 11(6A), not s. 8. That distinction is available to you, but those passages record it as part of the defendant's contentions and do not endorse it, so it should not be overstated.

COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The opposing side will say that Himangni's ratio was disapproved in Vidya Drolia [8], that Reema Singal [5] treats it as overruled, and that parties who agreed to arbitrate should be held to it. Participation in the proceedings may also be urged against you, as it was in Vidya Drolia [8].

LIMITS: No Madras High Court decision and no text of Himangni itself is among the sources. I cannot say whether any Madras Rent Control Act provision or Tamil Nadu statute applies here.

ADVICE: Do not present Himangni as good law on TPA disputes without addressing Vidya Drolia. Confirm the source and bench of the passage in Reema Singal and read the reported text of Himangni and Vidya Drolia.

They also reject routes such as a statutory Constituent Assembly or a referendum, because Parliament cannot achieve indirectly what it cannot do directly. Those extracts show that the 24th Amendment is treated as declaratory and that the Golaknath reading of Article 13(2) is criticised. One extract goes further and denies any implied limitation. From the notes, which are background and to be verified against the official report, the settled outcome is that Golaknath was overruled, Parliament may amend Part III, and it may not destroy the basic structure. Article 141 makes that binding on the Madras High Court. APPLICATION: An argument that Parliament has no power whatever to amend Part III is therefore untenable as a statement of present law. answer.issue: Whether Articles 19 and 21 operate in mutually exclusive fields, as the A.K. Gopalan approach held, or whether a law depriving personal liberty must also satisfy Articles 19 and 14, and what authority the advocate can rely on before the Madras High Court.

precedents.case_name: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
precedents.holding_summary: The extract states the law as well settled: Article 21 does not exclude Article 19. Even if a law prescribes a procedure for depriving personal liberty, so that Article 21 is not infringed, the law must still meet the challenge of Article 19 to the extent it abridges a Article 19 right [4]. The extract also traces the direct-effect test through Sakal Papers, the Bank Nationalisation Case and Bennett Coleman, displacing the object-based test of A.K. Gopalan [4]. The extract is of a single-bench entry, though the judgment is widely known as a larger bench decision; verify the bench from the official report.

precedents.case_name: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India
precedents.holding_summary: The Court records that the theory of fundamental rights as watertight compartments was discarded in R.C. Cooper (eleven judges). Gopalan's view that a preventive detention law was tested only against Article 22 was rejected, because protection depends on the effect of State action, not its object [7]. The passage is largely a recital of earlier law, so it is strong authority for the position but the operative ratio of the case lies elsewhere (privacy).

precedents.holding_summary: The Court accepts that a deprivation of liberty needs a law prescribing a fair procedure as laid down in Maneka Gandhi, and holds that the impugned provision 'has to be tested on the principles evolved under Articles 14, 19 and 21' [3]. It then applies the Article 14 classification test. The passage is applied reasoning, not a fresh statement of the doctrine.

precedents.holding_summary: The extract only restates that Article 21 protects personal liberty and the right to live with human dignity, subject to procedure established by law [5]. It does not address the relationship between Articles 19 and 21 and should not be cited for that proposition.

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The proposition that Articles 19 and 21 operate in mutually exclusive fields is no longer the law. The question is what authority establishes that, and with what precision it can be cited.

LAW: Article 21 requires a 'procedure established by law' [2]. Article 19 protects specific freedoms subject to the restrictions in its clauses. The exclusivity argument rested on A.K. Gopalan: a law on preventive detention was tested only against Article 22 or the procedure requirement, and not against Article 19.

COURT POSITION: Puttaswamy (2017) [7] records that the eleven-judge decision in R.C. Cooper discarded the theory of watertight compartments, and that Gopalan's approach, under which the object of the State action rather than its effect on the right decided the protection, was disagreed with. Maneka Gandhi (1978) [4] states that the law is well settled that Article 21 does not exclude Article 19, and that even a law prescribing a procedure for depriving personal liberty, if it abridges an Article 19 right, must meet Article 19. The extract also traces the shift to the direct-effect test [4]. Navtej Singh Johar (2018) [3], a constitution bench, applies this by holding that the impugned provision must be tested under Articles 14, 19 and 21, and that the Article 21 procedure must be fair as laid down in Maneka Gandhi. The Law Commission passage [6] says the Article 21 'law' must be reasonable and non-discriminatory under Articles 19 and 14. It is advisory and should not be cited as authority.

RATIO VERSUS OBITER: Maneka Gandhi [4] is the operative authority. The Puttaswamy passage [7] is a judicial recital of earlier law, and the Navtej passage [3] is applied reasoning; both are strong but cite Maneka Gandhi and Cooper as the source. People's Union for Civil Liberties [5] does not bear on the point.

APPLICATION: In the Madras High Court matter, argue that a measure affecting liberty must clear Article 21 (fair, just, reasonable procedure), Article 14 (non-arbitrariness) and Article 19 wherever a freedom is directly affected. Under the effect-based test, the State cannot defend the measure by pointing to a different object.

COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The State may say that Article 19 is engaged only where the impugned action directly and inevitably affects an Article 19 right, as the directness guidelines in Maneka Gandhi [4] indicate, so overlap is not automatic. That is answered by showing the direct effect on the specific freedom on the facts. Another point is that Article 19(1) applies only to citizens.

LIMITS OF THE RECORD: The extracts do not give paragraph numbers for the Maneka Gandhi passage, and none of the sources shows later treatment. I have not been given the Cooper judgment itself, which is known only through Puttaswamy [7]. No Madras High Court decision is provided. The Article 19 clauses and the golden triangle formulation come from the constitutional notes, not from the sources.

relevant_law.summary: No person may be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law [2]. After Maneka Gandhi, the procedure must be fair, just and reasonable, and the law must satisfy Articles 14 and 19 where those are engaged.

Article 19 freedoms can be restricted only by reasonable restrictions of the kind the clauses permit. Article 14 bars arbitrariness. Per the constitutional notes, these three Articles together form the 'golden triangle' (well-established constitutional authority; verify against the official text).

answer.reasoned_analysis: ISSUE: The question is whether Gian Kaur can still be cited as having approved passive euthanasia, for instance by adopting Airedale. LAW: Gian Kaur held, in upholding s. 306 IPC (BNS s. 108), that Article 21 does not include a right to die, and that suicide is an unnatural termination of life inconsistent with the right to life. Common Cause [1] reproduces that reasoning at paras 22 and 38. COURT POSITION: The reference order recorded in Common Cause [1] states that Aruna Shanbaug proceeded on the erroneous premise that Gian Kaur approved Airedale. In the headnote material attributed to Chandrachud J., Gian Kaur does not conclusively rule on passive euthanasia, Aruna Shanbaug proceeds on an incorrect perception of it, and its underlying basis is flawed. In the headnote attributed to Misra CJI (for himself and Khanwilkar J.), Gian Kaur does not lay down that passive euthanasia can be lawful only by legislation. Ratio versus obiter: the supplied passages are headnotes, summaries and partial text, and none can be confirmed as the majority holding, so each point must be attributed to the specific opinion; the advocate must check the operative majority text. A caution from para 38 of the lead opinion: it states that the position 'as of today' is that the right to life does not include a right to die. So the correction is that Gian Kaur is not authority approving passive euthanasia; Common Cause's separate Article 21 reasoning supplies the legality. APPLICATION: Before the Madras High Court, do not argue that Gian Kaur approved passive euthanasia or Airedale. Cite Common Cause [1] for legality and the advance-directive regime, and cite Gian Kaur only for the limited propositions above. The Supreme Court's decision binds the High Court under Article 141, and the 2018 Constitution Bench, being larger, prevails over the two-Judge Aruna Shanbaug on this point. [AUTHORITY NOT CONFIRMED — no retrieved passage could be identified as the majority opinion of the Bench] COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The opposing side may say Gian Kaur still denies any right to die, so the Article 21 basis for passive euthanasia is contested; the answer is that Common Cause [1] treats withdrawal of futile treatment as distinct from extinction of life and protects bona fide medical decisions. They may also say only Parliament can regulate; the answer is the Article 142 directions that hold the field until legislation. LIMITS: The sources do not contain the full majority text, paragraph numbers for the directions (paras 191-194 are referred to by Bhushan J.), or later treatment of the judgment. None of the material supplied covers subsequent modifications of the guidelines or any Madras High Court application, which must be checked.

relevant_law.summary: Article 21 guarantees life and personal liberty. The 2018 Constitution Bench draws on liberty, dignity, autonomy and privacy to uphold passive euthanasia and advance directives. Its advance-directive regime was issued under Article 142 and holds the field until Parliament legislates (per Chandrachud J., as summarised in the headnote). Article 141 makes the law declared binding on the Madras High Court (well-established constitutional authority; verify against the official report).

comparative_analysis.agreements_between_courts: The Supreme Court in the 2024 judgment [2][6] and the High Court views quoted in Kesoram [3] (Punjab & Haryana, Gujarat) agree that royalty is a payment for the minerals or for the use of land, not a compulsory exaction in the nature of a tax. answer.conclusion:
The present position is that royalty is not a tax. The nine-judge bench in Mineral Area Development Authority (2024) [2][6] holds it to be a contractual consideration paid by the lessee for mineral rights, and it binds the Madras High Court under Art. 141. India Cement (1990) cannot be cited for the contrary view, since para 34 was read as concerning cess on royalty and the decision was overruled to the extent of the observations. If your client's case is a challenge to a State levy, focus on whether the levy falls within Entry 49, since royalty may be used as a measure under conclusion (f). Before relying on this, obtain the certified copy of the 2024 judgment, confirm the paragraph numbers and the full text of para 342, and check for any later orders, review or clarification, and any Madras High Court application of the decision. The extract [2] also records that the 'royalty is a tax' sentence in India Cement para 34 was read as an error for 'cess on royalty'. The conclusions overrule India Cement, Orissa Cement, Federation of Mining Associations of Rajasthan, Mahalaxmi Fabric Mills, Saurashtra Cement, Mahanadi Coalfields and P. Kannadasan to the extent of the observations made. Conclusions (e) to (g) hold that States may tax mineral-bearing land under Entry 49, using mineral yield or royalty as a measure of the tax.

answer.reasoned_analysis: ISSUE: The question is whether royalty under s. 9 of the MMDR Act [1] is a tax. LAW: Section 9(1) and (2) [1] require the lessee to pay royalty at the Second Schedule rate on mineral removed or consumed from the leased area. The earlier argument that this is a tax rested on its statutory fixation and recoverability. COURT POSITION: The governing authority is Mineral Area Development Authority (2024) [2][6], a nine-judge bench. As reproduced in [6], conclusion (a) in para 342 is that royalty is not a tax. It is a contractual consideration paid by the mining lessee to the lessor for enjoyment of mineral rights, the liability arises from the conditions of the lease, and payments to the Government are not a tax merely because the statute provides for recovery as arrears. The extract [2] shows the Court reading the India Cement para 34 sentence as an inadvertent error for 'cess on royalty', and recording that nowhere else did the majority hold royalty to be a tax. Kesoram (2004) [3] reflects the same reasoning, quoting the High Court view that royalty is akin to rent or the price of minerals won from the soil. Under Art. 141 the 2024 decision binds the Madras High Court, and the Chhattisgarh High Court has already applied it [6]. APPLICATION: Any argument before the Madras High Court that royalty is a tax cannot be sustained, and the Madras decision in Tamil Nadu Minerals (2019) [5], as extracted, offers no support. The Orissa petitioner's argument in [4] likewise predates the decision. OBITER AND RANKING: The 2024 holding is the ratio. The overruled decisions are overruled only 'to the extent of the observations made', so a careful reading is needed to see what survives. Kesoram's approving quotations are supporting reasoning. COUNTER-ARGUMENT: An opponent may argue that the true point of the 2024 decision is that States, not Parliament, hold the power to tax mineral rights, so a levy measured by royalty may be valid under Entry 49. This does not make royalty itself a tax. It means a State levy on mineral-bearing land may use royalty as a measure (conclusion f). A party challenging a State levy would therefore need to distinguish the levy from a tax on royalty. LIMITS OF THE RECORD: The sources give only extracts of the 2024 judgment. The exact paragraphs of the majority and dissenting opinions, any separate opinion, and any later review or clarification are not shown, and later treatment was not checked. The effect on levies already collected, and any prospective or retrospective application, is not addressed by these extracts. PRACTICAL ADVICE: Cite the 2024 judgment and conclusion (a) directly, from the certified report rather than the Chhattisgarh paraphrase, and confirm the paragraph numbers.

comparative_analysis.agreements_between_courts: Roger Shashoua [5], the Karnataka decision [8] and the Delhi decision [9] agree on the operative position: the selection of a foreign seat carries the supervisory law of that seat, and Part I does not give Indian courts supervisory jurisdiction over the arbitration or award. Whether the clause designates a seat or only a venue is a matter of construction. The Bombay decision [7] applies the same seat-centred framework to a domestic arbitration.
comparative_analysis.conflicts_or_differences: Arif Azim [6] reproduces the older position (Bhatia International and Venture Global) that Part I applied to foreign-seated arbitrations unless excluded. That position sits uneasily with [5], [8] and [9], which rely on BALCO (a five-judge bench). The extract of [6] does not show whether the 2024 Court endorsed the older line or only recited it. Separately, [8] notes an internal tension in BALCO para 96 between concurrent jurisdiction of courts and the seat as the sole supervisory court. None of the supplied sources fully resolves these points, and BALCO itself is cited only through the high court extracts.
comparative_analysis.trend_analysis: The sources show a shift from Bhatia International's wide reach of Part I, which [6] quotes only as a prior position, to the seat-centric territorial approach of BALCO, applied in Roger Shashoua [5] and in the high court decisions of 2025-2026 [7][8][9]. Party autonomy in choosing the seat is the organising principle.

answer.conclusion:
On the sources supplied, the better-supported position is that where the agreement fixes a seat outside India, Part I does not give Indian courts supervisory jurisdiction, and the award is dealt with under Part II at enforcement. Roger Shashoua [5] is the principal authority, supported by the Karnataka [8] and Delhi [9] decisions, which apply BALCO. Argue the seat/venue construction of the clause first. Before relying on any of this in the Madras High Court, read the certified texts of BALCO, BGS SGS Soma JV and Arif Azim [6] to confirm bench strength, whether Bhatia International was endorsed or merely recited, and the exact text of s. 2(2) and its proviso. Do not cite the high court decisions as binding.

answer.reasoned_analysis: ISSUE: The question is whether Part I of the 1996 Act applies to an arbitration whose seat is outside India, and which authority the Madras High Court must follow. LAW: Section 2 [1] defines terms for Part I, and ss. 9 [2], 28 [3] and 34 [4] are the provisions most often invoked. The extracts do not reproduce s. 2(2) with its proviso or s. 20, so the statutory text on territorial scope must be checked against the Act as amended. COURT POSITION: The binding source supplied is Roger Shashoua [5]. Its extract states that choice of a foreign seat imports acceptance of that country's law on the conduct and supervision of arbitration. It adds that if the agreement provides for a seat outside India, a clause saying the 1996 Act governs does not make Part I applicable or enable Indian courts to exercise supervisory jurisdiction; it only imports provisions about the internal conduct of the arbitration. The extract describes this as a single-bench report, so the bench strength should be confirmed from the certified report. The high court decisions from Karnataka [8] and Delhi [9] quote BALCO to the same effect, and the Delhi decision [9] states that Part I is inapplicable to the extent inconsistent with the seat's law. Arif Azim [6] quotes the older Bhatia International reasoning that Part I applies to foreign-seated arbitrations unless excluded. That reasoning is also described there as having been laid down before the later position. The extract does not reveal how the 2024 bench uses it, so it must not be cited as the present rule without reading the whole judgment. APPLICATION: Before the Madras High Court the first step is construction of the clause: does it designate a seat or only a venue? Where it designates a foreign seat, the likely position on [5], [8] and [9] is that ss. 9 and 34 are unavailable in the Indian courts, and the award is dealt with at enforcement under Part II. Where the clause says only 'venue' with other connecting factors, [7] and [9] show the court asks whether the venue is really the seat. COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The opposing side can rely on the passages in Arif Azim [6] that Part I applies to all arbitrations unless excluded, and on the 2015 proviso to s. 2(2) allowing certain interim relief for foreign seats. Its strength depends on whether [6] adopts those passages, and on the text of the proviso, neither of which is shown in the extracts. LIMITS: BALCO, BGS SGS Soma JV and Bhatia International are cited only through quotations in other judgments, and none of the sources contains the amended s. 2(2). RISKS: Citing a High Court of another state is persuasive only before the Madras High Court. ADVICE: confirm the full text of BALCO and Arif Azim from the official reports before filing.

relevant_law.section: Section 2(2) (proviso to be verified) read with Section 2(1)
relevant_law.summary: Section 2 [1] contains the definitions for Part I. The territorial-scope provision, s. 2(2), is not reproduced in the extract supplied. The text of s. 2(2) and its proviso, which extends certain Part I sections to foreign-seated arbitrations, should be checked against the bare Act as amended in 2015.

Section 9 [2] lets a party apply to a court for interim measures before, during or after arbitral proceedings. Whether a court in India can exercise this power for a foreign seat depends on the territorial scope of Part I, so the extract does not answer that point by itself.

Section 34 [4] provides the exclusive recourse against an award, namely an application to set it aside on the listed grounds. The extract does not say where this remedy lies when the seat is foreign. Authority [5] indicates that Indian courts have no supervisory jurisdiction over a foreign-seated award.

Section 28 [3] deals with the law applicable to the substance of the dispute where the place of arbitration is in India. It distinguishes the substantive law from the law governing the arbitration, which is relevant when parties choose Indian law for the contract but a foreign seat.

Section 20, discussed in [8] and [9] but not reproduced in the extracts, governs the place of arbitration. Sub-sections (1) and (2) concern the seat, and sub-section (3) concerns the venue for hearings. The seat/venue distinction is central to the present position.

answer.reasoned_analysis: ISSUE: The question is whether the State may impose a fee-regulation and seat-sharing scheme on private unaided institutions. LAW: The rights rest on Article 19(1)(g) and, for minorities, Article 30(1). Islamic Academy [3] reproduces Pai Foundation: the Unni Krishnan scheme was unconstitutional because it nationalised admission and fee-fixing, and unaided institutions, minority or not, are assured maximum autonomy over fees, admissions and recruitment, subject to recognition conditions that cannot whittle down the right. Note that the extract reproduces Pai Foundation passages quoted in Islamic Academy; it does not show Islamic Academy's own operative scheme. COURT POSITION: On seat-sharing, Inamdar para 130, as quoted in [4], says the Islamic Academy scheme allowing States to fix quotas for seat-sharing between management and State in unaided institutions, minority and non-minority, 'does not lay down the correct law and runs counter to Pai Foundation'. [4] also records that local needs cannot justify quotas, and the Madras High Court there criticised a fixed percentage quota. The 2019 Delhi bench [5] and the 2021 single bench [1] summarise the fee law: regulation is permissible against capitation fee and profiteering and for standards; a reasonable surplus is allowed; rigid fee fixation is not. Paragraph 130 of [1] distinguishes profit from profiteering. Karnataka [2] applied this to hold a State fee provision inapplicable to unaided institutions, on its own statute. A caution applies: the note on [5] says its Inamdar passages could not be confirmed as the majority opinion, so they should be attributed to the passage and not treated as settled holdings. APPLICATION: Before Madras, a challenge to a government order or statute that fixes fees or compels seat surrender should rely on Pai Foundation and Inamdar para 130, which bind under Article 141. [AUTHORITY NOT CONFIRMED — no retrieved passage could be identified as the majority opinion of the Bench] Nothing in the sources identifies the Tamil Nadu statute, so the specific scheme must be examined. The Delhi and Karnataka decisions are persuasive only. RISKS: The State will argue that fee regulation to prevent profiteering and capitation fee is permitted, that quotas may be consensual or tied to recognition or land-allotment conditions (see [5] item (ix)), and that merit-based selection may be required as a condition of recognition ([4] quoting para 68). Whether a statutory committee mechanism survives is not settled by these sources. ADVICE: Obtain the full text of Inamdar, Pai Foundation and later Supreme Court decisions; plead that the measure is a rigid fee structure or nationalisation of seats; and be ready to meet the profiteering argument with evidence of reasonable surplus.

relevant_law.summary: Private unaided institutions claim the right to establish and administer an institution as an occupation. It is subject to reasonable restrictions, which the sources describe as regulation for academic standards, infrastructure and prevention of maladministration, and for prohibiting profiteering and capitation fee.

Religious and linguistic minorities may establish and administer educational institutions of their choice. Islamic Academy [3] quotes the passage that unaided minority institutions, like other private unaided institutions, are assured maximum autonomy in fees and admissions, subject to conditions of recognition that cannot whittle down the right.

Article 14 underlies the equal-treatment principle quoted in Islamic Academy [3]. Article 141 makes Supreme Court law binding on the Madras High Court. A later larger bench prevails over an earlier smaller bench (well-established constitutional authority; verify against the official report).

comparative_analysis.agreements_between_courts: Indian School [1] and Jain Heritage [2] both accept T.M.A. Pai autonomy, including a reasonable surplus for growth, and the bar on profiteering and capitation fees. Both leave room for regulation that does not destroy autonomy.
comparative_analysis.conflicts_or_differences: Indian School [1] stresses that Government may regulate fees from the initial stage and approves committee-based cost scrutiny. The Karnataka orders in Jain Heritage [2] take a narrower view and exclude unaided schools from the particular statutory fee-restriction provisions. These are reconcilable: the Supreme Court sets the constitutional floor, and the Karnataka position turns on its own statute's text. Under Art 141 the Supreme Court prevails, and Karnataka rulings are only persuasive in Madras.
comparative_analysis.trend_analysis: The sources show the law as autonomy balanced by anti-profiteering regulation. The Supreme Court accepts structured committee regulation that is cost-based and allows a reasonable surplus. High Courts examine whether a statute actually reaches unaided schools and whether the regulation is proportionate.

answer.conclusion:
The binding position, on the authorities provided, is that private unaided schools have fee-fixing autonomy, but the State may regulate through a committee scheme to prevent profiteering and capitation fees. Indian School [1] supports a cost-based committee model that allows a reasonable surplus. An institution should test whether the Tamil Nadu scheme meets those standards and treat Jain Heritage [2] as persuasive only, since it rests on the Karnataka Act. The State should rely on [1]. Before filing, verify the Indian School report and the Constitution Bench judgments against the official reports, obtain the Tamil Nadu statute, rules and committee orders, and search Madras High Court and Supreme Court decisions on fee committees and admission regulation, because the sources do not cover them or the later treatment of [1] and [2].

answer.issue: What is the present position on committee-based regulation of fees (and admissions) of private unaided schools, and what authority can an advocate rely on before the Madras High Court?

precedents.case_name: Indian School, Jodhpur & Anr. v State of Rajasthan & Ors.
precedents.holding_summary: Recounts the Constitution Bench position: T.M.A. Pai gives private unaided schools autonomy in fixing fees, but Modern Dental College (para 75-76) holds that commercialisation, profiteering and capitation fees are impermissible. The Government may regulate fees in the public interest, regulation is needed at the initial stage of fixation, and it has the power and duty to direct reduction of excessive fees. It approves Association of Private Dental and Medical Colleges v State of M.P., which upheld a committee model that weighs cost components and a reasonable surplus. Later treatment has not been checked.

precedents.case_name: Jain Heritage School v State of Karnataka (WP 24449/2022), following the order of 05.01.2023 in WP 6313/2017
precedents.holding_summary: [UNVERIFIED — CONFIRM AGAINST THE OFFICIAL REPORT OR COURT RECORD BEFORE COURT USE] Applies a coordinate bench order holding that private unaided institutions are outside s. 48 of the Karnataka Education Act, so the District Education Regulatory Authority cannot proceed against them under that section. It also holds Rule 4 of the 1999 Rules ultra vires and s. 7(1)(f) unconstitutional for such institutions, relying on a Division Bench decision. It says the school and Government must not ignore T.M.A. Pai. The extract is partial, and later treatment has not been checked.

answer.reasoned_analysis: ISSUE: The question is how far a statutory committee can fix or approve fees, and regulate admissions, of private unaided schools, and what a Madras High Court bench will treat as binding. LAW: The constitutional footing is Art 19(1)(g), tested under Art 19(6), and Art 30 for minority schools. The governing text is the Tamil Nadu fee-regulation statute and rules, which the sources do not contain. COURT POSITION: Indian School, Jodhpur (2021) [1] is the principal authority and is binding under Art 141, although it is a division bench decision. It restates the Constitution Bench law in T.M.A. Pai and Modern Dental College: management has autonomy to devise its fee structure, but commercialisation, profiteering and capitation fees are not permitted. Government may regulate in the general public interest, and regulation is needed at the initial stage of fixation. Where excessive fees come to notice, Government has the power and duty to direct reduction. The Court approved the committee model in Association of Private Dental and Medical Colleges v State of M.P., under which the committee considers location, nature of course, land and building cost, infrastructure, staff, administrative expenditure and a reasonable surplus for growth, and may call for information from the institution. The extract in [1] is cut off. Statements about what the Constitution Bench held are reported by the division bench, and the original judgments should be read. Jain Heritage School (2023) [2] is a Karnataka High Court order applying a coordinate bench decision. It holds that the Karnataka Education Act's s. 48 does not reach private unaided institutions and that s. 7(1)(f) and Rule 4 are unconstitutional for them. The ratio turns on that Act's text and a Division Bench ruling that the extract does not reproduce. It is persuasive only in Madras, and the broad autonomy submission in para 3 is counsel's argument, not a holding. APPLICATION: For an institution, the argument is that the Tamil Nadu scheme must leave the school its autonomy, including a reasonable surplus, and that Jain Heritage [2] shows courts will strike down fee control that lacks nexus to its object. For the State or a parent, the argument is that [1] expressly endorses committee-based, cost-component scrutiny at the stage of fixation, so a committee scheme with these factors is constitutional. COUNTER-ARGUMENT AND RISKS: The institution's strongest point is that the Tamil Nadu scheme may be more intrusive than the factors approved in [1], or may lack guidelines, reasons or a surplus allowance. The State's answer is that [1] binds and Karnataka rulings do not. Neither source decides admission regulation, so that limb is unsupported by the authorities here. Neither source addresses minority schools or Art 21A and the RTE Act, or the Madras High Court's own decisions on the Tamil Nadu committee.

relevant_law.summary: Private unaided institutions claim autonomy under Art 19(1)(g) (and Art 30 for minorities). Regulation is tested as a reasonable restriction under Art 19(6). Challenges to committee orders or fee-regulation statutes are brought under Art 226. (Constitutional provisions drawn from the standing notes.)

comparative_analysis.agreements_between_courts: [2]], [3], [4] and [5] agree that constitutional satisfaction is that of the Council of Ministers under Articles 74(1) and 163(1), not the personal satisfaction of the President or Governor.
comparative_analysis.conflicts_or_differences: The sources do not contain a conflicting view on Article 356 itself. The apparent tension is between the 'subjective satisfaction' language in [1], which concerns Article 311(2) and security of the State, and the reviewability of Article 356 under Bommai. These are different provisions, and Bommai, as a Constitution Bench, governs Article 356.
comparative_analysis.trend_analysis: The law moved from treating the satisfaction as non-justiciable to treating it as reviewable on a limited basis. After Bommai, review is confined to whether relevant material exists and whether the exercise was mala fide or based on irrelevant grounds. Rameshwar Prasad (2006) applied this to a biased Governor's report (well-established constitutional authority; verify against the official report).

answer.conclusion: The submission that Article 356 satisfaction is beyond judicial scrutiny is not good law. Under S.R. Bommai (1994), binding on the Madras High Court under Article 141, a Proclamation is reviewable on limited grounds: absence of relevant material, mala fides, extraneous considerations, and failure to hold a floor test. Rely on the Council of Ministers principle shown in [2], [3] and [5], but do not rely on [1] or [4] for Article 356. Before filing, check the operative paragraphs of Bommai and Rameshwar Prasad in the official law reports, and confirm the text of Article 74(2). Verify also the later treatment of every High Court decision cited, none of which has been checked.
answer.issue: Whether the President's satisfaction under Article 356 is immune from judicial scrutiny, or whether the Proclamation is reviewable and, if so, on what grounds and to what extent. The matter is before the Madras High Court.

precedents.holding_summary: [UNVERIFIED — CONFIRM AGAINST THE OFFICIAL REPORT OR COURT RECORD BEFORE COURT USE] The Proclamation under Article 356 is subject to judicial review. The Union must have relevant material, and a floor test is required before dismissal of a government (well-established constitutional authority; verify against the official report). The [3]] and [5] only record the opinions of Sawant, Ramaswamy and Jeevan Reddy JJ on the President's constitutional role, federalism and aid and advice. They do not set out the operative holdings on reviewability.

It is cited here for the constitutional-head principle only. The extract does not decide anything on Article 356.

precedents.holding_summary: Records that satisfaction under the Constitution is that of the Council of Ministers, not personal satisfaction. It relies on R.K. Jain (1993) 4 SCC 119 and discusses Bommai on federalism. The extract does not show the result of the PIL, so it is persuasive only on the constitutional-head point.

precedents.holding_summary: Reproduces Bommai passages: Article 356 is a function of the President under Article 74(1), exercised on ministerial advice. It identifies federalism and pluralist democracy as part of the basic structure (per Sawant J). Persuasive only, and the extract does not decide reviewability.

precedents.holding_summary: The extract records counsel's submission that Samsher Singh makes satisfaction under Articles 123, 213, 311(2) proviso (c), 317, 352(1), 356 and 360 the satisfaction of the Council of Ministers. precedents.holding_summary: Under Article 311(2) proviso (c), the Supreme Court extract describes the satisfaction as subjective, with reasons not required to be recorded. The High Court states that its review is confined to whether the reasons were germane and relevant. This is a different context and cannot be applied directly to Article 356.

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The proposition that the President's satisfaction under Article 356 is beyond judicial scrutiny is not the present law. The better statement is that the satisfaction is reviewable on limited grounds.

LAW: Article 356 requires the President to be satisfied that the government of a State cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution. Under Article 74(1), and for the State Governor under Article 163(1), that satisfaction is that of the Council of Ministers. [2]], [3], [4] and [5] confirm this principle. The sources show it was articulated in Samsher Singh and discussed in Bommai.

COURT POSITION: The governing authority is S.R. Bommai (1994), a nine-judge Constitution Bench decision. It is binding on the Madras High Court under Article 141. On the constitutional notes, it holds that a Proclamation under Article 356 is subject to judicial review, that the Union must show relevant material, that a floor test is required before a ministry is dismissed, and that the power cannot be used for political ends (well-established constitutional authority; verify against the official report). Rameshwar Prasad (2006) invalidated a proclamation based on a biased report. [3]] and [5] quote Bommai only on federalism and aid and advice, so the operative holdings on reviewability are not reproduced in the sources provided. Kishore Chandra Sahoo [1] describes subjective satisfaction under Article 311(2) proviso (c), and Karnataka High Court [4] records only counsel's submissions. Neither displaces Bommai, being a different provision in the case of [1] and a non-binding submission in the case of [4].

APPLICATION: The advocate should frame the challenge as one on the existence and relevance of material, not as a re-weighing of the sufficiency of the satisfaction. The strongest grounds are mala fides, irrelevant or extraneous considerations, absence of material, and failure to hold a floor test. The reasoning that satisfaction is the Council of Ministers' also supports a demand for disclosure of the material on which the Union acted, subject to Article 74(2).

RISKS AND COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The Union will argue that satisfaction is subjective and that the Court cannot examine its sufficiency. It will cite the language in [1], and will invoke Article 74(2) to resist production of the advice. The answer is that [1] concerns Article 311(2), whereas Bommai specifically governs Article 356. It is also the Union's burden to produce the relevant material. A further risk is the stage and the relief: a court may decline to revive a dissolved Assembly if the matter is academic or the Assembly's term has expired.

LIMITS: The sources contain no complete extract of Bommai and none of Rameshwar Prasad. The full Bommai holdings must be checked in the certified or official report before filing.

relevant_law.summary: Empowers the President, on a Governor's report or otherwise, to proclaim President's Rule if satisfied that the government of a State cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution. The 'satisfaction' is the foundation of the power and the target of any challenge.

The President acts on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers, and the Governor likewise. Constitutional 'satisfaction' is therefore the satisfaction of the Council of Ministers, not the personal satisfaction of the constitutional head.

Articles 32 and 226 supply the forum for judicial review. Article 141 makes the law declared by the Supreme Court binding on the Madras High Court. Article 74(2) bars enquiry into the advice tendered to the President but not into the existence of material (notes only; verify the text of Art 74(2)).

Also turns on the President's or Governor's 'satisfaction'. The Delhi High Court extract [1] shows this satisfaction is described as subjective and reasons need not be recorded. This is a different Article and should not be transposed to Article 356.

comparative_analysis.agreements_between_courts: The Constitution Bench line, as summarised in Padi Kaushik Reddy [3], consistently places first-instance decision with the Speaker, subject to judicial review. The Bombay High Court in the Goa matter [4] agrees that courts do not ordinarily intervene before the Speaker decides.
comparative_analysis.conflicts_or_differences: No source shows a conflict on the Nabam Rebia bar itself. A tension remains: Nabam Rebia restrains the Speaker from deciding while a removal notice is pending, while Padi Kaushik Reddy [3] emphasises timely decisions and directs a decision within three months. The passages supplied do not reconcile the two or consider the interplay. Note also that Padi Kaushik Reddy is a Division Bench decision and cannot dilute a Constitution Bench ruling.
comparative_analysis.trend_analysis: The trend is toward stricter accountability of the Speaker (Tribunal status, judicial review, time-bound disposal), not toward weakening Nabam Rebia. The sources do not show any later decision overruling or limiting it, but later treatment is unchecked.

answer.conclusion:
The governing authority is Nabam Rebia (2016) [2], para 178: a Speaker cannot adjudicate Tenth Schedule disqualification petitions while a notice for his removal is pending. It binds the Madras High Court under Article 141. Padi Kaushik Reddy (2025) [3] confirms the Speaker's first-instance role and judicial review but, in the passages supplied, neither applies nor limits this bar. Before relying on it, verify from the certified copy or official report of Nabam Rebia that the paragraphs are quoted correctly, check whether any later judgment has treated or limited it, confirm that the removal notice was valid and pending on the relevant dates, and consider whether the bar can be answered by an argument that the notice is a stalling device. Do not cite the Bombay High Court decision as binding.
