COURT POSITION: The Himachal Pradesh High Court [3] holds that a complaint filed before the 15 days run out is no complaint at all, and that later lapse of the period does not cure it. The Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh High Court [6] holds that a premature complaint cannot simply be re-presented later; the remedy is a fresh complaint within one month of the decision, with delay treated as condoned under the proviso to s. 142(1)(b). Both are single-bench High Court decisions, persuasive only outside their own States, and both rely on Supreme Court decisions that appear in the sources only as quoted passages. APPLICATION: Taking the outer limits purely as an illustration: if notice were sent and received on the last day, 17 February 2026, the 15 days would end on 4 March 2026 and the complaint would be due by 4 April 2026. Actual dates depend on when the bank's information and the notice were received, and no such dates are given. If the notice was received earlier, the dates move earlier correspondingly. Remember that the complaint cannot be filed before the 15-day period expires [3]. The cause of action arises only on expiry of the fifteen days under clause (c).

Cognizance can be taken only on a written complaint by the payee or holder in due course, made within one month of the date on which the cause of action arises under clause (c) of the proviso to s. 138. LAW: The general offence is cheating by personation, defined in IPC s. 416 [1] and, for conduct on or after 1 July 2024, BNS s. 319. The definition covers pretending to be another person, knowingly substituting one person for another, and representing that a person is other than he really is, and it applies whether the personated person is real or imaginary. The online mode is separately punished by IT Act s. 66D [3], which covers cheating by personation by means of any communication device or computer resource (up to three years and fine up to Rs 1 lakh). If the personation occurred before 1 July 2024, cite IPC s. 416 with BNS s. 319 in brackets as the successor; if on or after that date, charge BNS s. 319. A continuing course of conduct running across 1 July 2024 is charged once, under the BNS. If the fraud also involved dishonest inducement to part with money, the general cheating provisions may be needed, but their text is not set out in the sources and they should be verified. APPLICATION TO FORUM: The proceeding was begun on 15 July 2026, so it follows the BNSS. The ordinary rule, CrPC s. 177 [2], now reflected in the BNSS, is that the Court where the offence was committed tries it. BNSS s. 198 permits trial in any of the local areas where the offence was uncertainly located, partly committed, continuing, or made up of acts in several areas. In online fraud the deceptive communication, the victim's loss and the accused's location often lie in different places, so the court at Meerut, where the informant reports the fraud, can plausibly be said to have jurisdiction if part of the offence occurred or its effects were felt there. None of the sources decides whether the place of receipt of the communication or of the loss suffices, and the BNSS text shown does not itself say so; this must be checked. The answer to the first is BNSS s. 198(b) and (d); the second is unresolved on these sources. The Chhattisgarh order [4] shows that courts regard such fraud as serious, but it does not bear on venue. precedents.holding_summary: Section 142(b) prescribes only the outer period (one month from the cause of action under clause (c)); no period is prescribed before which a complaint cannot be filed. A premature complaint may await maturity or be returned for refiling, and presentation is distinct from the court taking cognizance [5].

precedents.holding_summary: A s. 138 complaint must show a cheque issued, presented, dishonoured, notice served, and non-payment within fifteen days of receipt of notice. Unless the conditions precedent are satisfied, the court has no jurisdiction to take cognizance [7].

precedents.case_name: Sainaba v. State of Kerala
precedents.holding_summary: Where the notice is dispatched by registered post to the drawer's correct address, a rebuttable presumption of valid service arises (s. 27 General Clauses Act; s. 114 Evidence Act), and the drawer must rebut it. M.D. Thomas v. P.S. Jaleel (2009) was held per incuriam. This bears on fixing the date of 'receipt', and hence the start of the limitation clock [3].

precedents.holding_summary: Cause of action arises only on expiry of fifteen days from service of notice. Section 142 prescribes no earlier bar, applying Narsingh Das Tapadia [4]. Persuasive outside Uttarakhand.

precedents.holding_summary: A complaint filed beyond the period under s. 142(1)(b) is not saved by a second notice, which cannot extend or revive limitation. The complainant must seek condonation by showing sufficient cause, failing which the cognizance order was quashed [6]. Persuasive outside Patna jurisdiction.

answer.reasoned_analysis: ISSUE: The cheque was returned unpaid on 10 June 2025. The question is the time within which the s. 138 complaint must be made. LAW: Limitation is a chain of three statutory steps in s. 138 [1] followed by s. 142(1)(b) [2]. First, the cheque must have been presented within six months of its date or its validity, whichever is earlier. Second, the payee must give written notice within thirty days of receiving information from the bank of the return. Third, the drawer has fifteen days from receipt of notice to pay. The complaint must then be made within one month of the date the cause of action arises under clause (c), that is, the day after the fifteen days expire without payment. COURT POSITION: Narsingh Das Tapadia [5] holds that s. 142(b) fixes only an outer limit and no earliest date, and that a premature complaint can await maturity. Subodh Salaskar [7] holds that all conditions precedent must be satisfied before cognizance. Sainaba [3] holds that registered-post dispatch to the correct address raises a rebuttable presumption of service, which fixes the date of receipt. The Patna High Court in Subodh Kumar Rai [6] holds that a second notice does not revive limitation and that, without a condonation application showing sufficient cause, a late complaint cannot sustain cognizance. APPLICATION: Taking 10 June 2025 as the date of return, and assuming the payee learned of it that day, the notice had to go by 10 July 2025 (thirty days). If the notice was received, say, on 15 June 2025, the drawer had until 30 June 2025 to pay; the cause of action would arise on expiry of that period and the complaint would be due within one month thereafter, around 30 July 2025. These dates are illustrative only, because the actual dates of presentation, receipt of the bank's information, dispatch and receipt of notice are not given. The dates of the cheque and presentation are also unknown. RISKS AND COUNTER-ARGUMENT: As drawer's counsel, the strongest argument is that the complaint was late and no condonation was sought [6], or that the notice was out of time or not validly served. The complainant's answer is the presumption of service under Sainaba [3] and the proviso to s. 142(1)(b), which allows condonation for sufficient cause; the sources do not set the standard for sufficient cause. Delay is not otherwise condoned automatically. A second notice will not help [6]. Premature filing is not fatal [5]. LIMITS: The sources do not state the counting rule for the one month, nor any binding Supreme Court holding on condonation standards. The BNSS or CrPC applicability depends on when the proceeding was begun, which is not stated.

relevant_law.summary: The offence is complete only if (a) the cheque was presented within six months of its date or within its validity, whichever is earlier; (b) the payee/holder gives written demand notice within thirty days of receiving information from the bank of the return of the cheque unpaid; and (c) the drawer fails to pay within fifteen days of receipt of the notice. Clause (c) fixes the date on which the cause of action arises.

Cognizance is taken only on a written complaint by the payee/holder in due course. The complaint must be made within one month of the date on which the cause of action arises under clause (c) of the proviso to s. 138. The proviso permits cognizance after that period if the complainant shows sufficient cause for the delay. Trial lies before a Metropolitan Magistrate or JMFC.

Territorial jurisdiction lies where the payee's collecting bank branch is situated (cheque delivered through an account), or where the drawee bank branch is situated (cheque presented otherwise than through an account).

precedents.holding_summary: A complaint need not reproduce every ingredient of the offence or say in terms that the intention was dishonest, if a factual foundation is laid. A commercial or money transaction does not exclude cheating, since the intention of the inducer decides it. Courts should not hastily quash at the investigation stage on hyper-technical grounds [8].

precedents.case_name: Tapas Pal v. The State of Jharkhand
precedents.holding_summary: Cheating under s. 420 IPC requires deception from the beginning of the transaction; an intention formed later does not amount to cheating. The prosecution was quashed because no such allegation was made. This is persuasive only outside Jharkhand [4].

precedents.holding_summary: Dishonest intention at inception may be inferred from subsequent conduct and surrounding factors, because a fraudster does not announce his intention. The observations were expressly not binding on the trial court. This is persuasive only [6].

answer.reasoned_analysis: ISSUE: The question is which offences are made out by online cheating by personation, and where the complaint is to be lodged. LAW: Section 416 IPC [1] (BNS s. 319(1)) defines cheating by personation; the Explanation makes it immaterial whether the person personated is real or imaginary, and the illustrations include pretending to be a deceased person. The punishment is in BNS s. 319(2) (up to five years, or fine, or both). Section 66D IT Act [3] specifically punishes cheating by personation by means of a communication device or computer resource, with up to three years and fine up to Rs one lakh. If the facts also show dishonest inducement to deliver property, s. 420 IPC (BNS s. 318) may be added; its text is not reproduced in the material before me. CODE: The request does not state when the offence was committed. If it was committed before 1 July 2024 the IPC applies, and if on or after that date the BNS; the date of the offence decides this. The proceeding was begun on 18 June 2025, so procedure is under the BNSS and evidence under the BSA, with CrPC and Evidence Act numbers cited only as repealed equivalents. Electronic records will need the BSA certificate (BSA s. 63, equivalent to s. 65B IEA). COURT POSITION: Rajesh Bajaj (1999) [8], binding under Article 141, holds that a complaint need only lay a factual foundation and need not recite ingredients or the word dishonest; the nature of the transaction does not decide the matter, the inducer's intention does. Tapas Pal (2026) [4], a single bench of the Jharkhand High Court and so merely persuasive in Odisha, requires deception from the beginning. Banoji Rao Moganti (2017) [6] allows inference of initial intent from later conduct, but is persuasive only and was expressed non-bindingly. In personation cases, the pretended identity itself is the deception at inception, which addresses the Tapas Pal requirement. APPLICATION ON JURISDICTION: Section 177 CrPC [2] states the general rule of trial where the offence was committed. BNSS s. 198 allows inquiry or trial in any local area where an offence is committed partly in one area and partly in another, or consists of several acts in different areas. An online fraud typically has acts in more than one place (where the accused operated, where the complainant was deceived, where money was lost), so a court at Bhubaneswar, where the report was made, can be argued to have jurisdiction if some part occurred there. The facts do not say where the complainant was when deceived or where the loss arose. None of the sources decides how s. 198 applies to cyber offences, nor which police station must register the FIR or whether a zero FIR is available; those points need verification. The sources also contain nothing on the IT Act's own rules on investigating officer rank or on the interplay of s. 66D and the penal code in a single trial, so this should be checked against the statute and reported decisions. RISKS AND COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The defence will argue that the complaint shows only a money dispute or later-formed intent (Tapas Pal [4]), that the electronic evidence is not properly certified, and that the Bhubaneswar court lacks territorial jurisdiction because no ingredient occurred there. The answer is Rajesh Bajaj [8] and a specific pleading that the accused assumed a false identity at the outset, plus BNSS s. 198. Identity details of the complainant in the request should be kept out of any public filing. PRACTICAL ADVICE: Plead facts of the false identity used, the communication channel, the inducement, the transfer and where each occurred; invoke both IT Act s. 66D and BNS/IPC personation and cheating provisions as the facts allow; preserve electronic evidence with certificate.

precedents.holding_summary: Informing the arrestee of the grounds of arrest is a mandatory constitutional safeguard, not a formality. The grounds must be furnished in writing, in a language the arrestee understands, and it applies in all offences. Failure renders the arrest illegal. [4]

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: Two questions arise: the arrestee's rights, and bail. No facts beyond the date, place and 'cheating' are supplied, so the offence section, whether the offence is cognizable, the maximum sentence, the arresting agency, and whether grounds were given are all unknown and must be taken from the client.

LAW: Procedure follows the BNSS because the proceeding began on 27 July 2025; the CrPC survives only as the repealed equivalent. On arrest he is entitled to be told the grounds (Article 22(1); BNSS s.47, formerly CrPC s.50 [1]) and to be produced before a Magistrate without unnecessary delay and within 24 hours (BNSS s.58, formerly CrPC s.56 [2]; Article 22(2)). Mihir Rajesh Shah [4] requires the grounds in writing, in a language he understands. Vihaan Kumar [5] and Kasireddy [6] put the burden on the police to prove compliance, require the grounds to exist before being communicated, and treat the grounds as vitiating the arrest if not given. Kasireddy [6] adds that grounds must be meaningful, and they should reach relatives.

APPLICATION: First establish what he was given: a written document or oral reading, its language, time and acknowledgment, the arrest memo, and the time of production before the Magistrate. If nothing written was supplied, argue illegal arrest under [4] and [6] and oppose remand or seek release. Bail is available under BNSS s.483; also consider s.479 once the half or one-third period is completed, which for cheating depends on the section charged and its maximum term, and s.479(2) if multiple cases are pending. If the case is under the PMLA, s.45 twin conditions apply and the matter is far harder. The [5]] explains why grounds matter there, since the accused must know the basis of the officer's reason to believe. Vijay Madanlal Choudhary and Tarun Kumar appear in the rule note but are not among the sources, so I do not rely on them.

COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The State will say that the client knew the grounds and suffered no prejudice, as in Sunil Kumar Shukla [3], and that a lapse leads at most to remand being set aside, with re-arrest permissible. It will also rely on the seriousness of the cheating allegation, flight risk and tampering. The answer is that Supreme Court decisions [4][5][6] bind and place the burden on the police, and the Allahabad decision [3] was decided on its own facts, a double murder, and does not bind a Hyderabad court.

The core rights are: (i) to be told the grounds of arrest (Art 22(1); BNSS s. 47, formerly CrPC s. 50 [1]); (ii) to be told of the right to bail and to arrange sureties if the offence is bailable (s. 50(2) [1]); (iii) to be produced before a Magistrate without unnecessary delay and within 24 hours (CrPC s. 56 [2], now BNSS s. 58); and (iv) the D.K. comparative_analysis.agreements_between_courts: The Himachal Pradesh, Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh, and Jharkhand High Courts [3][5][7] all treat a complaint filed before the 15-day notice period expires as non-maintainable, with the remedy being a fresh complaint and a plea of sufficient cause under the proviso to s. 142(1)(b), relying on Supreme Court authority quoted in the extracts.
comparative_analysis.conflicts_or_differences: None of the sources shows a conflict on the one-month period or the premature-complaint rule. The Madras High Court decision [6] concerns CrPC limitation for IPC offences of up to three years and does not govern s. 138, since s. 142 operates notwithstanding the CrPC [2]. The IL&FS decision [4] concerns IBC limitation and is not relevant to s. 138.
comparative_analysis.trend_analysis: The courts apply the statutory timeline strictly and treat the proviso to s. 142(1)(b) as the only relief for delay. They allow it to be used liberally, for example by excluding time spent on a prematurely filed complaint [5].

answer.conclusion:
The limitation period for a s. 138 complaint is one month from the date the cause of action arises, that is, on expiry of the 15-day period after the drawer receives the demand notice [2][1]. It is not one month from the 30 July 2025 dishonour. The notice itself must be sent within 30 days of the bank's intimation. Late filing is saved only by showing sufficient cause under the proviso to s. 142(1)(b), and premature filing is fatal [3][5]. Before filing or defending, obtain the return memo, the notice and its proof of delivery, the cheque date, and confirm the dates. Verify the Supreme Court decisions quoted in the High Court judgments against the official reports before citing them.

precedents.court: Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh High Court (single bench)
precedents.holding_summary: Relying on Supreme Court authority quoted in the extract (Yogendra Pratap Singh), a premature complaint is not maintainable. The complainant may file a fresh complaint within one month of the decision, and delay is treated as condoned under the proviso to s. 142(1)(b) [5]. answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The query gives only the date of dishonour (30 July 2025). Limitation under s. 138 does not run from that date. It runs from the cause of action under clause (c) of the proviso, so several unstated dates decide the outcome.

LAW: Section 142(1)(b) requires the complaint within one month of the date on which the cause of action arises under clause (c) of the proviso to s. 138 [2]. That cause of action arises when the 15-day period after the drawer receives the demand notice expires without payment [1]. The notice must itself be sent in writing within 30 days of the payee receiving the bank's information of dishonour [1]. The cheque must have been presented within six months of its date or its validity period, whichever is earlier [1].

APPLICATION (illustrative, assuming the 30 July 2025 return memo reached the payee on the same day): the notice must be issued by about 29 August 2025. If it was received by the drawer on a date D, the drawer has 15 days from D to pay. The cause of action arises on the day after those 15 days expire, and the complaint is due within one month from then. For example, if the notice was received on 10 August 2025, the 15 days end on 25 August 2025 and the complaint is due by about 25 September 2025. The exact computation, including the treatment of the day of receipt, should be checked against the record. None of the sources here sets out the counting convention.

COURT POSITION: The High Courts in the [3]][5][7] hold that a complaint filed before the 15 days expire is no complaint at all, so the payee cannot rely on the period expiring before cognizance. If it is filed early, the remedy is a fresh complaint, and if that falls outside one month the payee must show sufficient cause under the proviso [2][5]. Time spent prosecuting the premature complaint can be excluded as sufficient cause [5]. These High Court decisions are single-bench rulings that quote Supreme Court authority, and the Supreme Court decisions themselves are not among the sources.

COUNTER-ARGUMENTS AND RISKS: A drawer would argue (i) the cheque was presented beyond its validity; (ii) the notice was late, beyond 30 days; (iii) the complaint was premature or filed after one month with no sufficient cause shown; and (iv) the complainant is not the payee or holder in due course. For the complainant, delay can be cured only by a sufficient-cause application under the proviso, which is discretionary.

PROCEDURE: A complaint filed now follows the BNSS since it is a proceeding begun after 1 July 2024. If any proceeding in the matter was begun before that date, the CrPC may continue to apply under s. 531(2)(a) BNSS. The s. 142 period applies either way [2]. The Madras High Court's discussion of ss. 468 and 473 CrPC [6] is about general criminal limitation and should not be applied to s. 138.

LIMITS OF THE RECORD: The sources do not give the notice dates, whether the cheque was presented in time, or the day-counting convention. They also do not include the Supreme Court judgments directly.

relevant_law.summary: The offence is complete only if (a) the cheque was presented within six months of its date or within its validity, whichever is earlier; (b) the payee gives written demand notice within 30 days of receiving information of dishonour from the bank; and (c) the drawer fails to pay within 15 days of receiving the notice. The cause of action arises on expiry of the 15-day period under clause (c) [1].

Cognizance can be taken only on a written complaint by the payee or holder in due course, made within one month of the date on which the cause of action arises under clause (c) of the proviso to s. 138. The proviso to s. 142(1)(b) lets the Court take cognizance after that period if the complainant shows sufficient cause for the delay [2].

Territorial jurisdiction lies with the court where the payee's collecting bank branch is situated (cheque delivered through an account), or where the drawee branch is situated (cheque presented otherwise than through an account) [2].

precedents.case_name: Vihaan Kumar v State of Haryana & Anr.
precedents.holding_summary: Informing the arrestee of the grounds of arrest is a mandatory constitutional requirement under Art 22(1). precedents.holding_summary: Grounds of arrest are a binding constitutional safeguard. The grounds must be furnished in writing, in a language the arrestee understands, so that the safeguard is effective. Breach renders the arrest illegal. Para 42 reads Art 22(5) and 22(1) alike, relying on Harikisan.

precedents.case_name: Kasireddy Upender Reddy v State of Andhra Pradesh and Ors.
precedents.holding_summary: Repeats Vihaan Kumar's holding in the same terms: breach of Art 22(1) makes the arrest illegal and continued remand vitiated, and a chargesheet does not validate it.

precedents.holding_summary: Bail was refused despite the argument of an Art 22(1) violation, because the applicant knew the grounds from the outset, no prejudice was shown, and the case was a daylight double murder. answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The client was arrested on 1 June 2026 at Ahmedabad for cheating. The questions are what protections attach to the arrest and whether bail can be sought.

LAW: The procedure is governed by the BNSS because the proceeding began after 1 July 2024. CrPC ss. 50, 56 and 57 [1][2][3] are only the repealed equivalents. The penal code (IPC s. 420 or BNS s. 318) cannot be decided because the date of the alleged offence has not been supplied; that date determines it. Constitutionally, Art 22(1) and 22(2) give the right to be told the grounds, to consult a lawyer, and to be produced before a Magistrate within 24 hours, excluding journey time.

COURT POSITION: The Supreme Court in Vihaan Kumar [5], Kasireddy Upender Reddy [7] and Mihir Rajesh Shah [6] holds that communication of the grounds is mandatory, not a formality. Breach renders the arrest illegal, and continued remand is vitiated. A chargesheet or cognizance does not cure it [5][7]. Mihir Rajesh Shah [6] adds that the grounds should be furnished in writing, in a language the arrestee understands. Vihaan Kumar [5] says writing is not strictly required but advisable. Each rests on Art 22(1) read with Art 21. The Madras order [8] granted bail on that basis, while the Allahabad order [4] refused it where the accused knew the grounds and showed no prejudice.

APPLICATION: The facts supplied do not say whether grounds were given, in what form or language, when production before the Magistrate took place, whether the offence is bailable, or whether any PMLA case exists. First, check the arrest memo, the grounds of arrest document, the remand application and the time of production. If no written grounds were served, or they were not in a language he understands, argue that the arrest and remand are vitiated and seek release under [5][6][7], preferably before the Gujarat High Court or the Magistrate, and in any event on regular bail. Second, whatever the position on grounds, apply for regular bail under the BNSS (CrPC s. 437/439 equivalents; section numbers to be verified). Cheating alone attracts ordinary bail principles, not PMLA s. 45. The twin conditions arise only if the Enforcement Directorate has registered a case on a scheduled offence, and nothing says so. Third, check whether the offence is bailable, in which case bail is a matter of right, and consider BNSS s. 479 for later stages. Fourth, if the client has other cases pending, s. 479(2) bars its benefit.

RISKS: The prosecution will rely on Sunil Kumar Shukla [4] to say that knowledge of the grounds and absence of prejudice defeat the plea. The Supreme Court decisions leave open whether re-arrest is possible [5][7], and the Madras order [8] expressly allows it, so release may be brief. Gujarat law on the point is not in the sources. The Supreme Court in [5] says the issue of re-arrest need not be decided at this stage. The client's identifiers in the instruction have no bearing on the legal analysis.

ADVICE: Obtain the arrest papers immediately, plead the Art 22 breach if the record supports it, and file bail in parallel.

answer.law_staleness_warning: ⚠️ Superseded provisions cited: CrPC s.164 -> BNSS s.183. | Which code applies depends on dates: The penal code follows the date the offence was committed: an offence committed before 1 July 2024 is charged and punished under the Indian Penal Code, which section 358 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita saves, and one committed on or after that date under the BNS. One continuing offence that runs across 1 July 2024 is charged once, never split by date into an IPC charge and a BNS charge (section 9(1) of the BNS allows one punishment for an offence made up of parts), and under the BNS, since it was still being committed after that date (section 1(3) of the BNS); separate offences are each charged under the code in force when each was committed. The procedure follows the date the proceeding was begun: only an appeal, application, trial, inquiry or investigation already pending immediately before 1 July 2024 continues under the Code of Criminal Procedure (section 531(2)(a) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita), and the evidence in it under the Indian Evidence Act (section 170 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam); a proceeding begun on or after that date, including an FIR lodged then for an offence committed before it, follows the BNSS and the BSA. precedents.case_name: State of Rajasthan v. Chatra
precedents.holding_summary: Quoting State of H.P. v. Sanjay Kumar, the Court calls for a sensitive, survivor-centric approach to child victims of sexual violence. It also quotes Pradeep v. State of Haryana: before recording a minor's evidence, the Judge must ask preliminary questions to test the child's understanding and her grasp of the duty to speak the truth, and should record them. These passages bear on how the child is questioned and on the weight given to her testimony. They do not decide who records the investigation-stage statement.

precedents.case_name: State of Maharashtra v. Dr. Maroti Kashinath Pimpalkar
precedents.holding_summary: Prompt reporting of POCSO offences is of utmost importance. The Court links it to the prompt medical examination of the victim under POCSO s. 27(1) read with CrPC s. 164A, and notes that medical evidence has corroborative value in sexual offences. answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: Two distinct statements are in play. First, the police statement during investigation. Second, the Magistrate's statement recorded for evidentiary purposes.

LAW: (1) Police statement. POCSO s. 24 [1] governs. It is to be recorded at the child's residence, usual place of residence or place of her choice, as far as practicable by a woman police officer not below sub-inspector rank, not in uniform. The investigating officer must ensure the child never comes into contact with the accused and must not detain her in a police station at night. Her identity must be shielded from the media unless the Special Court directs otherwise. The general power to examine and record under CrPC s. 161 [2] (BNSS s. 180) supplies the mechanism, including the audio-video proviso. The text of BNSS s. 180 is not set out in the sources; only the equivalence is named. (2) Magistrate's statement. Under BNSS s. 183(6)(a), for offences under the BNS provisions listed in it, the Magistrate must record the victim's statement as soon as the offence is brought to police notice, as far as practicable by a woman Magistrate, or by a male Magistrate in the presence of a woman. Sub-section (6) as reproduced cites BNS sections, and I cannot confirm from the sources which of them correspond to the charge here; verify that the offences alleged fall within the listed sections. Because aggravated penetrative sexual assault under POCSO carries more than ten years, the second proviso (statement of the witness brought by the police) is also engaged, although the Magistrate there records the witness the police produce. Under s. 183(5) the statement is recorded in the manner best fitted to the case, and the Magistrate may administer an oath. Where relevant, a special educator or interpreter and audio-video recording apply. It is forwarded to the trial Magistrate under s. 183(7).

COURT POSITION: Chatra [4] directs a survivor-centric approach and, quoting Pradeep, requires the Judge to test a child's competence by preliminary questions at the stage of recording evidence. These are observations on trial-stage testimony, not on investigation-stage recording. Pimpalkar [5] stresses prompt reporting and medical examination.

APPLICATION: A 10-year-old is plainly a child. Her statement to the police should be taken by a woman officer of at least sub-inspector rank, in plain clothes, at home or a place she chooses, with no contact with the accused. A Magistrate's statement should be sought promptly, ideally from a woman Magistrate. Her Aadhaar number, as supplied, is personal data that should not be reproduced in any filing; identity protection under s. 24(5) [1] reinforces this.

CODE: The date of the offence and the date the proceeding began are not stated. If the proceeding began on or after 1 July 2024, BNSS ss. 180 and 183 apply; if an investigation was pending before that date, CrPC ss. 161 and 164 continue. The penal provisions follow the offence date (IPC or BNS).

RISKS/COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The defence may say a deviation from s. 24 vitiates the statement. The words 'as far as practicable' in s. 24(1) and the s. 183(6) proviso soften that, but none of the sources decides the consequence of non-compliance. The prosecution should record reasons for any departure. A child's competence may also be challenged; the Pradeep approach quoted in Chatra [4] requires preliminary questions to be recorded.

ADVICE: Insist on the s. 24 safeguards, seek a prompt Magistrate statement, and confirm the exact listed offences in s. 183(6) and the latest authorities from the official reports.

relevant_law.act_name: The Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
relevant_law.summary: The child's statement is to be recorded at her residence, or where she usually resides, or at a place of her choice, as far as practicable by a woman police officer not below the rank of sub-inspector. The officer must not be in uniform, the child must not come into contact with the accused at any point, and she must not be detained in a police station at night. Her identity must be protected from the media unless the Special Court directs otherwise in the child's interest [1].

A Magistrate of the district where the information is registered may record a statement made during investigation, whether or not he has jurisdiction. For listed offences, including those under BNS ss. 64 to 71, 74 to 79 and 124, the Magistrate must record the victim's statement as soon as the offence is brought to the notice of the police. As far as practicable this is to be done by a woman Magistrate, or by a male Magistrate in the presence of a woman. Where the offence carries ten years or more, imprisonment for life or death, the Magistrate records the statement of the witness the police bring before him. If the person is disabled, an interpreter or special educator is to be used and the recording is to be audio-video. Under s. 183(5) a non-confession statement is recorded in the manner best fitted to the case, and the Magistrate may administer an oath. The Magistrate forwards the record to the Magistrate who will inquire into or try the case (s. 183(7)). [CrPC s. 164 is the predecessor, shown in [3] in part.]

answer.reasoned_analysis: ISSUE: The question is which provisions apply to online cheating by personation and where the complaint must be filed. LAW: Cheating by personation is defined in IPC s. 416 [1], now BNS s. 319, and the online mode is separately punishable under s. 66D of the IT Act [3]. The proceeding began on 3 January 2025, so procedure follows the BNSS, with the CrPC cited only as the repealed equivalent. The penal code is not decided on the facts given. The request does not state when the offence was committed. If the personation occurred before 1 July 2024, IPC ss. 416/417 (BNS ss. 319/318(2)) govern; if on or after that date, BNS s. 319 applies. The reporting date of 3 January 2025 is not the date of the offence. If the conduct was a continuing course running across 1 July 2024, it is charged once, under the BNS. The IT Act charge under s. 66D is unaffected by this question. COURT POSITION: The general rule is that an offence is tried where it was committed (CrPC s. 177 [2]). BNSS s. 198 widens this where the offence is committed partly in one area and partly in another, is continuing, or consists of acts in different areas; online fraud commonly fits these heads because the personator, the device, the victim and the bank account may lie in different districts. The sources do not decide which local area prevails in an online fraud, so that step rests on the statutory text alone. APPLICATION: As the report was made in Lucknow, an FIR can be lodged there and the police may investigate, but whether a Lucknow court may try the case depends on whether any part of the offence, such as the receipt of the deceptive communication or the loss, occurred within Lucknow. The advocate should plead the facts that locate the deception and the delivery of money in Lucknow, and plead both the personation (BNS s. 319) and, if property was obtained, cheating (the BNS counterpart of IPC s. 420, which is BNS s. 318(4)), along with s. 66D. The general ingredients of deception and intention at the time of inducement must be pleaded [6][7]. RISKS: A complaint lacking specific facts linking the accused to the personation risks quashing, as in Sanjeev Bansal [4], which is only persuasive in Uttar Pradesh. The opposing side will argue that the forum is where the accused or the device was located, and that the matter is a civil dispute [6]. Which authority prevails on forum is not settled by the sources, and the Lucknow court's territorial competence should be confirmed against the enacted BNSS text. ADVICE: Lodge the FIR with full particulars of the communications, payment trail and electronic records, and keep the date of the offence clearly stated so the correct penal code is charged.

ISSUE: The advocate asks which provisions protect the identity of the 8-year-old victim and what is demanded of the police and media. The name '[NAME REDACTED]' and the locality 'Cuttack' given in the query are precisely the kind of identifying details that must not appear in any pleading placed in the public domain, in any media report or in any published order. Advocates should anonymise the child in filings, using initials or a pseudonym.

LAW: The core protection is in the POCSO Act. Section 24(5), quoted in Damodhar Himtaji Dongre (2015) [1], obliges the police officer recording the statement to ensure that the child's identity is protected from the public media unless the Special Court directs otherwise in the child's interest. Section 23 separately restrains media disclosure of the child's identity, and Sections 33(7) and 37 bind the Special Court to protect identity and to try the case in camera. I have not been given the text of Sections 23, 33 or 37 in the sources, so their exact wording and the penal consequence of a Section 23 breach must be verified from the Act. IPC s. 228A (BNS equivalent to be verified) overlays this for rape-type offences, and the identity protection applies whichever penal code governs the offence.

COURT POSITION: Damodhar Himtaji Dongre (2015) [1], a single-bench Bombay High Court decision, held in the passage reproduced that these provisions are made for the benefit of the victim and not the accused. The object, the Court said, is to spare a child already victimised from giving a statement at a police station to a male officer in uniform. It follows that a breach of Section 24 cannot be used to benefit the accused. That is the ratio of the quoted passage. The Court's remarks on the investigating agency being sensitive are explanatory. The decision is persuasive before the Orissa High Court, not binding, and it does not address media liability.

APPLICATION: For the police, the requirements are: statement recorded at the child's residence or a place of her choice as far as practicable, by a woman officer not below sub-inspector rank, not in uniform, with identity shielded from the media. For the media, no name, address, school, photograph or family detail may be published, absent a Special Court order made in the child's interest. For the court, identity must be protected through the trial, which is held in camera.

Damodhar Himtaji Dongre (2015) [1] answers that the safeguards cannot be turned against the prosecution, but it is a single-bench ruling and the argument could be revived in a case where the lapse also affects the credibility of the child's testimony. APPLICABLE LAW: Under s. 138 proviso [1], the payee must (b) issue a written demand within thirty days of receiving the bank's information that the cheque was returned, and (c) wait fifteen days from the drawer's receipt of that notice. Only on the drawer's failure to pay within those fifteen days does the cause of action arise. Section 142(1)(b) [2] then requires the complaint within one month of that date, with the proviso allowing delay to be condoned for sufficient cause. COURT POSITION: The High Court decisions [3][5][6], each applying a Supreme Court ruling it quotes, hold that a complaint filed before the fifteen days expire is no complaint in law; it cannot be cured by later expiry of the period, and the remedy is a fresh complaint with a condonation plea. Those decisions are single-bench and persuasive outside their own States; the quoted Supreme Court ratio would bind under Art 141 (well-established constitutional authority; verify against the official report) but is not itself among the sources. APPLICATION: The cheque was returned unpaid on 8 May 2026. Assuming the bank's information was received that day and notice is sent and received promptly, the outer date for notice is thirty days from receipt of the bank's information, that is, about 7 June 2026. If notice is received on a date D, the drawer has until D plus 15 days to pay. If he does not, the cause of action arises the next day and the complaint must be filed within one month of that day. Illustration only: notice received 20 May 2026 gives payment deadline 4 June 2026, cause of action 5 June 2026, complaint deadline about 5 July 2026. The facts of notice date and receipt are not in the query, so exact dates cannot be fixed. Also, the cheque must have been presented within six months of its date or its validity, whichever is earlier [1]; the validity period is not in the sources beyond that proviso. Jurisdiction follows s. 142(2) [2]. COUNTER-ARGUMENT AND RISKS: A drawer will argue prematurity [3] or notice defects and out-of-time notice; the complainant's answer is strict counting and, if late, sufficient cause under the proviso [2], with [5] showing excluded time spent on a prior premature complaint. A complaint on non-service of notice is not decided by the sources. The sources do not address computing receipt of notice when sent by post or email, which must be verified. Which procedural code governs the complaint depends on when the proceeding is begun; for a May 2026 dishonour this is likely the BNSS, but I cannot fix it without that date.

relevant_law.summary: The offence is not made out unless (a) the cheque was presented within six months of its date or within its validity, whichever is earlier; (b) the payee gives written demand notice within thirty days of receiving the bank's information of dishonour; and (c) the drawer fails to pay within fifteen days of receiving the notice. Clause (c) failure gives rise to the cause of action.

Cognizance is taken only on a written complaint by the payee or holder in due course, made within one month of the date on which the cause of action arises under clause (c) of the proviso to s. 138. The proviso to s. 142(1)(b) lets the court take cognizance after that period if the complainant shows sufficient cause. Trial lies only before a Metropolitan Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate of the first class.

Territorial jurisdiction lies where the payee's collecting account branch is situated (cheque delivered for collection through an account), or where the drawer's drawee branch is situated (cheque presented otherwise than through an account).

precedents.holding_summary: Informing the arrestee of the grounds of arrest under Art 22(1) is a mandatory constitutional safeguard, not a formality. ISSUE: The client was arrested on 5 September 2025 in Thiruvananthapuram for criminal intimidation. The questions are his rights on arrest and whether he can seek bail. The framework note refers to PMLA s. 45, but no ED arrest or scheduled offence is stated, so the twin conditions are not engaged on these facts. The instructions do not say whether the arrest was with or without a warrant, whether grounds were given, when he was produced before a Magistrate, or whether any other case is pending against him. Please supply these.

LAW: Procedure follows the BNSS because the proceeding began after 1 July 2024. The penal code cannot be fixed until the date of the offence is known. His rights are as follows. First, under Art 22(1) and BNSS s. 47 (CrPC s. 50 [1]) he must be informed of the grounds of arrest. Under s. 47 the arresting officer must also tell him he is entitled to bail if the offence is bailable. Second, under Art 22(2) and BNSS s. 58 (CrPC s. 56 [2]) he must be produced before a Magistrate within 24 hours. Third, he has the right to consult and be defended by a lawyer of his choice (Art 22(1)).

COURT POSITION: Mihir Rajesh Shah [3] holds that the Art 22(1) requirement is a mandatory fundamental-right safeguard. Breach violates Art 21 and renders the arrest illegal. Vihaan Kumar [4] holds that the arrest is vitiated, that remand and custody founded on it are vitiated, and that a later chargesheet or cognizance does not cure it. Both courts treat written grounds as the proper course.

APPLICATION: Obtain the arrest memo and the remand record and check whether written grounds were given, in a language he understands, and when. If they were not, move for release on the footing that the arrest and remand are illegal (a bail application can also be filed with this ground, or a writ of habeas corpus under Art 226 can be considered). As to bail, I have assumed intimidation is a bailable offence when it falls within the simple form, but the sources do not set out the offence, so verify its classification and the section charged. If bailable, he is entitled to bail on furnishing bond and sureties (CrPC s. 50(2) [1]; confirm the BNSS provision). If it is non-bailable, apply to the Magistrate or Sessions Court under the BNSS bail provisions. The text of those provisions is not in the sources. BNSS s. 479 may also help if he has served a qualifying portion of the maximum sentence, which is unlikely so soon after arrest, and its sub-section (2) is a risk if multiple cases are pending.

RISKS: The State will say that Vihaan Kumar [4] para 15 does not require writing and that the grounds were orally communicated. Vihaan Kumar [4] para 17 leaves open re-arrest after release on this ground, so release for an Art 22 breach may not end the matter. If the arrest is actually under the PMLA, the s. 45 twin conditions apply and bail is much harder; in that event Pankaj Bansal, which is cited in the sources only as treated, becomes relevant on the written-grounds requirement.

ADVICE: First fix the facts and the provisions invoked, then lead with the Art 22(1) argument and apply for bail in parallel.

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The victim is a 16-year-old girl, so she is a 'child' (under 18) and the identity-protection regime for child victims applies. The question is what the statutes require of the media and the police.

LAW: Section 74(1) of the JJ Act [1] is the clearest source in the materials. It bars any report in a newspaper, magazine, news-sheet, audio-visual media or other communication about an inquiry, investigation or judicial procedure from disclosing the name, address, school or any other particular that may lead to identification of a child victim or witness of a crime, 'under any other law for the time being in force'. That wording covers an offence charged under the BNS or IPC and the POCSO Act. Her picture may not be published. Identification is wider than naming: a report giving her locality, school, family details or a combination of details that points to her is covered. The query itself names her and her city, and these should not appear in any pleading, order or report placed in the public domain; use initials or a pseudonym. Under the proviso, only the Board or Committee holding the inquiry may permit disclosure, for reasons recorded in writing and only in the child's best interest. Whether that proviso can be exercised by a Special Court trying a POCSO case is not decided by the sources. Contravention carries up to six months' imprisonment or a fine up to Rs 2 lakh, or both (s. 74(3)). Section 74(2) separately bars the police from disclosing the child's record, including for a character certificate, in a pending or closed case.

POLICE: The passage in Damodhar Dongre [2] records a direction that the police officer must ensure the child's identity is protected from public media unless the Special Court otherwise directs in the child's interest. It also refers to recording the child's statement at her residence by a woman officer not below sub-inspector, not in uniform. I cannot state the exact text of the POCSO provisions from the sources, so counsel should read them in the official Act. In Re: Right to Privacy of Adolescents [3] stresses strict compliance with s. 19(6) POCSO and treats non-compliance as an Art 21 violation (headnote, para 37). That decision is on welfare and reporting, not on media disclosure.

CHARGE: The offence of sexual harassment appears in BNS s. 75 [text provided], punishable with up to three years (clauses (i)-(iii)) or one year (clause (iv)). answer.reasoned_analysis: ISSUE: The query asks for the limitation period. Section 142(1)(b) fixes it at one month, but the starting point is not the date of dishonour. LAW: Under Section 138, proviso (a)-(c) [1], the sequence is: presentation within six months or validity, whichever is earlier; written demand notice within thirty days of receiving information of the return; and non-payment within fifteen days of receipt of the notice. Section 142(1)(b) [2] then requires the complaint within one month of the date on which the cause of action arises under clause (c). The cause of action therefore arises on the day after the fifteen-day payment period expires, and the one month runs from that date. The proviso to Section 142(1)(b) allows delay to be condoned on sufficient cause [2]. COURT POSITION: Yogendra Pratap Singh [7], as reported, treats a conjoint reading of Sections 138 and 142 as meaning that a complaint can be filed only after the cause of action accrues, and that a premature complaint cannot found cognizance. The High Court decisions in Kuldeep Chand Kanwar [5] and Prabhavathi [6] apply the same position, relying on a three-judge bench decision that is quoted but not itself among the sources. Sainaba [3] holds that a notice sent by registered post to the correct address is presumed served, and a drawer who pays within fifteen days of receiving summons cannot plead non-service. APPLICATION: The facts state only that the cheque was returned unpaid on 20 June 2025, and that Ramesh Gupta is the drawer. A worked timeline, on the assumption that the payee received bank information on 20 June 2025, would be: the demand notice must go by 20 July 2025; if the notice is received, say, on 25 June 2025, the fifteen days end on 10 July 2025; cause of action arises on 11 July 2025; and the complaint is due by 10 August 2025 (one month). These dates are illustrative only and must be recalculated from the actual dates of receipt of bank information and of notice. The sources do not state the cheque date, the date notice was sent or received, or the date of any complaint, so the true deadline cannot be fixed. RISKS AND COUNTER-ARGUMENT: As drawer, the strongest argument is prematurity or lateness. A complaint filed before the fifteen days end is no complaint [7][5][6]. A complaint filed after one month needs sufficient cause under the proviso to Section 142(1)(b) [2], and none appears on this record. The complainant's counter is that service is presumed where the notice was sent to the correct address, so the clock runs regardless of actual receipt [3]. The drawer must therefore establish an incorrect address or a wrong postal endorsement. The sources do not decide how the period is computed where the notice date or delivery is disputed beyond the presumption in Sainaba [3]. PRACTICAL POINTS: Check presentation within validity, the notice date, proof of dispatch and delivery, the complaint date, and territorial jurisdiction under Section 142(2) [2].

ISSUE: The question is which provisions shield the identity of a 16-year-old complainant in a sexual assault case and what they demand of police, courts and media. Because she is under 18, she is a 'child' under s. 2(d) POCSO, as applied in S. Govindaraj (2026) [4], so the child-specific regime applies, in addition to the general rape-victim protections.

LAW: First, POCSO. Sections 23 and 33(7) are identified in Chandra Mouli (2024) [5] as protecting the child's identity from media and in trial, and s. 24(5), quoted in Damodhar Himtaji Dongre (2015) [2], places a duty on the police officer to protect identity from the public media unless the Special Court directs otherwise. Second, s. 74 of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 [1] prohibits any media report disclosing the name, address, school or any identifying particular of a child victim or witness, or publishing the picture, with a proviso allowing disclosure only by reasoned written order of the Board or Committee in the child's best interest. Contravention is punishable with up to six months' imprisonment or fine up to Rs 2 lakh or both. Third, IPC s. 228A is listed in [5]; its BNS equivalent (believed to be s. 72) is not in the sources and must be verified, with the IPC applying only to disclosures before 1 July 2024.

COURT POSITION: The Kerala High Court records the Supreme Court's Nipun Saxena directions [5]: no publication of the name or anything that could identify the victim in any medium, including social media; POCSO FIRs not to be put in the public domain; police to retain identifying documents in sealed cover and substitute redacted copies; all recipient authorities to keep the identity secret. Sakshi's directions govern the trial: screen, written cross-examination questions, breaks, in-camera trial under s. 327(2) CrPC [5]. These Supreme Court directions are quoted only second-hand, and their binding force under Art 141 should be confirmed from the original judgments (well-established authority; verify against the official report). Dongre [2] is a single-judge Bombay decision, persuasive in Jharkhand, and its observation that the safeguards are for the child, not the accused, is limited to those provisions.

APPLICATION: For [NAME REDACTED], the police must not name her or her address, school or locality in FIRs available publicly, press briefings or documents; the FIR is to be kept out of the public domain; identifying documents should be sealed. Media must not name her, publish her photograph or give particulars from which she could be recognised (Ranchi, school, family); that includes social media. The Special Court must ensure non-disclosure through investigation and trial and conduct the trial in camera with the Sakshi protections. Disclosure is allowed only on a reasoned order in the child's interest.

RISKS AND COUNTER-ARGUMENT: A publisher may argue that s. 74 JJ Act applies only to Board or Committee proceedings, or that the report did not identify her. The text of s. 74(1) expressly covers a 'child victim or witness of a crime' and 'any particular which may lead to identification', which answers the first point; the second is factual. The accused may argue that police lapses vitiate the trial; Dongre [2] answers that safeguards are for the victim's benefit. Another risk is that the sources do not set out the text of POCSO ss. 23, 24 and 33, nor the penalty under s. 23, nor the Jharkhand High Court's view.

ADVICE: Cite ss. 23, 24(5), 33(7) POCSO and s. 74 JJ Act together; ask the Special Court for an order restraining publication and for sealed-cover handling; and mention that BNSS or CrPC applies according to when the proceeding began.

precedents.case_name: Vihaan Kumar v State of Haryana & Anr
precedents.holding_summary: Informing the arrestee of the grounds of arrest is a mandatory constitutional requirement under Art 22(1). Failure vitiates the arrest, and the person cannot remain in custody. Subsequent remand orders, chargesheet and cognizance do not cure the defect. Written grounds are the ideal course, though writing is not strictly required. Whether re-arrest is possible was left undecided [5].

precedents.case_name: Kasireddy Upender Reddy v State of Andhra Pradesh & Ors

precedents.case_name: Mihir Rajesh Shah v State of Maharashtra & Anr
precedents.holding_summary: Grounds of arrest are a mandatory constitutional safeguard applying in all offences. answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The client was arrested in Kolkata on 14 March 2025 for criminal intimidation. The questions are what protections attach to the arrest and whether bail can be sought.

LAW: The proceeding began on 14 March 2025, so the BNSS governs procedure; the CrPC provisions are cited only as repealed equivalents. The penal code (IPC s. 506 or BNS s. 351) turns on the date of the alleged offence, which has not been supplied, and the section numbers must be confirmed against the FIR. Art 22(1) and s. 47 BNSS (s. 50 CrPC [1]) require that the grounds be communicated forthwith, and in a bailable offence the arrestee must be told he is entitled to bail. Art 22(2) and s. 58 BNSS require production before a Magistrate within 24 hours.

COURT POSITION: Vihaan Kumar [5] and Kasireddy Upender Reddy [6] hold that failure to inform the grounds vitiates the arrest, that custody cannot continue, and that neither remand, chargesheet nor cognizance cures the defect. Mihir Rajesh Shah [7] holds that the safeguard applies in all offences and that the grounds must be in writing, in a language the arrestee understands. D.K. Basu [8] adds the memo, relative-intimation, medical-examination and lawyer-access safeguards. These are ratio on Art 22(1); the preference for written grounds in Vihaan Kumar [5] is expressed as a suggestion.

APPLICATION: The advocate should immediately obtain the arrest memo, the written grounds, the remand application and the remand order, and check: when and how the grounds were communicated; whether in writing and in a language the client understands; whether production was within 24 hours; whether a relative was informed; and whether a medical examination was done. Non-compliance supports a plea that the arrest is vitiated and a prayer for release, whether before the Magistrate or by writ under Art 226 in the Calcutta High Court. On bail, the application lies first before the Magistrate or Sessions Court (s. 437 CrPC [4] / BNSS equivalent; s. 439 CrPC [3] / s. 483 BNSS for Sessions Court and High Court). If the offence is bailable, bail is a matter of right and the arresting officer must so inform him. If non-bailable, the s. 437 CrPC [4] bar applies only to offences punishable with death or life imprisonment or on specified prior convictions. Criminal intimidation, on the ordinary understanding, does not fall in that category, but the exact provision and punishment must be checked. Anticipatory bail under s. 438 CrPC [2] (s. 482 BNSS) is not available because the arrest has already occurred.

PMLA: The framework note on s. 45 PMLA and Vijay Madanlal Choudhary does not apply on the facts given, as no PMLA case is mentioned. The twin conditions would arise only if an ED case were registered.

RISKS: Vihaan Kumar [5] left open whether re-arrest is possible after release, so the State may re-arrest with proper grounds. Defects in Art 22(1) compliance are fact-dependent, and the State will produce the arrest memo to show compliance. The sources do not include Calcutta High Court authority, nor any decision on the specific offence, nor any bail-merits authority such as Arnesh Kumar for this offence.

ADVICE: Seek the documents today, record any non-compliance, and move for bail on merits in the alternative to the Art 22 plea.

answer.reasoned_analysis: ISSUE: The question is who may record the statement of a six-year-old complainant and in what manner. LAW: Section 24 of the POCSO Act governs the police recording [1]. The statement is to be recorded at the child's residence, usual place of residence, or place of choice. As far as practicable it is to be recorded by a woman police officer not below sub-inspector rank, who must be out of uniform [1]. The officer must ensure that the child never comes into contact with the accused, the child cannot be detained at a police station at night, and the child's identity must be shielded from the media unless the Special Court directs otherwise [1]. The general police power under s. 161 CrPC (BNSS s. 180) supplies the basis for recording, including the proviso allowing audio-video recording [2]. Section 164 CrPC (BNSS s. 183) allows a Magistrate to record a statement, also by audio-video means [3]. COURT POSITION: Maroti Pimpalkar [4] is the only judgment supplied. It emphasises prompt reporting and the role of early medical examination in POCSO cases; it does not interpret s. 24, so nothing in these sources decides how strictly s. 24 is enforced or the consequence of non-compliance. APPLICATION: For [NAME REDACTED], aged 6, the investigating officer should be a woman sub-inspector or above where practicable, in plain clothes, recording at her home or a place she chooses, with a parent or trusted person present as the circumstances allow (the supplied text does not mandate this, so that is practice to verify). Audio-video recording under the s. 161 proviso is advisable to preserve an accurate record [2]. A s. 164 / BNSS s. 183 statement before a Magistrate can be sought to fix the account early; the supplied text does not prescribe child-specific procedure for it, which should be checked in the full POCSO provisions on Magistrate recording. Her identity must not reach the media [1]. The Aadhaar number given in the query is not needed for this analysis and should not be reproduced in any filing or public record, consistent with s. 24(5). RISKS: Opposing counsel may attack departures from s. 24 (a male or uniformed officer, recording at the police station) as affecting reliability; the sources do not say whether such departures are fatal or curable, since 'as far as practicable' qualifies only the first requirement. Also unresolved on this record: the date of the offence and the date of the proceeding, which decide IPC/BNS and CrPC/BNSS. PRACTICAL ADVICE: Insist on compliance with s. 24, document reasons for any impracticability, and seek prompt medical examination as emphasised in Maroti Pimpalkar [4].

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The advocate asks which provisions apply to cheating by personation online and where the complaint must be filed. The facts given are thin: an online fraud was reported by the complainant at Guwahati on 27 July 2026. The mode of fraud, the identity falsely assumed, the place of the accused, the place of the victim's device and the place of the bank account are not stated, and the date the offence was committed is not stated.

APPLICABLE LAW (substantive): Cheating by personation is defined in IPC s. 416 [1] and, for offences committed on or after 1 July 2024, in BNS s. 319, whose text is identical in substance; punishment is up to five years under BNS s. 319(2). Where the personation is by a communication device or computer resource, s. 66D of the IT Act [3] separately punishes it with up to three years and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh. Which penal code applies turns on the date the offence was committed, not the date of reporting. If the offence was completed before 1 July 2024, IPC s. 416 applies, even though the FIR of 27 July 2026 is registered under the BNSS. If it was committed on or after that date, BNS s. 319 applies. A continuing course of conduct running across 1 July 2024 is charged once, under the BNS. The aggravated cheating provisions (IPC s. 420/BNS s. 318) may also be considered if there was dishonest inducement to deliver property, but their text is not set out in the sources and should be checked.

APPLICABLE LAW (procedure): The proceeding began on 27 July 2026, so it follows the BNSS. The default rule is that an offence is inquired into and tried by the court within whose local jurisdiction it was committed (CrPC s. 177 [2], BNSS s. 197 as its equivalent, text not shown here). BNSS s. 198 permits inquiry or trial in any of the local areas where the offence is uncertain as to place, committed partly in one and partly in another area, continuing, or made up of acts in different areas. Online fraud typically spans the places where the representation is made, received and acted upon and where money is credited, so s. 198 is the principal route for Guwahati.

COURT POSITION: Ram Chandra Singh [5] supplies only the general proposition that a knowingly false representation is fraud and vitiates solemn acts; it is civil in character. The Chhattisgarh order [4] shows a High Court refusing to quash an online banking fraud on compromise because of its societal impact. Neither decides the forum question.

APPLICATION: If the complainant was deceived, or acted on the false representation, or lost money while at Guwahati, the advocate can argue that part of the offence occurred there so that BNSS s. 198(b) or (d) gives the Guwahati court jurisdiction, and that the report at Guwahati is therefore properly lodged. The charge could be framed under BNS s. 319 or IPC s. 416 together with IT Act s. 66D. Whether the IT Act's own provisions on jurisdiction or investigating rank apply is not addressed in the sources and must be checked.

RISKS AND COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The accused may argue that the offence was committed wholly elsewhere, that the victim's mere residence or mobile-phone location in Guwahati does not found jurisdiction, and that s. 66D is a special law whose punishment should not be stacked on the general provision for the same act. No authority cited here resolves either point. Compromise is unlikely to dispose of the matter given [4], which is persuasive only. The personal details in the query (mobile and Aadhaar numbers) are not needed for the legal analysis and should be kept out of any filing beyond what the court requires.

relevant_law.act_name: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (successor to Indian Penal Code, 1860)
relevant_law.summary: A person cheats by personation if he cheats by pretending to be another person, knowingly substituting one person for another, or representing himself or another to be a person other than he or such other really is. It is immaterial whether the person personated is real or imaginary. Punishment under s. 319(2) is imprisonment of either description up to five years, or fine, or both. IPC s. 416 [1] is the text for offences committed before 1 July 2024; BNS s. 319 applies to offences committed on or after that date. The request does not state the date of the offence, and that date alone decides the code.

Whoever, by means of any communication device or computer resource, cheats by personating is punishable with imprisonment up to three years and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh [3]. It is a special-law provision applicable where the personation is carried out through a computer resource, and it can be invoked alongside the general cheating-by-personation provision.

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The query asks which provisions apply to online cheating by personation, and where the complaint should be filed. The facts are thin: the complainant is named, but the nature of the fraud, the date of the offence, the accused's location, and where the money or deception operated are not stated. The mobile and Aadhaar numbers in the query are identifiers only and should not be reproduced in pleadings beyond what is necessary.

LAW: Substantively, three provisions are in play. First, the general offence of cheating by personation: IPC s.416 defines it [1] and s.419 punishes it (as extracted in Urmila Devi (2025) [4]); the BNS equivalent is s.319, with s.319(2) prescribing up to five years. Second, s.66D of the IT Act [3] punishes cheating by personating through a communication device or computer resource, up to three years and fine up to one lakh rupees. Third, if property was dishonestly delivered, cheating under IPC s.420 (BNS s.318) may be added; the ingredients of cheating are explained in Inder Mohan Goswami (2007) [5]. Which penal code applies depends solely on the date of the offence: before 1 July 2024, IPC; on or after, BNS. A continuing offence running across that date is charged once under the BNS. Because the date is not stated, the advocate must fix it first. Procedure follows the BNSS because the proceeding began on 28 March 2026.

COURT POSITION: The sources give the elements of cheating and the standard for quashing unfounded complaints [4][5], but nothing on online-offence jurisdiction. The default rule is the place where the offence was committed (CrPC s.177 [2]). s.198 BNSS allows trial in any local area where it is uncertain where the offence was committed, where it was partly committed in several areas, where it is continuing, or where it consists of several acts in different areas.

APPLICATION: In an online fraud, deception, inducement and loss often occur in different places. Shimla, where the fraud was reported, is a proper place for the report. Whether Shimla courts have territorial jurisdiction depends on where the victim was deceived or suffered loss, which the facts do not state. If part of the offence occurred in Shimla, s.198 BNSS supports jurisdiction there. The practical step is to lodge an FIR at the police station in Shimla, or through the cyber crime reporting channel, and not to rely on a private complaint at the outset.

RISKS AND COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The accused will argue that the dispute is civil or contractual and no dishonest intention existed at inception [5], or that the complaint is an abuse of process [4]. Pleading both s.66D and BNS s.319 invites an argument that they overlap; the sources do not address overlap, so this should be checked. Delay in reporting may also be used against the complainant, as in Urmila Devi [4].

ADVICE: Establish the offence date, the place of deception and the place of loss; plead BNS s.319 or IPC s.419 according to the date, together with s.66D; and keep digital evidence preserved.

precedents.case_name: Somappa v State of Karnataka (CRL.A/200068/2021) [2]
precedents.holding_summary: The High Court upheld the conviction of the printer, editor and publisher of a fortnightly newspaper under IPC 228A and POCSO Section 23 for publishing material identifying a victim, and held that hostile witnesses did not displace the documentary evidence of the publication. The extract also quotes a passage that no person may print or publish the victim's name or facts that lead to identification. The extract does not name the court from which that passage is quoted, and later treatment of Somappa has not been checked. Being a single-bench High Court decision from Karnataka, it is persuasive only in Rajasthan.

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The victim is a 14-year-old girl, so she is a child under POCSO and under the JJ Act, and the accused faces a charge of aggravated penetrative sexual assault. The question is what protects her identity and who is bound.

LAW: Three layers apply. First, POCSO Section 23 regulates media reporting and penalises disclosure of the child's identity. Second, IPC 228A (BNS 72) criminalises publication of the identity of a sexual-offence victim; the date of the offence decides IPC or BNS. Third, s. 74, JJ Act [1] bars any report that identifies a child victim or witness of a crime, and bars publishing the child's picture. Section 74(3) [1] punishes breach with up to six months' imprisonment, a fine up to Rs 2 lakh, or both. Section 74(2) [1] separately restrains the police from disclosing the child's record. The POCSO provisions on in-camera trial (s. 37) and the child's protection during deposition (s. 36) are recalled from the Act and should be checked.

COURT POSITION: Somappa [2], a single-bench Karnataka High Court decision, upheld convictions under both IPC 228A and POCSO s. 23 against those who printed, edited and published an identifying item. The court treated the documentary proof of the publication as sufficient even though some witnesses turned hostile. Its quoted passage states that no person may publish the victim's name or facts leading to identification. As it is a High Court decision from another State, it is persuasive in Rajasthan and not binding.

APPLICATION: For police: do not disclose the name, address, school, photograph or family details of the victim; keep the record confidential (s. 74(2) [1]); ensure statement recording and trial follow the in-camera and child-friendly provisions. For media: no name, address, school, photograph or detail leading to identification, even indirectly; each person in the chain (printer, editor, publisher) can be prosecuted, as in Somappa [2]. The exception in the proviso to s. 74(1) [1] lets the Board or Committee permit disclosure for recorded reasons in the child's best interest; whether it extends to a Special Court trying a POCSO case is not decided by the sources.

RISKS AND COUNTER-ARGUMENT: A media defendant may argue that s. 74 [1] is directed at proceedings before the Board or Committee and does not cover a victim in a POCSO trial; the text covers a child victim or witness of a crime under any other law, which answers the argument, but no judgment in the sources decides it. Also, Somappa [2] is only an extract and its facts are specific. Where the identity was lawfully disclosed by the victim's family, the issue needs separate research.

ADVICE: Cite the statutory text first, and use Somappa [2] as persuasive support. Check the Rajasthan High Court and Supreme Court decisions independently.

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The question is the time within which a s. 138 complaint must be filed where the cheque was returned unpaid on 1 May 2026. The answer is not a single date, because limitation under s. 142(1)(b) runs from the cause of action, which depends on when the notice is served.

LAW: Section 138 [1] creates the offence only when three proviso conditions are met. The cheque must be presented within six months of its date or its validity period, whichever is earlier. The demand notice must be given within thirty days of receipt of information of dishonour. The drawer must then fail to pay within fifteen days of receipt of the notice. Section 142(1)(b) [2] requires the complaint within one month of the date on which the cause of action arises under clause (c), that is, the day after the 15-day payment window expires. The proviso to s. 142(1)(b) allows cognizance after that period on sufficient cause.

COURT POSITION: Kuldeep Chand Kanwar [3] holds that a complaint filed before the 15 days expire is no complaint in law. The later expiry of the period before cognizance does not cure it. Sheikh Abdul Rehman [5] and Amod Prasad Nirala [7], both applying Yogendra Pratap Singh, confirm that a premature complaint cannot be revived and the complainant must file afresh, relying on the s. 142(b) proviso if the month has passed.

APPLICATION: The dishonour date is 1 May 2026, but limitation does not run from it. The latest date for the demand notice is 30 days after the payee receives the bank's information. For illustration only: if the notice is received on a date D, the payment window ends on D plus 15 days, the cause of action arises on the following day, and the complaint must be filed within one month from then. The notice receipt date is not stated in the query, so no actual last date can be computed. The query also does not state the cheque date, so compliance with the six-month presentation requirement cannot be checked.

COUNTER-ARGUMENT AND RISKS: A drawer would argue that the complaint was filed before day 15 and is therefore a nullity [3], that the notice was out of time under clause (b), or that the presentation period lapsed. The complainant's answer to delay is the s. 142(1)(b) proviso, which needs sufficient cause. The extracts in [5] and [7] show that time spent on a premature complaint may be condoned. The extracts do not state how the one-month period is counted in other respects, for example the treatment of the day of service or the effect of a notice returned unserved. Those points are not decided by the authorities cited here and should be checked against the reported decisions.

PRACTICAL ADVICE: Calendar every date from the notice. Do not file until the 15-day window has fully expired. The complaint must be made by the payee or holder in due course [2]. File it in the court with territorial jurisdiction under s. 142(2) [2].

relevant_law.summary: The offence is complete only if (a) the cheque was presented within six months of its date or its validity, whichever is earlier; (b) the payee/holder gives written demand notice within thirty days of receiving information of return from the bank; and (c) the drawer fails to pay within fifteen days of receipt of the notice. Clause (c) gives rise to the cause of action. Punishment: up to two years, or fine up to twice the cheque amount, or both [1].

Cognizance only on a written complaint by the payee/holder in due course, made within one month of the date on which the cause of action arises under clause (c) of the proviso to s. 138. The proviso to s. 142(1)(b) permits cognizance after that period if the complainant shows sufficient cause. Trial lies only before a Metropolitan Magistrate or JMFC [2].

Territorial jurisdiction lies where the payee's collecting account branch is situated (cheque delivered through an account), or where the drawee branch is situated (cheque presented otherwise than through an account) [2].
