answer.issue: How must the statement of an 11-year-old complainant ([NAME REDACTED], Bhopal), who alleges outraging of modesty of a minor, be recorded, and by which officer or Magistrate? The question turns on s. 24 of the POCSO Act, 2012 (police recording) and the Magistrate's statement under BNSS s. 183 (CrPC s. 164).
answer.law_staleness_warning: ⚠️ Superseded provisions cited: CrPC s.164 -> BNSS s.183. | Which code applies depends on dates: The penal code follows the date the offence was committed: an offence committed before 1 July 2024 is charged and punished under the Indian Penal Code, which section 358 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita saves, and one committed on or after that date under the BNS. One continuing offence that runs across 1 July 2024 is charged once, never split by date into an IPC charge and a BNS charge (section 9(1) of the BNS allows one punishment for an offence made up of parts), and under the BNS, since it was still being committed after that date (section 1(3) of the BNS); separate offences are each charged under the code in force when each was committed. The procedure follows the date the proceeding was begun: only an appeal, application, trial, inquiry or investigation already pending immediately before 1 July 2024 continues under the Code of Criminal Procedure (section 531(2)(a) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita), and the evidence in it under the Indian Evidence Act (section 170 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam); a proceeding begun on or after that date, including an FIR lodged then for an offence committed before it, follows the BNSS and the BSA. Cite the repealed equivalent in brackets where it helps the court.
answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The complainant is an 11-year-old and the allegation is outraging modesty. Two recording tracks arise: (i) the police recording of the child's statement during investigation, and (ii) the Magistrate's recording of her statement.

LAW, track (i): Section 24 POCSO [1] governs. The statement is to be recorded at the child's residence, at the place where she usually resides, or at a place of her choice. As far as practicable it is recorded by a woman police officer not below the rank of sub-inspector, who must not be in uniform. The officer must ensure the child never comes into contact with the accused. The child cannot be detained at a police station at night, and the officer must protect her identity from the public media unless the Special Court directs otherwise in her interest. These are mandatory in form ("shall"), qualified only by "as far as practicable" for the woman-officer requirement.

LAW, track (ii): Under BNSS s. 183(6)(a), for offences punishable under the listed BNS sections, which include s. 74, the Magistrate must record the victim's statement as soon as the offence comes to police notice. It is recorded as far as practicable by a woman Magistrate, or in her absence by a male Magistrate in the presence of a woman. The statement is recorded in the manner set out in s. 183(5), best fitted to the circumstances, and the Magistrate may administer an oath. The statement is then forwarded to the Magistrate who will inquire into or try the case (s. 183(7)). The enacted text shows that a statement under s. 183(5) is distinct from a confession, so the confession safeguards in s. 183(2)-(4) do not govern a victim's statement. If the child is disabled, the interpreter or special educator and audio-video provisions in s. 183(6) apply.

WHICH CODE: The request does not state when the offence was committed or when the proceeding began. The offence date decides between IPC s. 354 and BNS s. 74. The date the proceeding began decides between CrPC s. 164 (only if the investigation was pending immediately before 1 July 2024, BNSS s. 531(2)(a)) and BNSS s. 183. A fresh FIR lodged on or after 1 July 2024, even for an earlier offence, follows the BNSS. Section 24 POCSO applies under either code.

APPLICATION: The police should record the statement at the child's home or a place of her choice, by a plain-clothes woman sub-inspector or above, with no contact with the accused. The Magistrate's statement should be arranged promptly, preferably before a woman Magistrate. Sections 24 and 183(6) operate on different actors and are cumulative on their text.

RISKS: Departures from s. 24 may be attacked as irregularities, but no source here decides their consequence, and the "as far as practicable" qualifier gives the prosecution room. The sources do not show whether any other POCSO provision (such as the Special Court procedure or the statutory timelines) applies; these should be checked. Nothing in the sources addresses whether a delay in the Magistrate's recording is fatal. The Aadhaar number in the query is irrelevant to the recording procedure, and a child victim's identifying details should not be reproduced in filings or the public record.

ADVICE: Record the date of the offence and the date of the FIR, because both decide the code. Request a woman Magistrate. Keep proof of compliance with s. 24 (time, place, officer's rank, dress). Verify everything against the official texts.

relevant_law.summary: The child's statement is to be recorded at her residence, at the place where she usually resides, or at a place of her choice. As far as practicable it is recorded by a woman police officer not below the rank of sub-inspector, who must not be in uniform. answer.reasoned_analysis: ISSUE: The question is what protects the identity of a 7-year-old victim of sexual assault in Nagpur, and who is bound. LAW: Four layers apply. First, s. 23 POCSO regulates media reporting and bars disclosure of the child's identity, and s. 33(7) obliges the Special Court to ensure non-disclosure during investigation and trial, as the Kerala High Court records [4]; the text of these sections is not in the sources and must be read in the Act. Second, s. 74 of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 [1] bars any report in any medium that discloses the name, address, school or any particular identifying a child victim or witness, and bars publishing her picture, with up to six months' imprisonment or fine up to Rs 2 lakh or both; only the Board or Committee may permit disclosure, in writing and in the child's best interest. Third, s. 228-A IPC [6], reproduced in the Patna High Court extract, punishes publication of identity in rape-type offences with up to two years, and extends to publishing court proceedings without the court's permission, but excludes publication of High Court or Supreme Court judgments. Fourth, the Supreme Court directions in Nipun Saxena as quoted in Chandra Mouli [4] forbid publication in print, electronic or social media of the name or any fact leading to identification, prohibit putting POCSO and s. 376 FIRs in the public domain, and require the police to keep documents bearing the name in sealed cover and replace them with redacted copies. COURT POSITION: The Bombay High Court extract [2] records a direction that the police officer ensure identity protection from public media unless the Special Court directs otherwise in the child's interest, and holds that s. 24 safeguards are for the victim and cannot assist the accused. Sakshi, as quoted in [4], adds in-camera trial, a screen, written cross-examination questions and breaks. Dr. Maroti Pimpalkar [3] underlines prompt reporting. APPLICATION: For the police at Nagpur: record the child's statement at her home or chosen place, by a woman officer not below sub-inspector, not in uniform, with no contact with the accused (s. 24 POCSO) [6]; keep the FIR out of the public domain; seal and redact records; and do not disclose the child's records. For the media: no name, address, school, photograph or indirect identifier, including on social media. Note that the query itself names the victim; any filing, order or reporting should use a pseudonym or initials. The Special Court must try the matter in camera and may allow disclosure only on recorded reasons in the child's interest. RISKS: First, as the sources do not decide whether s. 74 JJ Act applies to victims outside Board or Committee proceedings, rely on it as supplementary and on s. 23 POCSO and the Supreme Court directions as primary. Second, a counter-argument is that an accused may say a breach vitiates the trial; Damodhar Dongre [2] answers that the protections are for the victim, though it is a single-bench view. Third, the code question is open: because the date of the offence and of the FIR are not stated, cite both IPC and BNS and both CrPC and BNSS, as above. ADVICE: Move the Special Court for express directions on anonymity, sealed records and in-camera hearing, and cite the reporting duty if media disclosure has occurred.

Only the Board or Committee holding the inquiry may permit disclosure, for reasons recorded in writing and in the child's best interest. Contravention is punishable with up to six months' imprisonment, or fine up to Rs 2 lakh, or both. Sub-section (2) restricts police disclosure of the child's records. Its application to a victim in a POCSO trial, as opposed to a Board or Committee inquiry, should be confirmed (see risks).

It also holds that later remand, chargesheet and cognizance do not cure the defect. Mihir Rajesh Shah [4] extends the rule to all offences, as the headnote records. Kasireddy [5] explains the rationale, and the Karnataka order in Nagesha [6] is a persuasive application. APPLICATION: First, ascertain from the arrest memo, the remand papers and the client whether the grounds were given, when, in what form and in a language he understands. Second, check production before a Magistrate within 24 hours (Art 22(2); s. 58 BNSS / CrPC s. 56 [2]), whether he was informed of the right to consult a lawyer and to have a relative informed, and whether he was told of his entitlement to bail if the offence is bailable (s. 47 BNSS / CrPC s. 50(2) [1]). I do not know from the sources whether criminal intimidation is bailable or cognizable; check the First Schedule of the BNSS, as the answer decides whether bail is a right or a matter of discretion. Third, if the grounds were not communicated, move the Magistrate or the High Court at Allahabad (Art 226) for release on the Vihaan Kumar ground, in addition to or alternatively to bail. On bail: apply for regular bail before the Magistrate/Sessions Court under the BNSS bail provisions (ss. 480 and 483, texts not before me). Section 479 BNSS may assist on prolonged custody: for an offence without death or life punishment, detention of one-half (one-third for a first offender) of the maximum sentence entitles him to release, subject to the provisos; the maximum sentence for the offence charged must be confirmed from the penal provision, which is not in the sources. Anticipatory bail is no longer available to him because he is already arrested. The PMLA s. 45 twin conditions, Vijay Madanlal Choudhary and Tarun Kumar named in the query are not engaged on the facts given, since no PMLA case is stated, and their text is not in the sources, so I do not rely on them. RISKS: The State will argue that grounds were communicated, orally or in writing, and that Vihaan Kumar does not demand writing. It may also argue re-arrest after release, which Vihaan Kumar left open. Also, if he is accused in more than one case, s. 479(2) BNSS bars release on bail under that section. ADVICE: Obtain the arrest memo, remand order and case diary; examine the grounds issue; and file bail in parallel, preserving the Art 22(1) plea.

answer.issue: Which penal provisions govern cheating by personation committed online, and which court has territorial jurisdiction to receive the complaint, where the fraud was reported by Anil Patel at Indore on 2026-02-07 and the date of the offence is not stated.
answer.law_staleness_warning: ⚠️ Superseded provisions cited: IPC s.416 -> BNS s.319. | Which code applies depends on dates: The penal code follows the date the offence was committed: an offence committed before 1 July 2024 is charged and punished under the Indian Penal Code, which section 358 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita saves, and one committed on or after that date under the BNS. One continuing offence that runs across 1 July 2024 is charged once, never split by date into an IPC charge and a BNS charge (section 9(1) of the BNS allows one punishment for an offence made up of parts), and under the BNS, since it was still being committed after that date (section 1(3) of the BNS); separate offences are each charged under the code in force when each was committed. The procedure follows the date the proceeding was begun: only an appeal, application, trial, inquiry or investigation already pending immediately before 1 July 2024 continues under the Code of Criminal Procedure (section 531(2)(a) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita), and the evidence in it under the Indian Evidence Act (section 170 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam); a proceeding begun on or after that date, including an FIR lodged then for an offence committed before it, follows the BNSS and the BSA. Cite the repealed equivalent in brackets where it helps the court.

A missing affidavit is a curable defect if cured before the Magistrate passes any substantive order; otherwise the consequential proceedings can be quashed. This matters if the police refuse to register the Indore complaint. The excerpt also reiterates that a dispute that is essentially civil should not be given a criminal cloak [4].

precedents.case_name: Rajesh Bajaj v. State NCT of Delhi & Ors.
precedents.holding_summary: A complaint need not reproduce the ingredients of cheating verbatim or state in terms that the intention was dishonest; if a factual foundation is laid, the Court should not hasten to quash at the investigation stage. A commercial or money transaction does not exclude cheating, since the accused's intention, not the nature of the transaction, is decisive. This is useful against an argument that the matter is merely a civil money dispute [6].

It is persuasive only in Madhya Pradesh, being a High Court of another State, and the excerpt does not show it deciding anything on personation or territorial jurisdiction [5].

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The question is which provisions apply to cheating by personation carried out online, and where the complaint should be filed. The facts supplied are minimal: a reported online fraud, Indore, 7 February 2026. The date on which the offence was committed is not stated, and that date decides the penal code.

LAW (substantive): Cheating by personation is defined in IPC s. 416 [1], now BNS s. 319, which carries up to five years, a fine, or both. If the personation occurred before 1 July 2024, the IPC governs; if on or after that date, the BNS governs. If the conduct continued across that date, it is charged once, under the BNS. The IT Act s. 66D [3] independently punishes cheating by personation through a communication device or computer resource, with up to three years and a fine up to one lakh rupees. Online personation will therefore ordinarily attract both s. 319 BNS (or s. 416 IPC) and s. 66D. If the fraud also involved dishonest inducement to part with money, the general cheating provisions may also be considered. Their text is not before me, so they should be checked from the statute. Rajesh Bajaj [6] supports treating the intention of the accused, not the commercial form of the transaction, as decisive. The question whether combining these charges offends any bar on double punishment is not addressed by the sources and must be verified.

LAW (procedure): The proceeding began on 7 February 2026, so the BNSS applies, with the CrPC cited only as the repealed equivalent. The general rule in CrPC s. 177 [2] is trial where the offence was committed. BNSS s. 198 permits inquiry or trial in any of several local areas where the place is uncertain, the offence is committed partly in one area and partly in another, it is continuing, or it consists of several acts in different areas. For an online fraud, where the victim, the accused, the bank and the device may all be in different places, the argument is that the offence was committed partly at Indore, where the victim was deceived and suffered loss, so that an Indore court has jurisdiction. The sources do not decide whether the place of the victim's receipt of the deceptive communication or loss is enough, so that point needs authority from the Madhya Pradesh High Court or the Supreme Court. Police registration, as distinct from trial venue, is a separate question. Its rules are not in the sources and should be verified.

COURT POSITION AND APPLICATION: If the police at Indore decline to register an FIR, S.N. Vijaylakshmi [4] holds that the Priyanka Srivastava directions are mandatory: approach the Superintendent of Police, then the Magistrate with a supporting affidavit. An affidavit filed late is a curable defect only if filed before the Magistrate's first substantive order. The Chhattisgarh High Court order [5] shows how courts treat OTP and banking-credential frauds as serious economic offences, but it is persuasive only.

RISKS AND COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The defence may argue that the matter is a civil money dispute, or that Indore lacks territorial jurisdiction because the accused acted elsewhere. Rajesh Bajaj [6] answers the first; BNSS s. 198 answers the second, subject to the gap noted above. Also, the query contains the complainant's mobile number and Aadhaar number. These are not needed for legal analysis and should not be reproduced in filings beyond what the court requires.

PRACTICAL ADVICE: Fix the date of each act of personation first, since it decides IPC or BNS. Plead s. 319 BNS (or s. 416 IPC) together with s. 66D IT Act, and plead the Indore nexus facts specifically.

The BNS applies only if the offence was committed on or after 1 July 2024; for an earlier offence the IPC applies.

Where it is uncertain in which of several local areas an offence was committed, where it is committed partly in one area and partly in another, where it is continuing in more than one area, or where it consists of several acts in different areas, it may be inquired into or tried by a Court having jurisdiction over any of those areas. This is the provision that most naturally accommodates an online fraud that spans locations.

precedents.case_name: Yogendra Pratap Singh v. Savitri Pandey & Anr.
precedents.holding_summary: The cause of action under s. 138 accrues only when the drawer fails to pay within 15 days of receiving the notice. A complaint filed before that is premature and is no complaint in law, and cognizance cannot be taken on it even if the 15 days expire later. This fixes the start of the one-month period under s. 142 [6].

precedents.case_name: Sainaba v. State of Kerala
precedents.holding_summary: Where the notice is dispatched by registered post to the correct address, there is a rebuttable presumption of valid service, and 'giving' of notice is distinct from 'receipt'. M.D. Thomas v. P.S. Jaleel (2009) was held per incuriam for ignoring C.C. Alavi Haji. This governs when the 15-day period starts [3].

precedents.case_name: Sanjabij Tari v. Kishore S. Borcar & Anr.
precedents.holding_summary: The Court stressed the object of Chapter XVII and the presumptions under ss. 118 and 139. It issued directions for s. 138 cases, including dasti and electronic service of summons and a synopsis in each complaint. These are procedural and do not alter the limitation period [4].

precedents.case_name: Tedhi Singh v. Narayan Dass Mahant
precedents.holding_summary: The s. 139 presumption is rebuttable on a probable defence. It is relevant to merits, not to limitation [5].

answer.reasoned_analysis: ISSUE: The limitation question is when the one-month period under s. 142(1)(b) starts and ends. The date of dishonour (28 March 2025) is not itself the trigger. LAW: s. 142(1)(b) requires the complaint within one month of the date on which the cause of action arises under clause (c) of the proviso to s. 138 [2]. Clause (c) is the drawer's failure to pay within 15 days of receiving the demand notice [1]. That notice must itself be given within 30 days of the drawer's receiving information of dishonour from the bank [1]. COURT POSITION: Yogendra Pratap Singh [6] holds that the cause of action accrues only after the 15 days lapse without payment. A complaint filed earlier is premature and no cognizance can be taken on it. Sainaba [3] confirms that dispatch by registered post to the correct address raises a rebuttable presumption of service under s. 27 of the General Clauses Act, so the 15 days run from the presumed date of delivery in the ordinary course unless the drawer rebuts it. APPLICATION: On the stated date, dishonour was 28 March 2025. Assuming the bank's information reached the payee that day, the notice must be given by about 27 April 2025 (30 days). If the notice was received on date N, the drawer's 15 days end on N+15. The complaint must then be filed within one month after that, that is, from N+16 to roughly N+15 plus one month. For example, a notice received on 10 April 2025 gives a payment deadline of 25 April 2025 and a complaint deadline of about 25 May 2025. These dates are illustrative only, as the actual dates of notice and receipt are not stated. If the notice was returned unclaimed, the presumption in Sainaba [3] and K. Bhaskaran, as quoted there, fixes the start date. Delay can be condoned under the proviso to s. 142(1)(b) on sufficient cause [2]. The sources do not set out the standard for sufficient cause. RISKS AND COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The drawer may argue that the notice went out of time, to a wrong address, or that the complaint is premature under Yogendra Pratap Singh [6]. A premature complaint cannot be cured by later lapse of the 15 days. The drawer may also rebut the service presumption, or argue limitation. The complainant's answer is the proviso to s. 142(1)(b) and the Sainaba presumption [3]. Presentation within six months or the validity period of the cheque, whichever is earlier, is also a precondition [1]. The sources do not state the date of the cheque, the notice, or the delivery. The advocate's identification of the party (drawer) matters: the limitation runs against the payee or holder in due course who files, not the drawer.

relevant_law.summary: The offence is complete only when three conditions are met. The cheque must be presented within six months of its date or its validity, whichever is earlier. A written demand notice must be given within 30 days of receipt of the bank's information of dishonour. The drawer must then fail to pay within 15 days of receipt of that notice.

Cognizance is taken only on a written complaint by the payee or holder in due course. The complaint must be made within one month of the date on which the cause of action arises under clause (c) of the proviso to s. 138. The proviso to s. 142(1)(b) allows the court to take cognizance after that period if the complainant shows sufficient cause. Trial lies only before a Metropolitan Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate of the first class.

Territorial jurisdiction depends on where the payee's or holder's account branch is situated (cheque delivered for collection through an account), or where the drawee branch is situated (cheque presented otherwise than through an account).

relevant_law.summary: Service of a notice by registered post to the correct address is presumed effective at the time it would be delivered in the ordinary course of post, unless the contrary is proved. This affects when the 15-day period, and so the one-month limitation, begins to run.

precedents.case_name: Prabir Bhuian @ Prabir Bhuinyan v State of West Bengal
precedents.holding_summary: The Court held that s.228A IPC prohibits more than naming the victim. It also prohibits any matter from which identity can be discerned, such as school results, the name of the village, or unblurred relatives and neighbours. It reproduces the Supreme Court direction that no person may print or publish, in print, electronic or social media, the victim's name or disclose facts that lead to identification. It also records Lalit Yadav (2018) 7 SCC 499 on the duty of courts. This is the Calcutta High Court's own view and is directly relevant to a Kolkata victim.

precedents.case_name: Somappa v State of Karnataka
precedents.holding_summary: The printer, editor and publisher of a newspaper that published identifying matter were convicted under IPC s.228A and POCSO s.23. Documentary proof of the publication sufficed, and the hostility of some witnesses did not defeat it. The Court also relied on Satyan v State of Kerala (2023) 13 SCC 767 for the point that official witnesses may be relied on if reliable. That decision is not itself before me. This is a Karnataka decision and only persuasive in Calcutta.

precedents.case_name: State of Rajasthan v Om Prakash
precedents.holding_summary: The Court restored a conviction for the rape of an eight-year-old and stressed a sensitive approach to child rape cases, referring to Art 39. It is relevant to the gravity and sentencing approach for child rape. The extracts before me do not address anonymity, so it does not support any identity-protection proposition.

answer.reasoned_analysis: ISSUE: The victim is an 11-year-old, so two regimes operate together: the rape-victim anonymity rule in the penal code and the child-specific protections in POCSO. LAW: Section 228A IPC (BNS s.72) bars printing or publishing the victim's name or any matter that may make her identity known. Prabir Bhuian [2] stresses that sub-section (2) permits publication relating to court proceedings only with the court's permission, and that the Explanation exempts High Court and Supreme Court judgments. Under POCSO s.23, as applied in Somappa [1], a publication that identifies a child victim is an independent offence. COURT POSITION: Prabir Bhuian [2] reads the prohibition widely. Name, school, village, a school result with the State, and unblurred relatives or neighbours can each identify the victim. It also quotes the Supreme Court direction that no one may disclose, even in a remote manner, facts leading to identification, in print, electronic or social media. Lalit Yadav [2] requires courts to avoid naming the victim in orders and judgments. Somappa [1] shows the offence is made out by proving the publication and the roles of printer, editor and publisher. Hostile witnesses do not defeat it. APPLICATION: For the media, nothing may be published that names [NAME REDACTED] or discloses her school, locality, family or other particulars from which she can be identified, and this applies equally to online and broadcast outlets. For the police and the court, the sources require anonymity in the record. The FIR, chargesheet, orders and judgment should carry a pseudonym or initials, and the advocate should seek directions to that effect. answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The victim is a 10-year-old girl, so she is a child under POCSO. The accused is charged with sexual assault on a child. The question is what protects her identity and what is demanded of the police, the media and the court. [NAME REDACTED]'s name should not appear in any of the court papers or in this research, and the advocate should anonymise it in all filings.

LAW: Several layers apply. First, POCSO ss. 23 and 33(7), recorded in Chandra Mouli [4], regulate media reporting and the Special Court's handling of identity. I could not verify their wording from the sources, so the text must be read from the Act. Second, s. 74 of the JJ Act, 2015 [1] bars any report that could identify a child victim or witness of a crime, and bars publishing the picture. Contravention carries up to six months' imprisonment, or a fine up to Rs 2 lakh, or both under s. 74(3) [1]. Section 74(2) bars the police from disclosing the child's record. Third, s. 228A IPC (BNS s. 72, to be verified) penalises disclosure of a sexual offence victim's identity. The IPC or the BNS applies according to the date of the offence, which is not stated. Fourth, the Supreme Court directions quoted in Chandra Mouli [4] (Nipun Saxena) apply.

COURT POSITION: The directions at 50.1 to 50.7, as quoted in Chandra Mouli [4], forbid publication in any medium of the name or of facts that could identify the victim. They keep POCSO FIRs out of the public domain. They require the police to seal documents showing the name and to use redacted substitutes in public records. Every authority receiving the name must keep it secret. Damodhar Dongre [2] records the direction that police ensure protection of the child's identity from the media unless the Special Court directs otherwise. It also states that these protections exist for the victim, so a lapse cannot be turned to the accused's advantage. Sakshi, as quoted in Chandra Mouli [4], adds trial protections such as a screen and written cross-examination questions.

APPLICATION: The police must not disclose the name, address, school or picture of the child. They must keep her FIR off public platforms, seal documents carrying her name and use redacted copies. Media in any form, including social media, must publish nothing that could lead to her identification, since an indirect clue also counts. A route to the s. 74 proviso exists. The Board or Committee may allow disclosure in the child's best interest, with reasons recorded in writing. Under POCSO the Special Court may direct otherwise, according to the direction quoted in Damodhar Dongre [2]. The trial should be in camera with the Sakshi safeguards.

RISKS AND COUNTER-ARGUMENT: An accused or a media defendant may argue that s. 74 JJ Act is aimed at Board and Committee proceedings and does not govern a POCSO Special Court trial. The sources do not decide that. The better course is to rely primarily on POCSO and the Supreme Court directions. An accused may also say that an identity lapse vitiates the trial. Damodhar Dongre [2] answers that such protections are for the victim, but that is a single-bench passage marked as operative directions, so it carries limited weight. The dates of the offence and of the FIR decide between the IPC/CrPC and the BNS/BNSS. Nothing in the sources says whether the Rajasthan High Court has issued any local directions.

The reference to PMLA s. 45 in the framework does not fit these facts: nothing indicates that hurt is a scheduled offence or that the Enforcement Directorate is involved. The penal code is not decided because the date of the offence is not stated: the IPC applies if it was committed before 1 July 2024, the BNS if on or after. The charged section and its bailability are also not stated. Section 50 CrPC [1] (now s. 47 BNSS) requires the arresting officer to communicate the grounds forthwith and, where the offence is bailable, to say that the arrestee may be released on bail and arrange sureties. Section 56 CrPC [2] requires production before a Magistrate without unnecessary delay, and Art 22(2) fixes the 24-hour limit.

COURT POSITION. Vihaan Kumar [3] and Kasireddy Upender Reddy [4] hold that the requirement to inform the grounds is mandatory and constitutional; breach violates Arts 22(1) and 21, the arrest is vitiated, and so is the remand that follows. A chargesheet or cognizance order does not validate it. Mihir Rajesh Shah [5] extends this to all offences and refers to written communication in a language the arrestee understands. D.K. Basu [7] requires an arrest memo, intimation to a relative, medical examination and production of the memo to the Magistrate.

APPLICATION. The first task is to establish from the arrest memo, the remand application and the case diary what was communicated, when, in what form and language, and whether a relative was informed. If the grounds were not communicated, the argument is that the arrest and remand are illegal and the client must be released, an argument available in the remand court and before the High Court under Art 226 or in the bail application itself. On bail, if the offence charged is bailable, the client is entitled to be released on furnishing bail and the police were obliged to tell him so. If it is non-bailable, the application lies first to the Magistrate and then to the Sessions Court or High Court; the relevant BNSS texts are not shown here and must be checked.

RISKS AND COUNTER-ARGUMENT. The State will say the grounds were communicated orally, that writing is not strictly required (Vihaan Kumar [3]), and that the memo shows compliance. It may argue that a more serious section (for example grievous hurt) has been added, that the injury is grave, or that release on an illegal-arrest finding permits re-arrest, a point both Vihaan Kumar [3] and Kasireddy [4] left open. D.K. Basu [7] is a general guideline; Sanjay Mukeshbhai Patel [6] is persuasive only.

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The question is which provisions protect the identity of [NAME REDACTED], a 14-year-old victim of alleged sexual harassment, and what they require of the police and the media.

LAW: She is a 'child' because she is under 18 (POCSO s. 2(d), as the Madras High Court's reading in S. Govindaraj (2026) [5] confirms). Three layers of protection apply. First, s. 74(1) of the JJ Act, 2015 [1] bars any report in any medium that discloses her name, address, school or any other particular leading to her identification, and bars publishing her picture. It covers a 'child victim or witness of a crime' under any other law, so it reaches a POCSO prosecution. The only exception is a written, reasoned permission from the Board or Committee in the child's best interest. Contravention is punishable under s. 74(3) [1] with imprisonment up to six months, a fine up to Rs 2 lakh, or both. Second, POCSO ss. 23 and 24(5) impose the media bar and the police duty. The text of s. 23 is not in the sources and must be verified. The police duty is reflected in the extract of Damodhar Himtaji Dongre (2015) [2], which quotes the requirement that the officer ensure the child's identity is protected from the public media unless the Special Court directs otherwise in the child's interest. Third, IPC s. 228A (or its BNS counterpart) may apply if the charged offence falls within the offences it lists. That depends on the charge and the date of the offence, and neither is stated.

COURT POSITION: The Bombay High Court in Damodhar Himtaji Dongre (2015) [2], a single-bench decision, observed that these safeguards are for the victim's benefit and that their breach cannot be used by the accused. That passage appears among operative directions and states no wider proposition of law. The Supreme Court in In Re: Right to Privacy of Adolescents (2024) [3] linked child-victim protection to Art. 21 but did not decide the identity-disclosure question.

APPLICATION: The police must keep her name, address, school and similar particulars out of media communications and out of any material that could reach the media, and must not disclose her records under s. 74(2) [1]. Media must not publish identifying particulars or her photograph. Courts should anonymise her in orders and judgments, as the Madras High Court did in S. Govindaraj (2026) [5] by referring to her as 'X'. Any permitted disclosure needs a recorded best-interest reason.

RISKS AND COUNTER-ARGUMENT: A media body may argue that s. 74 [1] covers only reports on inquiry, investigation or judicial procedure involving a child and is subject to the Board's proviso. It may also argue that it reported without identifying particulars. The answer is that s. 74(1) [1] covers any particulars that 'may lead to' identification, which is wider than naming. Jharkhand has no state law identified in the sources that changes this position. The Jharkhand High Court's position on enforcement is not addressed by the sources.

ADVICE: Cite s. 74 JJ Act [1] for the media bar and penalty, and verify the POCSO ss. 23 and 24 text and the IPC s. 228A/BNS equivalent before filing. State the offence date and the date the proceeding began, since they decide between IPC/BNS and CrPC/BNSS.

ISSUE: Manoj Patel was arrested on 16 January 2026 in Guwahati for criminal breach of trust. The questions are what rights attach to the arrest and whether bail can be sought. The information must be effective and in a language he understands, and the burden of proving compliance is on the agency [4]. (2) He must be produced before a Magistrate without unnecessary delay and within 24 hours (CrPC s. 56 [2]; BNSS s. 58; Art. 22(2)). (3) He may consult an advocate and may meet one during interrogation under BNSS s. 38. (4) He may insist on D.K. Basu protections, including an arrest memo, informing a relative or friend, and medical examination [6]. The Gujarat bench is persuasive only, though D.K. Basu itself is a Supreme Court authority from the notes (verify against the official report). COURT POSITION: A vitiated arrest and the remand orders following it fall, but the investigation, chargesheet and trial survive [4]. A chargesheet does not cure it [7]. Re-arrest was left open [7].

BAIL: Criminal breach of trust is, on my general knowledge, an offence for which bail is ordinarily sought under the general bail provisions, and the bail provisions applicable should be confirmed from the BNSS text. If the offence is non-bailable, the court has discretion. The special twin conditions of PMLA s. 45 apply only if he is arrested under that Act, which the facts do not show. ISSUE: The query asks which provisions apply to online cheating by personation and where the complaint should be filed. LAW: The definition of cheating by personation is in BNS s. 319(1), the successor to IPC s. 416 [1]; the punishment is in s. 319(2), up to five years, or fine, or both. Where a communication device or computer resource is used, IT Act s. 66D [3] applies, with up to three years and a fine up to Rs 1 lakh. The Chhattisgarh order [4] records a charge under BNS s. 318(4) with IT Act s. 66D. The sources do not set out the text of s. 318(4), so I name it only. WHICH CODE: The penal code depends on the date of the offence, which is not stated. If it was committed before 1 July 2024, the IPC applies. If it was committed on or after 1 July 2024, the BNS applies. A continuing offence running across that date is charged once under the BNS. PLACE OF FILING: The general rule is that an offence is inquired into and tried where it was committed (CrPC s. 177 [2], now BNSS s. 197). Under BNSS s. 198, where the offence was committed partly in one area and partly in another, or consists of acts in different areas, it may be tried by a court of any such area. In online fraud the deception may be received in Indore, the money may be transferred elsewhere, and the accused may be in another State, as the many-State acknowledgements in [4] show. Since the report has already been made in Indore, a complaint there is supportable on the basis that the victim was deceived and suffered loss there, on the multi-area limb of s. 198. The sources do not decide whether the victim's location alone fixes jurisdiction, and no judgment cited here addresses it.

The answer is to plead specific facts showing a false identity assumed at the outset, because dishonest intention at inception is the gist of the offence [5]. Evidence of each accused's knowledge is needed, as Monica Bedi [7] shows.

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The question is who may record the statement of a 10-year-old complainant and in what manner. There are two distinct modes: a police statement during investigation, and a statement before a Magistrate.

LAW: Under s. 24(1) POCSO [1], the police statement is recorded at the child's residence or usual place of residence, or at a place of her choice, and as far as practicable by a woman police officer not below the rank of sub-inspector. Under s. 24(2) the officer must not be in uniform. Under s. 24(3) the investigating officer must ensure the child never comes into contact with the accused. Under s. 24(4) the child cannot be detained at the police station at night. Under s. 24(5) her identity must be protected from the media unless the Special Court directs otherwise in the child's interest. The Magistrate's statement is governed by s. 25 POCSO [2] read with s. 164 CrPC [4] (BNSS s. 183). The Magistrate must record the statement as spoken by the child, and the accused's advocate has no right to be present. Under s. 164(2) the Magistrate must be satisfied that the statement is voluntary [4]. Under s. 25(2) the child and her parents or representative are entitled to the s. 207 CrPC documents after the final report [2].

COURT POSITION: Anurudh (2026) [5] describes POCSO as a self-contained code designed to ensure a child-friendly process. Its observation that s. 2(d) makes age the sine qua non is part of the reasoning for applying POCSO and supports establishing her age by the s. 94 JJ Act [CITATION UNVERIFIED] hierarchy. Maroti Pimpalkar (2022) [7] stresses prompt reporting and medical examination under POCSO s. 27(1), although its observations on the nature of s. 164A are not a holding on the recording of statements.

APPLICATION: Because the child is 10, she is plainly within s. 2(d). The police should record her statement at home or a place of her choice, through a woman officer of at least sub-inspector rank in plain clothes, with no contact with the accused. The advocate should also seek a s. 164 CrPC / s. 183 BNSS statement before a Magistrate, recorded as spoken, without the accused's counsel. Medical examination should follow POCSO s. 27 and the applicable CrPC s. 164A / BNSS s. 184 procedure. BNSS s. 184 on its text covers rape or attempted rape. Whether it extends to the offence alleged here depends on the sections actually invoked. Her Aadhaar number, supplied in the query, should not be reproduced in filings or open documents, given the identity protection in s. 24(5) [1].

RISKS/COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The defence may argue non-compliance with s. 24, for example a male or uniformed officer, or a statement recorded at the police station. The sources do not state the consequence of such non-compliance, and the wording 'as far as practicable' in s. 24(1) gives the prosecution room to argue substantial compliance. Which code governs (CrPC or BNSS) turns on whether the investigation was pending before 1 July 2024, and the date of offence determines IPC versus BNS. Neither date is given.

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The question is the limitation for a s. 138 complaint. The statute prescribes no single fixed date. The date is derived from a chain of events, and the only fixed fact stated is that the cheque was returned unpaid on 30 October 2025. The query also does not say who the complainant is, so the advocate's side (drawer or payee) must be confirmed.

LAW: Section 138 makes the offence depend on three proviso conditions [1]. Time runs as follows. First, the cheque must have been presented within six months of its date or its validity, whichever is earlier. Second, the payee must issue a written demand notice within 30 days of receiving the bank's information of the return. Here, treating 30 October 2025 as the return date, the notice should go by about 29 November 2025, but the 30 days run from receipt of the bank's information, so the exact date of that information matters. Third, the drawer has 15 days from receipt of the notice to pay. Section 142(1)(b) then requires the complaint within one month of the date the cause of action arises under clause (c), that is, from the day after the 15-day period expires [2]. The limitation for the complaint is therefore one month from expiry of the 15-day payment window, not one month from 30 October 2025.

ILLUSTRATION (assumed facts, to be replaced by actual dates): if the bank intimated the return on 30 October 2025 and the notice was served on 10 November 2025, the 15 days expire on 25 November 2025, and the complaint is due within one month from then, around 25 December 2025. Counting conventions for the first and last day should be checked against the record.

COURT POSITION: The High Court decisions in the sources, quoting Supreme Court authority, hold that a complaint filed before the 15 days lapse is 'no complaint at all' and cognizance on it is barred, even if the period lapses before cognizance [4]. The remedy is a fresh complaint, and delay can be condoned under the proviso to s. 142(b), including by excluding the time spent on the premature complaint, if the fresh complaint is filed within one month of the decision [5][7].

APPLICATION AND COUNTER-ARGUMENT: If the advocate acts for the complainant, the risks are a late notice (beyond 30 days), a premature complaint, a wrong forum under s. 142(2), and a late complaint requiring a sufficient-cause plea. The condonation proviso is discretionary, and the Delhi High Court decision shows courts will reject poorly explained delay in a related limitation setting [6]. If the advocate acts for the drawer, the strongest defences are non-compliance with any proviso condition, prematurity, the one-month bar and territorial jurisdiction. The complainant's best answer to a late filing is a sufficient-cause application, and to a notice dispute is the presumption of service where the notice was sent to the correct address, as recorded in [4], together with the pay-after-summons opportunity from C.C. Alavi Haji as mentioned there.

LIMITS: IL&FS [3] contains only operative directions on a different statute and does not bear on this question. The sources do not give the six-month presentation rule's interaction with the later three-month validity of the cheque. The relevant s. 138 provisions in the sources do not mention the 143A or 148 deposit provisions. The query's personal identifiers are not relevant to the analysis and are not repeated.

relevant_law.summary: The offence is complete only if (a) the cheque was presented within six months of its date or within its validity, whichever is earlier; (b) the payee or holder in due course gave written demand notice within thirty days of receiving information from the bank of the return; and (c) the drawer failed to pay within fifteen days of receiving that notice. Punishment is imprisonment up to two years, or fine up to twice the cheque amount, or both [1].

Cognizance is only on a written complaint by the payee or holder in due course. The complaint must be made within one month of the date the cause of action arises under clause (c) of the proviso to s. 138, that is, expiry of the 15-day payment period. The court may take cognizance later if sufficient cause for the delay is shown. The trial court must be a Metropolitan Magistrate or JMFC [2].

Territorial jurisdiction lies with the court where the payee's collecting branch is situated (cheque delivered through an account), or the drawee bank branch where the drawer maintains the account (cheque presented otherwise than through an account) [2].

answer.reasoned_analysis: ISSUE: The question is the correct set of offences for online cheating by personation and the forum for the complaint. LAW: Cheating by personation is defined in IPC s. 416 [1], now s. 319 BNS, whose enacted text is identical in substance and carries up to five years' imprisonment, fine, or both. Whether the IPC or BNS version applies depends on the date of the offence. The query gives only the date of reporting, 12 August 2025, which is not the date of the offence. If the personation occurred before 1 July 2024, the IPC (ss. 416/419, with s. 420 if property was delivered) applies; if on or after that date, the BNS (s. 319, with s. 318 for cheating) applies. For a continuing course of conduct crossing that date, the BNS applies and the offence is charged once. In addition, s. 66D IT Act [3] applies independently where a communication device or computer resource was used, with imprisonment up to three years and fine up to Rs 1 lakh. Both can ordinarily be invoked in the FIR, as the practice in the Chhattisgarh orders shows [4][6]; whether this raises a double-punishment objection is not decided by the sources. COURT POSITION: Rikhab Birani [5] requires that dishonest intention existed from the start; the complaint should therefore plead the false identity, the inducement, and the delivery of money or property. PROCEDURE: As the proceeding began on 12 August 2025, the BNSS governs, not the CrPC. FORUM: The general rule is that trial lies where the offence was committed [2] (s. 197 BNSS). Because online offences span locations (where the victim was deceived, where money was paid out, where the accused operated), s. 198 BNSS permits trial in any court with jurisdiction over any such area. The report was made at Cuttack, so the Cuttack court is a proper forum if the victim was deceived or suffered loss there; the facts do not say. The sources do not decide whether the police station must accept an FIR for an offence with no local nexus, and a zero FIR with transfer is a general procedural point I cannot support from them. Section 66D offences are also not addressed in terms of the police officer's rank competent to investigate, so check the IT Act itself. RISKS: The accused may argue a civil dispute [5], that no personation is shown, or lack of territorial jurisdiction. The identifiers in the query (mobile number, Aadhaar) are personal data of the complainant and should not be reproduced in filings beyond what is necessary. PRACTICAL ADVICE: Draft the FIR with specifics of the false identity, the electronic channel and the payment trail, and plead the locations in Cuttack.

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The victim is 14 and the charge is aggravated penetrative sexual assault. The question is which provisions protect her identity and what they demand of the police and the media.

LAW: Three layers appear in the sources. First, s. 74(1) of the JJ Act, 2015 [1] bars any report in any medium on any inquiry, investigation or judicial procedure that discloses name, address, school or any particular leading to identification of a child victim or witness, or publishes her picture. The text covers a child victim 'under any other law for the time being in force', so a POCSO victim falls within the words. Breach is punishable under s. 74(3) with up to six months, or fine up to Rs 2 lakh, or both. The only gateway to disclosure is the proviso: the Board or Committee may permit it, for reasons recorded in writing, in the child's best interest. Second, s. 228-A IPC, quoted in Nagendra Kumar [4], criminalises publishing the identity of a victim of a s. 376-series offence and publishing court-proceeding matter without the court's permission, with an exception for High Court and Supreme Court judgments. If the alleged offence is a s. 376-series offence, as aggravated penetrative assault typically is, s. 228-A is engaged. The BNS equivalent is understood to be s. 72, but that is not in the sources and must be verified. Which code governs turns on the date of the offence, which is not stated. Third, s. 24 POCSO, as quoted in [2] and [4], governs the police. They must record her statement at her residence or place of choice, by a woman officer not below sub-inspector, not in uniform, without contact with the accused, and, per s. 24(5) quoted in [2], must ensure her identity is protected from the public media unless the Special Court directs otherwise in her interest. On what the police must not do, s. 74(2) JJ Act [CITATION UNVERIFIED] bars disclosure of the child's record in a pending or closed case.

COURT POSITION: Dongre [2] holds that the s. 24 safeguards are for the victim and cannot be used by the accused to vitiate the trial. That is a single-bench Bombay High Court view and is persuasive only in Uttar Pradesh. Nagendra Kumar [4] is also persuasive only, and its extract shows statutory text, not a ratio. Maroti Pimpalkar [3] is Supreme Court authority, binding under Art 141 (well-established constitutional authority; verify against the official report), but the extract concerns prompt reporting, not identity.

APPLICATION: For the police, the investigating officer should ensure no name, address, school or picture leaks, should keep the file out of any disclosure, and should follow s. 24. For the media, any report on the investigation or trial must omit identifying particulars even where the name has circulated elsewhere. Procedurally, whether CrPC or BNSS governs depends on when the proceeding began, and the sources do not settle this.

RISKS AND COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The accused may argue that a s. 24 lapse vitiates the trial; Dongre [2] answers that the provisions are for the victim, though it is not binding in Uttar Pradesh. A media defendant may argue that s. 74 targets child-in-conflict-with-law proceedings and Boards or Committees, not POCSO trials. The text of s. 74(1) answers this, but no cited judgment decides it. Parental or victim consent is not a statutory exception in s. 74, and s. 228-A authorisation is limited to prescribed persons.

ADVICE: Seek a written direction from the Special Court restraining identification, and verify the BNS/BNSS equivalents and any Allahabad High Court authority from official reports.

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The query asks whether Section 365 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996 applies default bail. The premise appears mistaken.

LAW: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996 is a civil statute governing arbitration agreements, appointment, interim relief, awards, challenge and enforcement. I am not aware of any Section 365 in it, and the sources contain none. The Act creates no offence and provides for no arrest, remand or chargesheet. Default bail is a creature of criminal procedure: s.167(2) CrPC [1], now s.187 BNSS, which the Supreme Court [6] and the Bombay order [3] confirm. Where a section numbered 365 exists in other legislation, such as the BNS, it needs to be identified, since that is a different statute and, as far as I know, not about default bail. In UAPA matters an extension postpones the right [4] and must rest on the Public Prosecutor's independent report [5].

ADVICE: Confirm the intended statute and section, ascertain the arrest date, the offence date and the date the proceeding began, and the chargesheet filing date. Then frame the application under the correct code.

ISSUE. The advocate has asked for the judgment at '2011 8 SCC 98301 [CITATION UNVERIFIED]'. That string is not a valid SCC citation. SCC volumes carry page numbers of at most a few hundred, so '98301' cannot be a page number, and none of the sources contains a judgment at that reference. LAW. Section 6(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, as substituted in 2005 [1], makes the daughter of a coparcener a coparcener by birth in the same manner as a son. The proviso protects dispositions, alienations, partitions and testamentary dispositions made before 20 December 2004. Section 6(3) governs devolution of a coparcener's interest on death after the 2005 Amendment.

COURT POSITION. The authoritative decision in the sources is Vineeta Sharma [6]. Its ratio is the reference answer: daughters are coparceners by birth, the father need not have been alive on 9.9.2005, the pre-2005 fiction of partition did not effect an actual partition, and oral partition is accepted only in exceptional cases supported by public documents. Because Prakash v. Phulavati was overruled, any reliance on it for a living-father requirement is misplaced. The pre-2005 position on the oral partition plea is treated by Vineeta Sharma only through the Explanation to s. 6(5). The text of that sub-section is not reproduced in [1], so the Explanation should be read from the Act. The High Court decisions [2][3][4][5] apply this ratio and add nothing to it on the point of law. They are persuasive on application and binding only within their own territories, and they bind subordinate courts only through the Supreme Court law they follow.

APPLICATION. If the advocate wants authority for the daughter's right, cite s. 6 [1] together with Vineeta Sharma [6], quoting the answer to the reference. If another judgment was intended, the report year 2011 does not match the year of Vineeta Sharma (2020), so the citation may be a corrupted reference to some other case, or a mistaken year. I cannot say which.

COUNTER-ARGUMENT. The opposing side will say that a partition or disposition was made before 20 December 2004 and is saved by the proviso to s. 6(1). It will also argue that the property is self-acquired, not coparcenary property, or that the family is not governed by Mitakshara law. It may further plead an oral partition. Vineeta Sharma [6] answers the last point by requiring public documents. The first three points depend on evidence of the date and form of the partition, the character of the property, and the governing school, and the sources do not decide these on the facts.

relevant_law.act_name: Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (as substituted by the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005) [1]
relevant_law.summary: In a Mitakshara joint Hindu family, the daughter of a coparcener becomes a coparcener by birth in her own right, in the same manner as a son. She has the same rights and is subject to the same liabilities. The proviso saves any disposition, alienation, partition or testamentary disposition made before 20 December 2004.

Section 6(2) provides that property a woman obtains under s. 6(1) is held with the incidents of coparcenary ownership and may be disposed of by will. Section 6(3) provides that where a Hindu dies after the 2005 Amendment, his interest devolves by testamentary or intestate succession and not by survivorship. The coparcenary property is deemed divided as if a partition had taken place, and the daughter is allotted the same share as a son. Section 6(3) deems a partition on the death of a coparcener and allots the daughter the same share as a son [1].

COURT POSITION: The Supreme Court in Vineeta Sharma [6], as reproduced in the High Court judgments [3][5], held that the right is by birth, so the father need not be alive on 9.9.2005. It held that the rights are claimable from 9.9.2005 and that daughters must be given equal shares even in pending final decree proceedings or appeals. It held that oral partition is accepted only in exceptional cases supported by public documents. Other High Courts have followed it: Uttarakhand [2], Chhattisgarh [3], and Karnataka [4][5]. The Karnataka single-bench decision [5] adds that a preliminary decree can be modified to give effect to the amendment. Of these, [5] is a single-bench decision and [2]-[4] are on the face of the extracts decisions of High Courts outside Telangana, so they are persuasive only in Telangana.

APPLICATION: For a Telangana proceeding, Vineeta Sharma [6] binds under Art 141 and is the proposition to cite. The other High Court decisions are persuasive and show uniform application. Whether a Telangana High Court judgment has followed it cannot be answered from these sources.

COUNTER-ARGUMENT AND LIMITS: The opposing side may invoke the savings proviso, arguing that a partition or disposition before 20 December 2004 was effected. Under [3] that requires a registered partition deed or a court decree, and oral partition is accepted only in exceptional cases supported by public documents. The opposing side may also say the coparcenary did not exist on the relevant date [5]. None of the sources decides a Telangana-specific point.

LAW: The sources provided show the 2019 Act's offence provisions in Chapter VII, of which s. 92 [2] is one, and its miscellaneous provisions in Chapter VIII, including ss. 98 [3] and 100 and 107 [1]. COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The only conceivable contrary argument is that some penal provision of the Act could be stretched to cover the conduct. Two conditions must both be met: reason to believe the person committed the offence, and satisfaction that arrest is necessary on one of the listed grounds (preventing further offence, proper investigation, preventing tampering with evidence, preventing inducement or threat to witnesses, or ensuring presence in court). BNSS equivalent is Section 35, per the High Court orders cited [4]-[8].

relevant_law.act_name: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (BNSS 2023 equivalent: Section 35 and related provisions)
relevant_law.summary: The arresting officer must bear a visible name identification and prepare a memorandum of arrest attested by a family member or respectable local witness and countersigned by the arrestee. The arrestee must be told of the right to have a relative or friend informed. The BNSS equivalent should be confirmed from the BNSS text, as the sources do not give it.

The State must set up police control rooms at district and State level. Names and addresses of arrestees and the arresting officers must be displayed, and a public database maintained. The BNSS equivalent is not stated in the sources.

comparative_analysis.agreements_between_courts: Mohammed Ajmal Kasab [4], Kamlesh [3] and Aldanish Rein [1] consistently treat free legal aid as part of fair procedure under Art 21, reinforced by Art 39A and LSAA s. 12(d).
comparative_analysis.conflicts_or_differences: The two-Judge Bench in Mohd. Hussain [2] split on whether a vitiated trial for want of counsel should be remanded or not retried. None of the sources shows how the larger bench resolved this.

answer.conclusion: BNSS s. 510 does not apply or confer free legal aid; the BSA has no such provision either. The right to free legal aid derives from Art 21, Art 39A and LSAA s. 12(d), as supported by Kasab [4], Kamlesh [3], Aldanish Rein [1] and Mohd. Hussain [2]. The advocate may argue that denial of counsel is a failure of justice that engages the appellate power under s. 510 to order a fresh trial, but that is an argument by analogy and no supplied authority decides it. Before filing, confirm the intended statute and section, check the official reports for the larger bench's final ruling in Mohd. Hussain, and map the cited CrPC sections to BNSS.
answer.issue: Whether 'BSA Section 510' has any bearing on the right to free legal aid. The query appears to contain a code error: the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) is the evidence statute, and the section of that number in the statute text supplied is s. 510 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), which concerns the effect of omission to frame, or error in, a charge. The question therefore resolves into whether BNSS s. 510 interacts with free legal aid.

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The query asks whether 'BSA Section 510 [no such section: the BSA has sections 1 to 170]' applies free legal aid. The BSA is the evidence enactment and the supplied text is s. 510 of the BNSS, which corresponds to CrPC s. 464. I proceed on the footing that the advocate means that provision, and that should be confirmed. LAW: BNSS s. 510 is a curative provision. Its subject is the absence of, or error in, a charge. A finding or sentence is not invalid merely on that account unless the appellate, confirming or revising Court finds that a failure of justice has in fact occurred. Where it does, the Court may order a charge framed and recommence the trial from that point, or direct a new trial on a charge framed as it thinks fit. If no valid charge could be framed on the facts proved, it must quash the conviction. Nothing in the text mentions legal aid, so s. 510 does not itself confer, apply or regulate free legal aid. The source of the right is Art 21 read with Art 39A and LSAA s. 12(d). COURT POSITION: Kasab [4] records that the State's duty to provide a lawyer attaches at first production before the magistrate and at remands, and that the magistrate must inform the accused of the right. Kamlesh [3] restates the same for Art 21. Aldanish Rein [1] applies it to preventive-arrest remands and treats the requirements as mandatory. Mohd. Hussain [2] shows the consequence of denial of counsel at trial: due process is infringed, with disagreement on whether remand or no retrial follows. APPLICATION: The only indirect connection is conceptual. If a trial proceeded without effective counsel, the argument is that a failure of justice has in fact been occasioned, which is the threshold at which s. 510 stops protecting the finding and lets the appellate Court act, including by ordering a fresh trial. That argument is by analogy to the reasoning in Mohd. Hussain [2] on remand; no judgment supplied applies s. 510 or CrPC s. 464 to denial of legal aid. RISKS: The State will say s. 510 saves findings absent proof of actual failure of justice, and that prejudice must be shown. Counsel should therefore plead concrete prejudice from the absence of counsel. The remedy question left open in Mohd. Hussain [2] cuts both ways. ADVICE: Rest the legal aid claim on Art 21, Art 39A, LSAA s. 12(d) and Kasab [4]. Use s. 510 only as a procedural route for relief on appeal or revision, and verify the BNSS equivalents of CrPC ss. 303, 304, 386 and 311 independently.

relevant_law.summary: Provides that no finding, sentence or order of a competent Court is invalid merely because no charge was framed or because of an error, omission or irregularity in the charge, unless the appellate, confirming or revising Court finds that a failure of justice has in fact been occasioned. If it does, it may order a charge framed and the trial recommenced from that point, or direct a new trial on a properly framed charge; if no valid charge could be framed on the facts proved, it must quash the conviction. The section deals with defective charges only; its text says nothing about legal aid. The BNSS has no s. 510 'applying' legal aid, and the BSA (evidence law) is a different enactment.

As described in Aldanish Rein [1], this provision guarantees free legal aid to every person in custody. K.N. Govindan Kutty Menon [5] records that persons in custody are among those entitled to free legal services under the Act.

Art 39A directs the State to provide free legal aid so that opportunities for securing justice are not denied by economic or other disabilities. The courts read the right to free legal aid into Art 21 as an element of fair, just and reasonable procedure (Maneka Gandhi; Hoskot; Hussainara Khatoon, from the constitutional notes). Art 22(1) requires that the arrested person be informed of the grounds of arrest.

answer.reasoned_analysis: ISSUE: The advocate asks about 'AIR 2029 Supreme Court 5792 [CITATION UNVERIFIED]'. LAW AND RECORD: None of the sources carries that citation. The year 2029 is also later than any date reflected in the materials (the latest source is from 2026), so the citation is probably a typographical error. I therefore cannot state what that report holds, and I will not guess at its content or attribute a holding to it. The nearest authorities in the sources are Vihaan Kumar [4], cited in [1][2][3] as AIR 2025 SC 1388, and Baldev Singh, cited as 1999 (6) SCC 172. It may be that the advocate intends one of these, but that is a conjecture, and the actual reference must be confirmed. COURT POSITION: If the intended authority is Vihaan Kumar [4], its ratio is that informing an arrestee of the grounds of arrest is a mandatory requirement under Article 22(1). The communication must give sufficient knowledge of the basic facts, effectively and in a language the person understands. Article 22(1) does not itself demand written grounds. A breach vitiates arrest and remand, and a charge-sheet does not cure it. The Lallubhai passage in [4] concerns Article 22(5) and is relied on by analogy for the meaning of 'communicate'. If the intended authority is Baldev Singh, then as quoted in [1][2][3] the s. 50(1) NDPS Act right must be conveyed before a personal search, and omission prejudices the accused. State of HP v Ram Lal [5] adds the Constitution Bench position in Vijaysinh Chandubha Jadeja (2011) that the right must be conveyed, orally or in writing, and that merely seeking consent is insufficient (Suresh, 2013). APPLICATION: Whichever authority is meant, the Supreme Court decisions bind all courts under Article 141, while the Allahabad orders [1][2][3] and the Himachal Pradesh order [5] are persuasive outside their own States. The Allahabad bail orders recite these rules and then grant bail on a general prima facie view, so they do not show that a breach alone wins bail. RISKS: The prosecution will argue that grounds were in fact conveyed, that the s. 50 right was explained, or that the conviction does not rest solely on recovery from the person. Prejudice is a live question in s. 50 matters, as [5] shows. Whether the 'later treatment' of any of these decisions has changed matters is not shown in the sources. ADVICE: Obtain the full citation and the report itself, and confirm the court, year and bench before relying on anything.

comparative_analysis.agreements_between_courts: Navjot Sandhu (2005) [3] और Yakub Memon (2013) [5] दोनों में सर्वोच्च न्यायालय सहमत है कि अवैध करार ही अपराध का सार है और षड्यंत्रकारी परस्पर एजेंट के रूप में उत्तरदायी हैं। Vijendra Ram (2026) [6] में उद्धृत अंश भी साक्ष्य-पद्धति पर यही दृष्टिकोण दर्शाता है।
comparative_analysis.conflicts_or_differences: प्रदत्त स्रोतों में कोई विरोधाभासी निर्णय नहीं है। पंजाब एवं हरियाणा उच्च न्यायालय का कोई निर्णय स्रोतों में उपलब्ध नहीं है; अतः उस न्यायालय की विशिष्ट स्थिति इन स्रोतों से तय नहीं होती।
comparative_analysis.trend_analysis: IPC की धारा 120A/120B अंग्रेज़ी विधि के अनुरूप 1913 के संशोधन से आई। अब BNS धारा 61 में समान संरचना सहित समाहित है। पुराने निर्णय पूर्ववत मान्य रहेंगे, जब तक नए प्रावधान ने विषय न बदला हो।

answer.conclusion:
धारा 120B IPC षड्यंत्र के लिए मूल अपराध के अनुसार दंड निर्धारित करती है (उप-धारा 1) या छह माह तक कारावास/जुर्माना (उप-धारा 2) [1], और 1 जुलाई 2024 या बाद के अपराधों पर BNS धारा 61 लागू होगी। बचाव में तर्क यह होगा कि केवल जानकारी या चर्चा करार नहीं है और परंतुक की शर्तें पूरी नहीं हुईं [4]; अभियोजन Navjot Sandhu [3] और Yakub Memon [5] पर निर्भर रहेगा। जोखिम यह है कि पंजाब एवं हरियाणा उच्च न्यायालय का कोई निर्णय इन स्रोतों में नहीं है, और Vijay Bajaj [4] तथा Vijendra Ram [6] के अंश अपूर्ण हैं। अतः सभी उद्धरण न्यायालय के प्रमाणित प्रति या आधिकारिक रिपोर्ट से सत्यापित करें।

The Indian Penal Code, 45 of 1860 (Rep., Act 45 of 2023) s.120B: उद्धृत रूप में यह प्रावधान इस प्रश्न को नियंत्रित करने वाली तिथि पर लागू था या नहीं, इसका सत्यापन नहीं हुआ है; भरोसा करने से पहले प्रारंभ, संशोधन और निरसन की अधिसूचनाओं से इसकी जाँच करें।

precedents.holding_summary: षड्यंत्र का करार प्रत्यक्ष या परिस्थितिजन्य साक्ष्य से सिद्ध हो सकता है; Evidence Act की धारा 10 (अब BSA में समतुल्य) के लिए पहले युक्तियुक्त आधार आवश्यक है। उद्धृत अंश अन्य निर्णय का उद्धरण प्रतीत होता है [6]।

precedents.case_name: Ravi Kapur v. State of Rajasthan
precedents.holding_summary: धारा 313 Cr.P.C. (BNSS 351) के अंतर्गत अभियुक्त की परीक्षा औपचारिकता नहीं है; दोषमुक्ति के विरुद्ध अपील में दोहरी निर्दोषता की उपधारणा लागू होती है। यह षड्यंत्र पर सीधा निर्णय नहीं है [2]।

answer.reasoned_analysis: मुद्दा: प्रश्न यह है कि IPC की धारा 120B के अंतर्गत क्या प्रावधान हैं और पंजाब एवं हरियाणा उच्च न्यायालय के समक्ष इसका क्या प्रभाव होगा। विधि: धारा 120B(1) के अनुसार मृत्युदंड, आजीवन कारावास या दो वर्ष या अधिक के कठोर कारावास से दंडनीय अपराध के षड्यंत्र का पक्षकार, जहाँ संहिता में स्पष्ट दंड नहीं है, दुष्प्रेरक के समान दंडित होगा; धारा 120B(2) में अन्य षड्यंत्रों के लिए छह माह तक कारावास, जुर्माना या दोनों है [1]। परिभाषा धारा 120A में है, जिसके परंतुक के अनुसार अपराध करने के करार के अतिरिक्त अन्य करार में कोई अन्य कृत्य भी आवश्यक है [4][5]। BNS में समतुल्य प्रावधान धारा 61 है। न्यायालय की स्थिति: Navjot Sandhu (2005) [3] में माननीय सर्वोच्च न्यायालय ने कहा कि अवैध करार, न कि उसका निष्पादन, अपराध का सार है और 120B का आरोप स्वतंत्र हो सकता है। Yakub Memon (2013) [5] में कहा गया कि करार का अनुमान आचरण से लगाया जा सकता है और षड्यंत्रकारी एक-दूसरे के कृत्यों के लिए उत्तरदायी हैं। Vijendra Ram (2026) [6] के अंश के अनुसार करार प्रत्यक्ष या परिस्थितिजन्य साक्ष्य से सिद्ध हो सकता है, तथा सह-षड्यंत्रकारी के कथन/कृत्य तभी ग्राह्य हैं जब षड्यंत्र के प्रथम दृष्टया युक्तियुक्त आधार हों; यह अंश उद्धृत प्रतीत होता है, अतः मूल निर्णय देखना होगा। अनुप्रयोग: अभियोजन को दो या अधिक व्यक्तियों के बीच करार सिद्ध करना होगा; केवल जानकारी या चर्चा पर्याप्त नहीं, ऐसा तर्क Vijay Bajaj [4] में याचिकाकर्ता ने Kehar Singh के आधार पर उठाया, परंतु उस अंश से न्यायालय का निष्कर्ष स्पष्ट नहीं है। याचिका में Bhajan Lal के आधार पर धारा 482 Cr.P.C. (अब BNSS 528) के अंतर्गत रद्दीकरण मांगा जा सकता है। प्रतिपक्ष का तर्क: अभियोजन कहेगा कि षड्यंत्र प्रायः परिस्थितिजन्य साक्ष्य से सिद्ध होता है और प्रत्येक सदस्य को सभी विवरण ज्ञात होना आवश्यक नहीं [3][5]। जोखिम: पंजाब एवं हरियाणा उच्च न्यायालय का कोई निर्णय स्रोतों में नहीं है; अतः उस न्यायालय की विशिष्ट नज़ीर सत्यापित करनी होगी। साथ ही लागू संहिता अपराध की तिथि से तय होगी: 1 जुलाई 2024 से पूर्व के लिए IPC, उसके बाद के लिए BNS धारा 61; प्रक्रिया उस तिथि के बाद शुरू कार्यवाही पर BNSS से चलेगी। सलाह: अपराध की तिथि निश्चित करें, मूल अपराध का दंड देखें, करार के साक्ष्य की कमी पर बल दें।

relevant_law.summary: जो व्यक्ति मृत्युदंड, आजीवन कारावास या दो वर्ष अथवा उससे अधिक के कठोर कारावास से दंडनीय अपराध करने के आपराधिक षड्यंत्र का पक्षकार है, और जहाँ संहिता में ऐसे षड्यंत्र के दंड का स्पष्ट प्रावधान नहीं है, उसे उसी प्रकार दंडित किया जाएगा मानो उसने उस अपराध का दुष्प्रेरण किया हो [1]।
उपर्युक्त से भिन्न अपराध के षड्यंत्र के लिए किसी भी प्रकार के कारावास से, जो छह माह तक हो सकता है, या जुर्माने से, या दोनों से दंड [1]।

जब दो या अधिक व्यक्ति कोई अवैध कार्य, या अवैध साधनों से कोई वैध कार्य, करने या कराने पर सहमत होते हैं तो वह सहमति आपराधिक षड्यंत्र है। अपराध करने के करार के अतिरिक्त अन्य करार में करार के अनुसरण में कोई अन्य कृत्य होना आवश्यक है (परंतुक) [4][5]।

IPC 120A/120B का समतुल्य। धारा 61(1) षड्यंत्र को परिभाषित करती है (परंतुक सहित) और 61(2)(a)/(b) दंड निर्धारित करती है: गंभीर अपराध के लिए दुष्प्रेरण के समान दंड, अन्य के लिए छह माह तक कारावास, जुर्माना या दोनों। 1 जुलाई 2024 या उसके बाद किए गए अपराध पर BNS लागू होगी; उससे पूर्व के अपराध पर IPC (BNS धारा 358 द्वारा संरक्षित)।

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: Aap poochh rahe hain ki Patna High Court ke sandarbh mein s. 47 application kaise file karein. Pehle procedure samajhna zaroori hai: s. 47(1) [1] ke anusaar yeh question 'Court executing the decree' tay karti hai. Isliye application normally us civil court ki execution case mein file hoti hai jahan decree execute ho raha hai (jaise Bihar ka Title Execution Case), High Court mein seedhe nahi. High Court tabhi executing court hoti hai jab decree uski original civil jurisdiction mein pass hua ho. Patna HC ki filing ki exact mechanics (Patna High Court Rules, e-filing, format, court fee) in sources mein nahi hain; unke liye Patna High Court Rules aur registry se confirm karein.

LAW: s. 47 [1] ke tahat objection execution, discharge ya satisfaction se judaa hona chahiye. Representative ka sawaal s. 47(3) mein hai. Auction purchaser ke liye Explanation II lagoo hai; UP mein yeh omit hai, Bihar mein nahi, par Bihar ke kisi state amendment ki jaankari sources mein nahi, isliye verify karein.

COURT POSITION: Dhurandhar [3] (as quoted in [4] aur [5]) ke anusaar s. 47 ka exercise 'microscopic' hai; objection tab chalta hai jab decree nullity ho ya law mein inexecutable ho. Devendra Gupta [5] mein quoted Vasudev Modi ke anusaar executing court decree ke peeche nahi ja sakti; jurisdiction ka objection tabhi uthta hai jab woh face of record par dikhe. Balachandran [2] mein eviction decree ke execution ko rokne ki koshish khaarij hui. Grasim [4] ne teen grounds spasht ginaye.

APPLICATION: Application mein aapko spasht batana hoga ki decree kyun nullity ya inexecutable hai (jaise mrit vyakti ke khilaaf decree, jurisdiction ka abhaav jo record se dikhe, ya baad mein aaya kanoon, ya satisfaction/adjustment). Pleading mein facts, grounds, supporting documents aur prayer (execution roakna/dismiss) dein. Agar grievance sirf decree ki galti ya ex parte hone ka hai, to Dhurandhar [3] ke anusaar woh s. 47 ka vishay nahi; uske liye appeal, review, ya properly constituted alag remedy hai.

RISKS/COUNTER-ARGUMENT: Decree-holder kahega ki objection delay ka hathkanda hai ([2], [5]), aur executing court decree ke peeche nahi ja sakti. Isse bachne ke liye aapko nullity ko face-of-record dikhana hoga. Dhurandhar [3] mein non-impleader se decree void nahi mana gaya, to is tarah ka argument kamzor hoga.

REMEDY AFTER ORDER: [3] mein executing court ke order par High Court revision hui thi. Aaj ki sahi forum (appeal/revision/Art. 227) in sources se tay nahi hoti; CPC ki current provisions aur Patna HC practice dekhein.

PRACTICAL ADVICE: Application executing court mein, supporting affidavit ke saath, jaldi file karein.

Act 57 of 1976 ne Explanation II omit kar diya hai; yeh sirf UP par lagoo hai, Bihar (Patna HC) par nahi.

comparative_analysis.agreements_between_courts: प्रदत्त स्रोतों में कोई न्यायिक निर्णय शामिल नहीं है, इसलिए न्यायालयों के मध्य सहमति पर इन स्रोतों के आधार पर कोई कथन संभव नहीं है।
comparative_analysis.conflicts_or_differences: इन स्रोतों में कोई विरोधी निर्णय नहीं है। यह प्रश्न कि 1 जुलाई 2024 के बाद दायर आवेदन 2014 में प्रारंभ कार्यवाही का भाग होकर CrPC से शासित होगा या BNSS से, BNSS की धारा 531(2)(a) के पाठ से स्पष्ट रूप से हल नहीं होता; इस पर कोई निर्णय यहाँ उद्धृत नहीं है, अतः सत्यापन आवश्यक है।
comparative_analysis.trend_analysis: BNS में IPC 304B को धारा 80 के रूप में लगभग यथावत रखा गया है [7]; विधायी उद्देश्य महिलाओं के विरुद्ध अपराधों को प्राथमिकता देना है। इससे अधिक किसी न्यायिक प्रवृत्ति पर स्रोत मौन हैं।

answer.conclusion:
2014 से संबंधित प्रकरण में, यदि मृत्यु 1 जुलाई 2024 से पूर्व हुई, तो आरोप व दंड IPC 304B के अंतर्गत ही रहेंगे; BNS 80 लागू नहीं होगी, और अनुच्छेद 20(1) का संरक्षण उपलब्ध है। प्रक्रिया के लिए लंबित कार्यवाही पर BNSS 531(2)(a) के अनुसार CrPC जारी रहेगी, किंतु 1 जुलाई 2024 के बाद दायर आवेदनों पर स्थिति अस्पष्ट है, अतः आवेदन में दोनों संहिताओं के प्रावधान उद्धृत करें। सबसे पहले अपराध की सटीक तिथि, FIR की तिथि और प्रकरण की वर्तमान अवस्था अभिलेख से सुनिश्चित करें। BNSS 531, BNS 358 और BSA 170 का आधिकारिक पाठ तथा इस विषय पर सर्वोच्च न्यायालय/उच्च न्यायालय के निर्णय प्रमाणित प्रतियों या न्यायालय की आधिकारिक वेबसाइट से सत्यापित करें, क्योंकि प्रदत्त स्रोतों में कोई निर्णय नहीं है।
